The Kia Telluride already has the kind of presence that makes it stand out, but a different set of wheels can give it a whole new personality.
A clean spoke design can make it look more refined. Black wheels bring out its tougher side, while brushed finishes and larger custom designs create something more distinctive.
Whether you’re after a subtle refresh or a complete transformation, these eight aftermarket wheel brands offer four different ways to make your Telluride your own.
Look One: The Subtle Upgrade
This look is for owners who already like their Telluride but want a sharper look that feels like a natural extension of the original design.
Think clean spokes, balanced proportions and a finish that works with the SUV instead of fighting it. Done right, the wheels look like they came with it.
Niche Wheels: Understated Custom Style

Niche specializes in bridging modern European styling and street-friendly cast durability with designs that range from understated street styles to more elaborate luxury-inspired options. It’s a good place to start if you want something more interesting than stock without making a dramatic change

The NC282 Serene pulls this off better than most. Its thin, closely spaced spokes and mildly recessed center give it a refined appearance that works naturally with the Telluride’s broad body. Finish options come in Gloss Black, Gloss Black with a Machined Face, or Gloss Titanium Brushed, giving you the choice between a stealthy blackout look and just enough bare metal to catch the eye.
2027 Kia Telluride, Niche NC282 Serene, 22×9 inches, Gloss Black.
Curva: A Sportier Take on the Telluride
Curva Concepts takes a slightly more performance-inspired approach, offering modern spoke designs and a range that includes cast and flow-formed wheels.

Ten open spokes give the CFF46 a crisp outline, especially in Gloss Black. The 2021 Telluride pictured here wears 22×9-inch examples. Gunmetal is worth a look if you like the pattern but want a softer contrast against the paint.
2021 Kia Telluride on 22×9-inch Curva CFF46 wheels in Gloss Black.

Which look works better? Niche’s Serene leans toward refined luxury, while Curva’s CFF46 feels sportier. At the same diameter, that difference in spoke design can change the SUV’s character more than you might expect.
Look Two: The Blacked-Out Aesthetic
Dark wheels and dark trim go together naturally on a Telluride. You get a tougher look without changing anything else on the vehicle.
The real choice is between a fully black wheel and one with enough contrast to show off the spokes.
Dark wheels and dark exterior trim are a natural pairing on the Telluride. They bring out its tougher side without requiring major changes to the vehicle.
The main decision is whether you want a completely black wheel or something with enough contrast to show off the spokes.
Asanti Black: Bold Spokes, Clean Finish

Asanti has been around the custom wheel scene for a long time, and fans know it for chunky spoke designs and luxury-leaning styling. The Asanti Black line brings that look to a more accessible range of aftermarket wheels.

The ABL-27 Dynasty has a branching multi-spoke face with a lot of character, and the Gloss Black finish keeps it clean. If you want the Telluride to look more assertive and leave the rest of the exterior alone, this is a solid way to go.
2022 Kia Telluride LX with 22×9-inch Asanti Black ABL-27 Dynasty wheels.
Savini: Dark Wheels With More Detail
Savini has been in the aftermarket business since 2003. It’s known for bold designs, concave profiles and custom finishes.

The Black Di Forza BM16 Super Concave carries that over to the Telluride. The intricate spokes and recessed center add depth that a plain black wheel can’t match. In Gloss Black with Double Dark Tint, the wheel stays dark, but the spokes become easier to pick out as the light changes.
2022 Kia Telluride S on 22×9-inch Savini BM16 wheels with Double Dark Tint.

So which one? It comes down to how much detail you want. The ABL-27 gives you a clean, all-black look. The tinted BM16 lets the spokes show a bit more. Both work for a blacked-out build, but they give the SUV a different personality.
Look Three: Silver and Brushed Finishes
Not every Telluride needs black wheels.
Silver, brushed, and two-tone finishes show off a wheel’s details and make the SUV look more polished. They work especially well on darker paint, where the lighter spokes stand out.
Road Force: A Brighter Take on SUV Styling
Road Force has been making aftermarket wheels for decades, with designs for luxury cars, performance models, trucks and SUVs.

The RF11 in Silver Brushed shows what a brighter finish does for the Telluride. The metallic look makes the spoke design easy to appreciate without looking over the top. If you want to compare another Road Force design, the RF35 in Silver Machined goes in a similar bright direction.
2021 Kia Telluride on 22×9-inch Road Force RF11 wheels in Silver Brushed.
Vossen: Detailed Designs, Premium Feel

Vossen is a favorite with enthusiasts for its detailed designs and long list of finishes. The catalog covers fully forged wheels and a separate Hybrid Forged range, which take different approaches to styling and construction.

The HF-8 is part of the Hybrid Forged series. It has an intricate multi-spoke face and a full-face floating center cap, so there’s a lot to look at. Black Diamond Brushed adds metallic contrast, though it’s less bright than a standard silver.
Vossen HF-8 in Black Diamond Brushed. Product photo, not a Telluride installation.

Bright or understated? A light brushed finish like the Road Force RF11 stands out more against dark paint. Vossen’s darker brushed option holds back a little, with metallic detail that catches the light without taking over.
Look Four: Going All Out With a Custom Build
Some owners want more than a subtle change. They want bigger wheel faces, bolder spokes and finishes that make the wheels the first thing you see.
That’s where the Telluride stops looking like a factory-inspired build and starts looking fully custom.
Avant Garde: Big, Broad Faces
Avant Garde is known for modern wheel designs with clean lines and a strong custom streak.

The AG Luxury Vanguard has a broad ten-spoke face that gives it real presence. It’s built as a flow-formed monoblock and offers custom finishes, so you have options when planning a build. It looks bold even in plain gloss black, with no chrome or unusual color needed.
2022 Kia Telluride on 22×10.5-inch Avant Garde Vanguard wheels in Gloss Black.
Azad Wheels: A More Expressive Custom Look
Azad is worth a look if you like intricate spokes, bright finishes and contrasting outer lips.

The AZ99 delivers all three, with a detailed split-spoke face and a prominent chrome lip. It’s offered in select 20-, 22- and 24-inch sizes, in finishes like Brushed Silver with Chrome Lip and Candy Red Milled with Chrome Lip. With that much shine, the wheels become the first thing you notice.
2022 Kia Telluride with 24×10-inch Azad AZ99 wheels in Silver with Chrome SS Lip.

These two show different sides of custom styling. The Vanguard gets its presence from a broad, structured face. The AZ99 relies on decorative detail and contrast. Neither is better. It depends on whether you want a cleaner custom look or a flashier one.
Which Wheels Look Best With Your Telluride’s Color?
There’s no rulebook here, and plenty of great builds break the usual rules. Your paint and trim are still a decent place to start.

Finish matters as much as color. Gloss black reflects light differently from matte black, and a brushed finish shows off the spoke pattern more. If you can’t decide between two options, check photos in daylight and in lower light.
What to Know Before Buying Kia Telluride Wheels
Once you’ve picked a style, make sure the size, tires and whole setup actually work on your Telluride.
Choosing Between 20-, 22-, and 24-Inch Wheels
Go with 20-inch wheels if you want a clear upgrade without making size the whole point. Depending on the tires, they also leave you with more sidewall than a bigger wheel would.
At 22 inches the wheel face gets more attention. Most of the Telluride builds pictured here use that size, including the Asanti ABL-27, Curva CFF46 and Avant Garde Vanguard.
At 24 inches you’re in custom-show territory, like the Azad AZ99 build. It can look great, but the shorter sidewalls that come with it make rough roads, potholes and tire choice a bigger deal.

Pick wheels and tires together. If you go up in wheel diameter and keep overall tire height close to stock, the sidewall has to shrink, and that can hurt ride comfort. Kia’s redesigned 2027 Telluride also has different factory wheel options, so it needs its own fitment check.
What Should You Budget?
Prices vary a lot, even at the same diameter.

As an example, AudioCityUSA has listed a set of four 22-inch Curva CFF46 wheels in Gloss Black at about $1,796. A set of four 22-inch Vossen HF-8 wheels in Black Diamond Brushed has been advertised from about $4,846. Those are wheel-only base prices that can change and need to be confirmed for your vehicle. They aren’t completely installed quotes.

Add tires, TPMS requirements, mounting, balancing, installation, shipping and tax on top. And the pricier wheel isn’t automatically the better pick. Choose the look you want in a setup that fits your Telluride and your budget.
Confirm Fitment Before Ordering
A wheel that looks great in a photo still has to fit your Telluride.
Before you order, ask a fitment specialist to check the diameter, width, offset, bolt pattern, center bore, brake clearance and load rating. Tire specs and mounting hardware count just as much.

Give them your exact model year and trim, plus any suspension or brake changes. That matters most if you’re copying a setup from a photo of someone else’s Telluride, because year and equipment differences can change what fits.
Where to Buy Kia Telluride Wheels

AudioCityUSA, as an authorized dealer, offers a wide selection of Kia Telluride Wheels featuring bold designs, premium finishes, and full customization options. Buyers also benefit from expert fitment guidance, warranty support, and fast, reliable delivery ensuring a safe and confident purchasing experience.

AudioCityUSA is a handy place to compare these eight brands, look through real Telluride installations and price out wheel-and-tire packages. The catalog is broad, and the fitment specialists can narrow things down to setups that suit your vehicle.
Go in with two or three favorite wheels, plus your Telluride’s year, trim, preferred diameter and budget. It makes the jump from a styling idea to a properly specified package much easier.

The best Telluride upgrades don’t all look alike. Some are subtle enough to resemble a factory option, while others deliver a more customized appearance. AudioCityUSA offers a range of Kia Telluride wheels, including options for those exploring 2027 Kia Telluride wheels. Choose the right design, confirm fitment for your model year and trim, and pair the wheels with suitable tires to create a setup that looks great and works for your vehicle.

Autogem has celebrated its fifth win in six years at the NTDA Tyre Industry Awards 2026, saying the accolades underline “an unwavering commitment to customer service, training, innovation and continuous improvement.” The company claimed the newly introduced Best Supply Chain Partner Award, sponsored by Blackcircles. The award was highly contested, with the largest number of entries among all the awards in 2026.

NTDA chief executive officer Ian Andrew highlighted that the judging panel selected Autogem due to its strong commitment to genuine, long-term partnerships. “This was the first year of the Best Supply Chain Award, which had the largest volume of entries, reflecting the wide range of companies that supply the tyre sector including aftermarket suppliers, tyre distributors, software providers and recruitment partners. Sponsored by Blackcircles, we were delighted that the judging panel selected Autogem as the worthy winner.
“The judges got a true sense of Autogem’s commitment to partnerships. Their partnership philosophy defines everything they do and I believe this is what clinched it for them.”

Supporting more than 5,000 workshops nationwide, Autogem focuses on delivering tailored technical support, advanced TPMS technology, and comprehensive training rather than standard transactional sales.

Managing director Prashant Chopra attributed the success to the company’s strong staff culture and drive to support customers and suppliers: “People often ask me what the formula is. The recipe is simple: having selfless colleagues that genuinely care for our customers and each other. It is a deep culture that has built up over time and we are particularly protective of it when taking on new team members.

“It means a great deal to everyone here because we know how much work goes into delivering the right service, day after day. This award belongs to the whole team as well as our customer and supplier partners that help us shape our programs.”

Chopra said that while the five-win milestone is an incredible achievement, the business remains focused on continuous improvement. “We’ve never wanted to be a business that simply completes a transaction and moves on. We want to understand our customers, support them properly and build relationships that last.”

Chopra added that the company does not intend to sit on its laurels. “Winning five times in six years is an incredible achievement, but we can’t sit back and think we’ve cracked it,” he said. “The industry keeps changing, our customers’ needs keep changing and we have to keep getting better. We listen, we learn and we look for ways to improve.
“That’s what makes this award so special, it gives us the motivation to relentlessly keep pushing forward.”

MR: I left in mid-May, and I've been basically underway for the most part since then. At this time, currently, I've only been at sea for a few days, because I left Greenland a few days ago. The longest stretch I was continuously at sea this year is 59 days, although I was planning on doing longer than that, so that sucked. Essentially, I was attempting to do a nonstop, single-handed circumnavigation of the Arctic. That's where this all sort of came out of. I tried in 2018, but you couldn't get the Russian permits. And the Russians were the problem in the end [this year]. I got defeated by Russian bureaucracy, essentially. And there was some weird stuff going on with the ice up there this year. [Editor's note: Sections of the High Arctic were impassable due to a relatively cold summer and solid ice fields.]

The NSRA gives you the permit to do this, but the FSB are the people who patrol it. And the FSB don't like the NSRA. I learned that when they boarded me, because they think that they're the ones who should control the Northern Sea Route, not the NSRA. So there's [a] beef between them; they don't talk. There's a lack of communication, which benefits me. I can lean heavy onto the NSRA side, because they don't have boats; they're not going to board you. And they're the ones you have to check in with every 24 hours in Moscow; you've got to send them an email every 24 hours. So I'll do all of that stuff with those guys, but I think there's some ways I can avoid the FSB even knowing where I am, essentially, while still complying with my permit in the NSRA.

But mostly what we focus on is Arctic research. Since 2015, we've been heading up to Greenland — sometimes the Northwest Passage also, but primarily Greenland — doing research related to glaciers, for the most part. An ocean-terminating glacier sort of has a river of melted water underneath it, and it creates upwelling, and the upwelling has nutrients. So it mixes nutrients with the ocean and creates this perfect recipe for growth for phytoplankton and zooplankton. And then, we look at the different stages of decay between an ocean-terminating glacier, a land-retreated glacier or a deglaciated fjord. In the middle phase, when a glacier starts retreating back on land, it just creates a river of muddy water, essentially; it turns the fjord into a mud puddle. You can't have photosynthesis if you're in a mud puddle.

Tesla said Wednesday it will start selling its Cybercab to customers by the end of the year, even as federal regulators investigate whether the vehicle meets vehicle safety standards. The gold-hued, autonomous two-seater lacks a steering wheel and other traditional controls.

During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Lars Moravy, vice president of engineering at Tesla, said the Cybercabs produced today are all destined for the company’s own robotaxi fleet. As that fleet grows, the company will “mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers,” he said, noting that it will start small. The company will scale as it learns about delivery, ownership, and fleet management of autonomous vehicles, Moravy added.

Tesla first floated the idea of selling the autonomous vehicle to third parties last month around its Cybercab event in Austin and even posted a form for people interested in buying robotaxis. But it wasn’t clear if Tesla would follow through, or how.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has talked for years about building a massive fleet of low-cost robotaxis, but until recently, those plans centered on turning privately owned Tesla vehicles into self-driving taxis with a software update.
That plan has yet to materialize, and Musk’s comments on the call show how his views have shifted.

If both timelines hold, it would mean third-party fleet customers would be able to buy the autonomous Cybercab and potentially operate it as a robotaxi service before Tesla owners would get access to the same autonomous capability in their own cars.

Musk said the Cybercab is meant to be a ride-hailing vehicle, not a car people own. “Cybercab is primarily going to be something that is offered as like transport as a service, whereas our other cars would be more, you know, the cars that you’d want to own, like the 3 and the Y and whatnot, and the Roadster, obviously,” Musk said Wednesday on the call. “But, you know, the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transported as a service.”

There is at least one obstacle that could throw off Tesla’s Cybercab fleet plans. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the federal auto safety regulator, announced last month that it had opened an investigation into the Cybercab, just hours after the vehicles began operating on public streets in Austin.

Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) require manual controls like brake pedals, as well as other features such as rearview and side mirrors. Automakers traditionally self-certify whether their vehicles comply with FMVSS rules, and Tesla did the same.

Current regulations don’t accommodate vehicles without manual controls, though the Department of Transportation recently proposed removing those requirements for vehicles that are designed to be autonomously driven. In the meantime, NHTSA said it would investigate the Cybercab to “examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues.”
The outcome of that investigation could affect whether Tesla, or anyone else, can legally operate the Cybercab.

We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.

That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. We investigate AI’s ability to say no, a bionic eye that can restore sight, and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years.
This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride.
Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon

Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month.

The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation.
How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster

In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.

The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.
MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world

“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.

MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.

There’s a lot of exposure for Elizabeth Holmes’s partner in the hit documentary by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything. Over nearly three hours, you see Billy Evans as a domineering partner and stealth social-media surrogate — and get a glimpse of him fully naked brushing his teeth in the shower. But what the audience doesn’t get, beyond a few glimpses of Holmes and Evans pitching investors on a post-Theranos prototype, is a look at what Evans is working on while Holmes is in prison for running Silicon Valley’s most infamous fraud.

In 2022, five years after he first met Holmes, Evans founded a company called Haemanthus, which is named after a genus of blood lily. Like Theranos, it is a blood-testing start-up with a prototype machine that looks a whole lot like the Edison — the box that falsely promised to run more than 1,000 instant tests with just a pinprick of blood. Little is known about the private company, unlike Theranos, which attracted endless publicity and famous investors. But Evans’s decision to launch a blood-testing company after meeting Holmes is raising a lot of questions about whether this is a Theranos reboot — and whether his partner is onboard. Below is everything we know about Haemanthus, which, inevitably, includes some You Can See Everything spoilers.

Haemanthus is developing a test for urine, saliva, and small blood samples promising “a radically new approach to health testing” that could be “the future of diagnostics,” according to marketing materials obtained by the New York Times last year. In pursuit of this radical future, they have come up with a brilliant trick to avoid Food and Drug Administration oversight: They are testing on animals first under the less strict regulatory framework of the Department of Agriculture. Eventually, the plan, per the marketing materials, is total “human health optimization.”

To analyze nonhuman blood and saliva, Haemanthus uses Raman spectroscopy, a type of laser first developed in the 1960s that can determine early-stage markers of ALS and differentiate between malignant and cancerous tissue. The company also states it uses AI to analyze the data. Like with Theranos, its goal is getting the product into a small, PC-sized box for commercial use — and eventually, make it even smaller. In an investor presentation obtained by the Times, the final product would be a small piece of wearable tech, which the company anticipates would take three years and $70 million to make. The ambition is Theranos-like, but that cost is much lower: Holmes raised nearly $1 billion before she was exposed.

In theory, this is all possible. “Handheld Raman instruments the size of a cell phone are already commercially available,” said Igor Lednev, a chemistry professor at SUNY–Albany working on Raman detection for Alzheimer’s. “We are practically working in the same field, trying to develop similar technology.” Eric Potma, a Haemanthus consultant and chemistry professor at UC Irvine, told Wired that “from an engineering perspective, they have some interesting ideas that are worth exploring.”

Haemanthus has been fundraising, beginning with $3.15 million from friends and family in the spring of 2025, according to the investor materials seen by the Times, in addition to another $15 million from San Francisco and Austin investors. But because the company is private, there is little information about who is onboard. NPR reports that the company has around a dozen staffers, including some people who worked with Evans at a previous job developing laser sensors for self-driving vehicles.

Evans has said on his social media that he is working on a “stealth” health start-up. “When you’re in stealth, you’re trying to be in stealth,” he told the Times. “They aren’t going to find anything associated with the name Haemanthus.”

The company has also applied for a patent to use AI sensors to run and analyze its tests. The researchers involved in the patent did not respond to requests for comment. The only investor who has publicly come forward is Street Global Venture Capital, a small San Francisco–based firm funding tech start-ups. That firm also did not respond to requests for comment.
In a May 2025 post on X, when the Times broke the news of his fundraising efforts, the company stated:

“We’re Haemanthus. Yes, our CEO, Billy Evans, is Elizabeth Holmes’ partner. Skepticism is rational. We must clear a higher bar. When @nytimes contacted us, we invited them: see our lab, tech, and team. They declined. The headline was already written. Our reality inconvenient.”

In a seven-post thread, the account said that the company prefers to “build first, talk later” and that its research will “stand on its own merits.” It added that Haemanthus is “making lab technology accessible through modern lasers and AI.”

As for the animal-research angle, the thread said Haemanthus is starting with veterinary testing “not because it’s easier, but because it’s practical and meaningful.” The thread also stated that it “helps animals who can’t describe symptoms.”

Evans comes from a wealthy California family: His grandparents founded a small chain of luxury hotels that employs over 1,000 people. In a statement before the movie’s release, the company asserted that Evans is not a shareholder or employee.

Evans, 34, attended a private high school in San Diego — tuition today is $49,100 — before graduating from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2015 with a bachelor’s in economics. After college, Evans reportedly tried to create a concierge-medical-service start-up connecting wealthy clients in China with medical care in the United States, setting them up with a chauffeur and luxury hotel stays. “Then he realized that it’s actually very hard to get in with the affluent Chinese community if you’re not fluent in Chinese, so he dropped that,” a source close to Evans told the New York Post in 2019. He worked for LinkedIn for two years before going to work for Luminar, an automated driving company.
Through a representative, Evans declined to comment.

In the Haemanthus thread on X, the company said, “Elizabeth Holmes has zero involvement” and “this is not Theranos 2.0.” Last year, NPR reported that Holmes is listed as a scientific adviser, which the company denied on X.

In the doc, before she reports to prison, Evans and Holmes are discussing a project featuring lasers and AI that Evans describes as “2.0” and an opportunity to “put the band back together and do it all again.” Holmes responds, “From wherever I am, I’m going to continue to work inventing, even if it’s inventing from a cage.” But according to a source close to Evans, the couple was not referring to Haemanthus in this particular conversation but rather an attempt to create a “chemistry-less” system to make testing affordable. When the project resulted in a testing panel that still cost several hundred dollars, it was shelved.

While the company has been clear in its statements that Holmes is not involved, the doc raises some questions as to how Evans is using her likeness. He claims that he has power of attorney over her and that he will post on her social-media accounts without her approval. “It’s a lot easier to make it seem like Elizabeth Holmes is El Chapo running a diagnostics cartel from prison than it is to say, ‘Billy’s building a nerdy company,’” he said on the All-In podcast in October.
Our brains depend on a steady oxygen supply, and problems can arise when cells cannot properly use the oxygen reaching them.
Scientists investigating what happens when that balance breaks down have tested an unexpected approach in mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms: reducing oxygen delivery to their tissues.
Mice given an experimental drug combination became quicker at descending a pole and could hold onto a cage lid for longer. Treatment began after their movement problems had already appeared.
The researchers call their approach "hypoxia in a pill" because it recreates some effects of breathing low-oxygen air.
Parkinson's damages brain cells that produce dopamine, a chemical that helps regulate movement. The disease also involves the buildup of a protein called alpha-synuclein.
Damage associated with this protein can disrupt the tiny energy-producing structures inside cells, called mitochondria. These structures use oxygen to help generate energy.

"Our current working hypothesis is that when there is mitochondrial dysfunction, oxygen is not being consumed properly, and this leads to an oxygen mismatch, i.e., oxygen delivery is greater than oxygen utilization," Harvard Medical School physician-scientist Vamsi K. Mootha told ScienceAlert.
By reducing oxygen delivery, the team aims to limit that mismatch and the damage that comes with it.

In a 2025 study, the researchers showed that mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms benefited from continuously breathing air with 11 percent oxygen. Ordinary air contains about 21 percent. In the new study, they tested whether drugs could achieve similar effects.

Hong Wang and colleagues used two compounds that complement each other. The first, GBT601, makes the blood release less of its oxygen into tissues. Because the body can compensate by producing more oxygen-carrying red blood cells, the second compound, PT2399, limits that response.

For the experiment, the scientists injected alpha-synuclein fibrils into the mice's brains to trigger protein buildup and movement difficulties. Six weeks later, once movement problems had developed, they began giving the drugs orally each day.

Over the following six weeks, treated animals improved in the pole and cage-hang tests, while mice given only the injection of liquid without the protein solution kept getting worse. The combination also reduced excess brain oxygen and lowered a marker of fat damage in brain tissue, but did not improve an anxiety-like behavior measure.
Mootha said improvements with either inhaled low oxygen or the drug approach can begin as early as one to two weeks after treatment starts.

Better movement does not show that nerve cells have been restored. Mootha explained that in the 2025 experiment, mice already had movement problems when delayed treatment began, but no nerve cell loss had been detected yet. The mice regained movement abilities and avoided subsequent nerve cell loss even though the buildup of alpha-synuclein remained unchanged.
The new study did not report dopamine neuron counts in the main paper, so it does not establish whether the combination protects those cells.

The team also tried the combination in two other disease models. In mice modeling Leigh syndrome, a rare disorder affecting cellular energy production, the combination extended median lifespan from 62 to 158 days. In a model of Friedreich's ataxia, which affects movement and coordination, it stopped further deterioration without reversing existing difficulties.
After six weeks of treatment in control mice, the researchers found no increase in a heart measurement linked to pulmonary hypertension, a risk of prolonged low oxygen.
"Hypoxia can be dangerous, so an important challenge is being able to achieve hypoxia therapy that is safe and effective," Mootha cautioned.
"All of our work to date is pre-clinical, in mouse models, and much more work is required before moving this concept into humans."
The research has been published in PNAS.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has directed the Air Force to establish a new Special Tactics Squadron under the Florida Air National Guard, growing a small but elite group of special operators.

The Pentagon announced Hegseth’s order Oct. 21, releasing a brief Sept. 23 memo from Hegseth to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, directing him to create the new squadron at Hurlburt Field “with an associated new organization at MacDill Air Force Base,” both in Florida.
Pentagon and Air Force spokespersons offered no further details. The Air National Guard did not immediately respond to a query.

Hurlburt is the headquarters of Air Force Special Operations Command, and MacDill is home to U.S. Special Operations Command. Connecting the new unit to both “creates an unparalleled ecosystem of combat-ready training and mission execution,” the Pentagon’s announcement states. “This move maximizes joint-force synergy, ensures seamless operational readiness, and provides the President with highly responsive, lethal options to counter pacing threats.”

Special tactics squadrons are some of the Air Force’s premier ground forces, consisting of combat controllers, pararescuemen, special reconnaissance, and Tactical Air Control Party specialists. They conduct a wide range of missions in covert, remote, or hostile areas, including combat search and rescue, airfield seizure, emergency air traffic controller, and coordination of close air support.

There are just a handful of special tactics squadrons across the Air Force, and only two in the Guard—the 123rd Special Tactics Squadron in Kentucky and the 125th Special Tactics Squadron in Oregon. The Florida Air National Guard has one special ops unit, the 249th Special Operations Squadron, which flies the CV-22 Osprey.

It is unclear how quickly the new unit will be established and be fully manned. Hegseth’s memo states that “any further resourcing for this direction, to include military construction, equipment, and manpower authorizations will be developed in the President’s Budget 2028 budget cycle.”

The memo also directs the National Guard Bureau and the Air Force to follow Air Force policy for establishing the new unit, “consistent with applicable DAF Strategic Basing process and environmental legal requirements.”
It is highly unusual—if not unprecedented—for the Secretary of Defense to direct the establishment of a squadron-level unit in any component.

Hegseth, a former Army officer, has praised special operations forces, seeing them as a model for innovation and acquisition reform, and they have played key roles in operations during his tenure, including Operation Absolute Resolve to seize Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, Operation Rough Rider in Yemen in 2025, and the ongoing strikes against alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.
Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars.

When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in Pasadena’s Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the Lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isn’t only celebrating the long line of historic firsts accomplished here; it’s paving the way for many to come.

Initially a contractor for the U.S. Army, JPL launched America’s first satellite, Explorer 1 in 1958. But rather than just orbiting Earth like the Soviet Union’s Sputnik, Explorer 1 became the first spacecraft to conduct science, thanks to an onboard Geiger counter that discovered the protective radiation belts encircling Earth.

The Lab joined part of the newly formed NASA that same year. Within six years, in 1964, JPL sent the first U.S. mission to the Moon, Ranger 7. It also went on to lead the first planetary flyby, the first probe to visit all four gas giants, the first infrared telescope, the first rovers to roll on Mars, and the first rotorcraft to fly there, among many other historic milestones.

“Over the course of 90 years, JPL’s first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL’s director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the Lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the mission’s most iconic images. “We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and we’re ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.”

Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASA’s Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall, a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the Sun’s activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans.

Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks that other telescopes can’t find. Once an object is spotted, NASA can offer a threat assessment and plan accordingly.

Closer to home, the same Lab that launched the first oceanographic satellite in 1978 is at work on several missions that will offer a deeper reading of Earth’s vital signs. Where one mission will monitor the movement of water by measuring slight changes in gravity, another will study how powerful tropical convective storms form. A third will detail how different types of air pollution affect human health.

They add to a fleet of other Earth missions and projects JPL helps lead, including NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) a joint mission with the Indian Space Research Organisation that can pinpoint how Earth’s surface changes in relation to natural disasters. Another, one of a series of instruments called AVIRIS (Airborne Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer), can even detect rare Earth elements critical to modern technology.
From Mars to the Milky Way—never miss a discovery! Delivered straight to your inbox.

Flown on airplanes, the AVIRIS sensors were developed at JPL’s Microdevices Laboratory, which invented the “camera on a chip” technology that enables cellphones to take pictures. It’s also where the detectors are being developed for PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), a newly announced NASA mission that will strengthen humanity’s understanding of the universe by studying radiant energy visible only in the far-infrared.

“Bringing together the very best of scientific brilliance and engineering ingenuity from across Caltech and JPL continues to advance NASA’s priorities and empower America’s space leadership,” said Caltech’s president Ray Jayawardhana, who is also a professor of astronomy. “I can only imagine what those Caltech students experimenting with rockets in a little patch of dry riverbed would think if they could to see what Caltech and JPL have accomplished since, and where we’re headed next. Ninety years later, the same spirit of daring is still opening new frontiers and inspiring humanity.”

The 90th anniversary comes just a few weeks before another milestone, when on Nov. 18 Voyager 1 reaches a full light-day — the distance light will travel in 24 hours, which is some 16 billion miles, or 26 billion kilometers — from Earth. Ed Stone led the mission for 50 years, serving as JPL’s director for 10 of them. Stone died in 2024, but the Voyagers are continuing on their journey deeper into interstellar space, a place no other spacecraft have ventured. Turning 50 next year, they rely on NASA’s Deep Space Network (developed by JPL in the Apollo era) to receive commands and send back science data. Stone said that with both Voyagers exploring regions never before visited, “every day is a day of discovery.” The same could be said for JPL.
NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi.
Test teams fired the developmental engine for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket.
During the test, operators also fired the engine up to the 111% power level, matching the thrust needed for new production engines to launch the SLS rocket and the Orion spacecraft to orbit.

The main objectives of the test were to acceptance test RS-25 flight components for future Artemis missions and validate the new thermal protection system, which protects the RS-25 engine nozzle from the thermal environment surrounding SLS during launch.

While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability.
Four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket for each Artemis mission.
All RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions.

On a frigid February morning in Edinburgh, Scotland, Patrick Hickey had run out of living things to put under his microscope. The plants and fungi in his garden had dried up, and summer puddles, with their flamboyant biological complexity, had long frozen over.

Hickey, a mycologist at Hypha Research Ltd., was using plant leaves to study mitochondria, cellular organelles that generate energy. He was planning to sprout mustard seeds for fresh samples, but he was impatient. While making coffee in his kitchen, he noticed a cold-hardy turtle vine hanging from the windowsill. “I snipped off an inch or so, put it in my pocket, took it into the lab, and was just amazed at what I saw,” Hickey said.

Under the microscope, mitochondria darted around the cells. They nimbly maneuvered around slower chloroplasts, like motorcyclists dodging traffic. “It was absolutely alive with activity,” Hickey said.

His time-lapse video of this microscopic dance, which leads our gallery below and was recently honored in Nikon’s 2026 Small World in Motion Competition, reveals the close partnership between the organelles: chloroplasts (red) spin sunlight into sugar, and mitochondria (green) convert sugar into energy.

The Nikon Small World competition, established in 1974, honors excellence in microscopy. The annual contests have charted not only the evolution of creative photomicrography but also the progress of imaging technology.
Hickey — and many of the other honorees featured here — relied on a technique called confocal laser scanning microscopy.

Unlike a standard microscope, which illuminates an entire sample at once and can produce blurry images, a confocal microscope focuses on one depth level at a time. Researchers first “label” a sample with fluorescent dyes that attach to specific structures within the cell. A laser then illuminates a thin layer of the sample, and the microscope detects the resulting fluorescence. Scanning line by line, the system builds a detailed image.

As imaging technology advances, so too does our understanding of cellular processes. Hickey’s video shows that mitochondria are more dynamic than previously thought, which suggests that they are “more than just a ‘powerhouse of the cell,’” he said. “They are likely involved in cytoplasmic streaming, signaling, and interactions with other organelles.”

The full list of awardees can be found here for the photo contest and here for the video contest. We’ve chosen to feature a several winners and honorable mentions that reveal the intricacies of the cellular world.

Astronautsâ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars

- A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet.

A journey to Mars may be less challenging for the human heart than scientists once feared. A new study suggests that astronauts can adapt remarkably well to months of weightlessness, offering encouraging evidence that humans could endure the long trip to the Red Planet and function under its weaker gravity.

Researchers from Northwestern Medicine, UT Southwestern, and UT Houston monitored the hearts of 13 astronauts who spent approximately six months aboard the International Space Station. Their findings showed that although spaceflight initially affected heart performance, the astronauts gradually adapted, with intensive daily exercise playing an important role in maintaining their cardiovascular health.

One of NASA's major concerns about sending humans to Mars is how astronauts' hearts and circulatory systems will respond when they leave the weightless conditions of spaceflight (known as microgravity) and encounter Martian gravity, which is only about one-third as strong as Earth's.
Encouragingly, the researchers found that the astronauts showed no significant signs of cardiovascular strain when exposed to simulated Martian gravity after returning to Earth.

"With our findings, there is now reason to think that we would be able to traverse to Mars, get there and actually work on the surface of Mars," said study senior author Dr. James Thomas, professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
The study, published last month in the journal Circulation, is the first to investigate how the heart responds to simulated Martian gravity following an extended period in space.
How Daily Exercise Protects Astronauts' Hearts in Space

Living without gravity creates unusual challenges for the human body. On Earth, the heart constantly works against gravity to circulate blood, while muscles must support the body's weight. In space, those demands decrease substantially, allowing muscles and even the heart itself to shrink over time.

Returning to a gravitational environment can also be difficult. Astronauts on previous missions have frequently experienced dizziness or lightheadedness when standing after landing. This happens because gravity pulls blood toward the lower body, sometimes causing blood pressure to drop suddenly. The condition is called orthostatic hypotension. (If you've seen Sandra Bullock crawling after returning to Earth in "Gravity," you get the idea.)
However, the astronauts involved in the new study generally handled this transition well, potentially because they had maintained demanding exercise schedules throughout their missions.

As part of NASA's Exercise Countermeasures program, astronauts exercised for up to two hours each day. Their routines included 30 to 45 minutes of endurance training, which strengthens the cardiovascular system, along with 60 to 75 minutes of resistance training to help preserve muscle mass and strength.

"You lose muscle mass and cardiac mass when you're in a weightless environment because you are working less up there," explained Thomas, who also is a Northwestern Medicine cardiologist. "You're floating around in the air, and you give a little tap with your foot, and you can sail over to say hello to your buddy."
"To counter that, exercise is crucial when you're in space," Thomas added.
Heart Scans Reveal How the Body Adapts to Weightlessness

To understand what happens to the heart during prolonged spaceflight, the researchers collected echocardiograms before, during, and after each astronaut's mission. These ultrasound scans use sound waves to produce moving images of the heart, allowing doctors to examine its structure and measure how effectively it pumps blood.

While aboard the International Space Station, astronauts were trained to perform these scans on one another every few weeks. The recordings were transmitted to Earth, where researchers could monitor changes in heart function throughout the missions.
Thomas worked alongside Dr. Benjamin Levine of UT Southwestern Medical Center and Dr. Michael Bungo of the McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.

"It would be typically about 3 a.m. for me because the space station runs on Greenwich Mean Time," Thomas said. "I would watch the recordings come in live and coach the astronauts in real time to improve the images."

The scans revealed that the astronauts' hearts initially struggled to adjust to their new environment. During the first two weeks in space, researchers observed declines in cardiac filling, stroke volume, and several other measures of cardiovascular performance.

Cardiac filling refers to how much blood enters the heart between beats, while stroke volume describes the amount of blood pumped out with each contraction. Both measurements decreased early in the missions, indicating that the astronauts' hearts were temporarily moving less blood with each beat.
As the astronauts spent more time in space, their cardiovascular systems adapted. Cardiac filling and stroke volume gradually improved, approaching the levels recorded before launch.
These results suggest that the heart can adjust to prolonged weightlessness more effectively than early measurements might indicate, particularly when astronauts maintain regular physical activity.
Astronauts' Hearts Pass a Simulated Mars Gravity Test

The researchers also wanted to answer a particularly important question for future Mars missions: What happens when an astronaut who has spent months in weightlessness suddenly encounters gravity again?

Mars has roughly 38% of Earth's surface gravity. Although this is considerably weaker than what people experience on Earth, it would still force astronauts' hearts to work differently after months of floating in space.
To reproduce some of these effects, the researchers conducted a simulated Martian gravity test after the astronauts returned to Earth.
Each astronaut was tilted upward by 22 degrees from a lying position. This posture caused blood to shift toward the lower body, approximating the circulatory effects of Martian gravity.

The results were encouraging. After spending about six months in space, the astronauts' hearts performed just as well under simulated Martian gravity as they had when standing upright on Earth before their missions.

This suggests that astronauts who maintain their cardiovascular fitness during spaceflight may be capable of transitioning to the weaker gravity of Mars without experiencing major cardiovascular difficulties.
Although the findings come from a relatively small group of astronauts and a simulation rather than an actual Mars landing, they provide valuable evidence for planning future missions.

Combined with the benefits of daily exercise, the heart's ability to adapt to weightlessness and respond well to simulated Martian gravity offers another reason to be optimistic about sending humans to the Red Planet.

The study is titled "Impact of Prolonged Spaceflight on Cardiac Structure and Function: An Exploratory Longitudinal Observational Study." Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy
The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the Trump administration must continue providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates in federal prisons.
The decision, in an emergency appeal, maintains a lower court's injunction on a federal Bureau of Prisons' policy that would terminate hormone therapy and other treatments for trans inmates.
The unsigned order offered no explanation behind the decision. It simply read, "The application for stay presented to The Chief Justice and by him referred to the Court is denied."
It also said Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would side with the Trump administration and would grant the application for stay.
As the federal judge's injunction remains in place, the legal battle over the policy continues.

In January 2025, upon assuming office, Trump issued an executive order banning the use of federal funds that "promote" gender ideology. And prisoners brought a class action seeking reinstatement of the decades-long health policy. It contends that the Trump policy violates the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
A federal district judge barred the BOP from implementing its policy this summer.
A second court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, also rejected the administration's request to pause U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth's order.
That's when U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

Li Nowlin-Sohl, senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union and a lawyer involved in this case, said the organization believes there are more than 2,000 people in BOP custody who identify as transgender. (The BOP stopped publishing data reflecting transgender inmates after Trump took office in 2025. It only records male or female individuals incarcerated in the federal system.)

Kingdom v. Trump represents 1,000 inmates who have a gender dysphoria diagnosis, Nowlin-Sohl explained. Of those, the ACLU believes there are about 800 who have been prescribed hormone therapy and many who are also receiving social transition accommodations, Nowlin-Sohl said.

In its request for an emergency stay on the earlier rulings, the Trump administration argued that providing this care poses several risks, including for recipients of this specialized care, who it argued would become "targets for attacks." They also said that it raises "fairness concerns" as it would "breed resentment" with other inmates.

Access to gender-affirming care is considered medically necessary to treat gender dysphoria, a medical term used to describe the deep discomfort caused by a mismatch between a person's assigned sex at birth and their gender identity. Without it, individuals can struggle severely with mental health issues such as heightened anxiety and depression, with some turning to self-harm and suicide.

Gender-affirming care can include "...hormone therapy, and gender-affirming surgeries among others," according to the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. (In its filings, the Trump administration questioned WPATH's standards of care, which were developed by experts in transgender health and used by organizations across the world.)
Some people who are transgender may require hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries; others may not require any of these interventions.
The BOP has treated people diagnosed with gender dysphoria since at least 1992, the ACLU said in response to the government's filings to the Supreme Court.

"Had BOP's doctors found this treatment unhelpful or harmful to patients or had the agency found that the treatment compromised security, surely BOP would have mentioned it in the administrative record," the ACLU wrote.
This is a "glaring omission" and appears to indicate that the government's arguments now are simply "contrived," the ACLU continued.

NPR previously covered the impact of the loss of hormone treatments on people who are incarcerated. One woman said she experienced severe physical and mental anguish when she lost access to hormone treatments.
The Supreme Court's decision is at odds with other rulings that support the Trump administration's anti-trans policy agenda.

Last June, the court ruled that states can ban transgender girls from participating in sports at publicly funded schools. And in 2025, the court upheld state laws that make it illegal for doctors and other health professionals to provide gender-affirming care for minors.

In one of his first executive orders of his second term, President Trump targeted the trans community with a declaration that his administration recognizes just two sexes, male and female. This order has been the basis for a host of anti-trans policies throughout the administration.
But at least for now, the emergency request on the prison policy was to no avail.

Waiting in the wings at the Supreme Court are other cases on transgender rights. Most prominently, the Alliance Defending Freedom, an anti-trans group, has filed an emergency petition at the court on behalf of a mother and her teenage daughter who contend that the daughter was "unknowingly" forced to face a transgender opponent in girl's high school wrestling. Later this year, the court will hear oral arguments in a case testing whether a religious preschool can receive state funding while excluding LGBTQ families. In a separate case, the justices will examine whether parents have the right to challenge a state law that allows runaway teens to receive gender-affirming care without parental consent.
NPR Legal Affairs Correspondent Nina Totenberg contributed reporting.

The closer the NFL calendar creeps to the Nov. 10 trade deadline, the clearer it becomes which teams are buying and which are selling. Three weeks out, there is already a divide between contenders and pretenders, so playing the role of matchmaker provides a myriad of potential trade pairings.

A sweep across the league shows how Super Bowl contenders with roster holes, like the Seattle Seahawks and their running back position, match perfectly with downtrodden teams that own tradeable veterans, like the Philadelphia Eagles and Indianapolis Colts.

Sometimes the obvious trade proposals never come to fruition. But in a lot of cases, if it makes sense on paper, then it makes sense in practice. There are a number of reunions, like Khalil Mack's potential return to the Chicago Bears, that just feel right.
Here are 10 of those trades that feel so fitting that it would be a shame if they did not go through.

The Seattle Seahawks ought to have extreme seller's remorse as they field a bottom-tier rushing attack and watch Kenneth Walker III run wild in Kansas City. Much of their disappointing 3-3 start can be attributed to an offense that ranks second-worst in EPA per rush, which leads one to wonder how much they regret letting Walker go in free agency.

He is very much the missing piece, and they will rely on Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price to fill that gap when they return from injured reserve. Neither is an established No. 1 running back, though, so Seattle would benefit from admitting it needs a high-caliber starter, then placing Charbonnet back in his more natural secondary role and allowing Price to develop as a rookie third option.

They would have to pay a hefty price to pry Saquon Barkley away from Philadelphia because of his immense value and his giant cap hit, but with the Eagles poised to watch this season wither away in the wake of countless personnel losses, they should be willing to at least field calls on their superstar running back. Seattle is in as much of a win-now mode as any team in the league and thus is in a position to give up premium draft capital for a player who can help it return to the Super Bowl.

If Jerry Jones cannot turn the Dallas Cowboys into a winning football team, he is at least going to go down swinging. The Joey Porter Jr. trade earlier this season was one big move, but the defense clearly needs more blockbuster additions in order to climb out of the depths. Since Jones addressed the back end of the unit with the Porter deal, it may be time to turn back toward the line of scrimmage and address, again, an edge rusher group that is still lost without Micah Parsons.

While Arizona Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort said in August that he has "no interest" in trading Josh Sweat, there might not be a more obvious trade candidate on a team that is not built to contend for anything in 2026. Sweat denied any displeasure with his contract, but there was offseason smoke that he sought a restructured deal or a trade.

He is an expensive veteran for a franchise attempting to build a young core and boasts the kind of perennial sack production and team contract control that a competitive team would pay a premium for. If the Cowboys moved a couple of draft picks to land Sweat, this would be a win-win.

The NFL's stingiest defense is to credit for the Minnesota Vikings' perfect start. The margins in those five victories were nail-bitingly slim, though, because the offense has only done just enough to capitalize on Brian Flores' coaching masterclass on the other side of the ball.

The passing game is what it is. There is no in-season upgrading over Kyler Murray, and the wide receiver group will always be in good shape so long as Justin Jefferson is there. The main area that needs improvement and, more importantly, can be improved, is the rushing unit. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason (once healthy) are a serviceable tandem, yet the attack has accounted for only three touchdowns and ranks in the bottom quartile in EPA per rush. An infusion of stardom would take this offense to another level and make the Vikings true Super Bowl contenders.

Enter Jonathan Taylor. Whether the Indianapolis Colts would part with their best player just over two months after they signed him to a two-year contract extension (the third-largest deal for a running back in NFL history) is unknown, but with general manager Chris Ballard fired and coach Shane Steichen , too, this franchise could be headed toward a tear-down. Teams will call about Taylor. Minnesota needs to make sure it is in the conversation.

If there is one trade that is most likely to be completed by the deadline, a Khalil Mack reunion in Chicago has to be at the top of the list. The pairing almost makes too much sense. The Bears need pass-rushing help. Mack remains productive in the latter years of his career, albeit not quite at the All-Pro level of his Chicago heyday. The Los Angeles Chargers are prime candidates to sell expiring contracts, considering their 0-6 record. Everything points to these teams working together to send Mack back to his old home.

The lift Mack would provide for an offense-first team could be a difference maker that sparks a deep postseason run. Now that Caleb Williams is healthy again, the Bears have the potential to score at will. The defense lags behind just enough to warrant a splashy trade deadline move, and this one is just waiting to be completed.

There is a wide receiver injury crisis in Pittsburgh. Aaron Rodgers was on a hot streak until health issues depleted his supporting cast. In order to maximize the supposed last year of his career and stay in contention for the AFC North crown, the Steelers need to plug some immediate help into Rodgers' receiving room.

Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson are on injured reserve, and Ben Skowronek has a calf issue. It is up to DK Metcalf, rookie Germie Bernard and a couple of practice squad elevations to keep the passing game afloat.

All of that makes the Steelers potentially desperate buyers at the deadline. Chris Godwin Jr. should be on their radar. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers, whom they just defeated in overtime, are drifting further into the abyss and should be ready to sell. His three-year contract makes him an expensive asset who struggles to stay on the field, and that is a profile that the Buccaneers would seemingly want to part with.

He is healthy now, though, and that is what matters to the Steelers. Plus, he should be a tremendous fit next to Metcalf. Godwin spent every year prior to this one on the other side of a towering No. 1 target in Mike Evans, so he would be right at home in the same lineup as a similarly sizable go-to weapon like Metcalf.

The Buffalo Bills are winning games in one way and one way only: Scoring a boatload of points. They have to. The defense is a sieve, specifically in the back end. No matter how much pressure Greg Rousseau and the front provide, opponents are able to pick apart the pass defense to the tune of 285.8 yards per game — the second most in the league. The slot defensive back spot is the biggest weakness, and there is an obvious upgrade potentially sitting on the trade market in Cardinals safety Budda Baker.

Baker is versatile enough to play nickel or fall back deeper into coverage and would immediately be the best player in the Buffalo defensive backfield. He is the Cardinals' highest-paid player and remains under contract through 2027, but he carries a dead cap hit of only $3 million for next year, so moving on from him would not put Arizona in a long-term financial bind. That is an attractive proposition for a rebuilding team.

Jauan Jennings was in a 49ers uniform less than a year ago and would be a perfect fit back in one this season. He led all San Francisco wide receivers in catches and yards in 2024 and 2025 and knows the Kyle Shanahan offense front and back, so with the 49ers fighting through a litany of wideout injuries, why not reunite with someone who can slot right back into the lineup and deliver difference-making plays from Day 1?

The primary reason he is not on the squad right now is that the 49ers did not want to pay him long-term money, but the Minnesota Vikings did not either, so San Francisco can have him back on an expiring $8 million deal.

Minnesota is , as he has been invisible in the offense with only five targets, two catches and 9 yards on the year. He is not part of the Vikings' plan, so they might as well get something in return for him before he inevitably walks away at the end of the season.

His usage is up over the last two weeks, but Jerry Jeudy still ranks only fifth on the Cleveland Browns in targets as the team prioritizes its exciting rookie tandem of KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston over the 27-year-old veteran. It appears as though he is being phased out of the offense. Coming off his best showing of the year — a four-catch, 69-yard effort — the time to move on from him is now.

The Kansas City Chiefs would be the perfect destination for Jeudy and are as needy at the wide receiver position as any team in the league. Not only could the former Pro Bowler carve out a top-three role in a receiving corps that lacks any reliability outside of Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy, but his transition to a new offense would be smoothed by the fact that wide receivers coach Chad O'Shea was the same wide receivers coach who oversaw his Pro Bowl campaign in Cleveland in 2024. Patrick Mahomes could use a gifted route-runner to go with his speedy weapons in Rice and Worthy, especially as this team barrels toward a potential Super Bowl run.

The defensive backfield situation in Detroit is bleak, and that might be putting it nicely. The NFL's worst pass defense is desperate for help at each secondary position, while Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph remain out with injuries at safety, and the cornerback unit still has not recovered from the loss of Terrion Arnold.

Since the Lions keep scoring at an elite level and own plenty of pieces on the rest of the defense, there might not be a more glaring missing link for a postseason contender than their secondary. They will likely be aggressive at the trade deadline.

Riq Woolen should be there for the taking as the Eagles potentially tear everything down. He signed with them in March on a one-year contract, and given that he is still in his prime, it seems unlikely that he would re-sign with Philadelphia if they commit to a rebuild.

Of all the high-upside wide receivers that figure to be available at the deadline, none have a greater delta between their ceiling and floor than Brian Thomas Jr. His 1,282-yard, 10-touchdown rookie campaign displayed All-Pro potential, but in the two years since, he slipped behind Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers in the pecking order for targets in Jacksonville. The time for the Jaguars to move on from him is now, before his stock drops any further.

The ideal fits for Thomas are either a team that would benefit from his price as he remains on a rookie contract or a team that would make him a long-term centerpiece if he rekindles his 2023 success. The Las Vegas Raiders fit the latter criteria. Their wide receiver depth is nonexistent, and there is no clear No. 1 weapon in the room. That needs to change by the time Fernando Mendoza takes over at quarterback, or else they risk stunting the top draft pick's early-career development. It still feels early in the Raiders' trajectory to begin buying, but after a surprisingly competitive first six weeks, it might already be time to spend.

On Tuesday, I published a story about how YouTube appeared to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, with at least two users on X sharing screenshots of the dislike button moved into the three-dot menu. But a YouTube spokesperson, in a Wednesday statement to The Verge, confirmed that YouTube is “not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users.” However, YouTube is introducing a new UI for creators on their uploaded videos where the dislike button will be moved.
YouTube says it isn’t testing hiding the dislike button
YouTube creators, on their own videos, will have the dislike button moved behind the three-dot menu, but that’s not the case for regular users.
Here’s the full statement, from spokesperson Kimberly Taylor:

We are not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users. We’re introducing a new UI for creators on their own uploaded videos, where dislike is behind the three-dot menu, and as always, they can find their full dislike counts in Studio, alongside other analytics.

The change for creators follows past adjustments to the dislike button on the platform. YouTube hid the public dislike count on videos starting in 2021 as a way to prevent harassment, and it removed the dislike button video from Shorts earlier this year.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.

During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.

Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, the Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments into AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.

Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies left for Texas, Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.

But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.
Lou Gramm to reunite with Foreigner for concerts as he plans to retire with a ‘bang’
Former Foreigner vocalist Lou Gramm has got nowhere left to hide — it looks like retirement has finally found him.
The 76-year-old singer-songwriter reiterated his plans to retire from the touring life in an interview with “TalkShopLive,” a livestreaming platform.

“I feel like I’ve done this long enough,” Gramm said earlier this year on the podcast. “While I really enjoyed a lot about this life, I think the second most important thing to putting your heart and your mind and your body into ... a great band is knowing when to walk away.”
Gramm is currently touring with his recording band as the Lou Gramm All Stars for the remainder of the year, with the last performance set for Dec. 19 in Des Plaines, Ill.

“I’m very fortunate that at my age I can still still sing and hit the notes and everything,” Gramm said on the livestream. “But I don’t want to get to the point where I’m faking it or lowering the key two steps to do this song.”

The singer was a founding member of Foreigner, the British American rock band known for hits including “I Want to Know What Love Is” and “Juke Box Hero.” This year, the multiplatinum band celebrates its 50th anniversary and has scheduled performances throughout California for the remainder of the year.
Gramm left the band twice. The first time was in 1990 to focus on his solo career.

In 1992, he rejoined Foreigner but left in 2003 due to communication issues with bandmate Mike Jones, the guitarist and bandleader told Rolling Stone in 2005. Gramm shared details of their strained songwriting process with The Times years earlier.

“My contributions haven’t been that welcomed. It has caused me a lot of grief. I was a real studio rat,” Gramm told The Times in 1987. “But I didn’t have much say. It would leave me bitter, with a bad taste in my mouth.”

Jones retired from the band in 2023 after announcing a battle with Parkinson’s. Gramm revealed that the two reconciled prior to the band’s induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2024. In a 2026 interview with Spin Magazine’s Lipps Service, the singer shared that Jones was in the end stages of Alzheimer’s.

Gramm still has plans to join the current Foreigner group during a handful of appearances; Ultimate Classic Rock and Culture reports that he will appear with the group on the Rock Legends Cruise, which will depart from Miami on Feb. 21. He is also scheduled to be included in six shows during the band’s March 10-20 gig at the Venetian in Las Vegas.

“I think this is for me a high point, this tour, and finally getting into the Rock Hall of Fame and all the good things,” Gramm said on the podcast. “I think I just want to go out with a bang, and I think this summer tour is it.”

Asked for comment to an NBC report about the reduction of military and diplomatic personnel in the region, CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said in a statement, "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."

Earlier Wednesday, the State Department ordered the departure of non-essential personnel and family members in Saudi Arabia -- a decision officials say is a direct response to the risk posed by the Houthis.

There have been much smaller posture adjustments at several other embassies in the Middle East — changes officials say are also linked to the Houthi threat and other matters not connected to any plan to resume combat against Iran that the president may be considering.
