Continental Tyres said its Manufacturer of the Year 2026 Tyre Industry Award recognises its holistic commitment to innovation, customer care, and industry excellence. The company won the award during the 15 October NTDA Annual Dinner and Awards.

In the last year, Continental accelerated its innovation drive across passenger car, commercial vehicle, and specialty tyre portfolios. High-profile product launches include the ultra-high-performance SportContact 7 Force, engineered specifically for the Brabus Bodo supercar, alongside the adaptable EcoContact 7 and EcoContact 7 S lines. In the bus and coach segment, development centred on the sustainable Urban HA5 NXT.

Knowledge sharing and technical training have been equally prominent. Responding to widespread industry concerns regarding commercial vehicle wheel security, Continental bolstered its specialist training provision with dedicated modules, aiding technicians and fleet managers in reducing operational risk and enhancing maintenance standards.

Educational initiatives extended to broad consumer-facing campaigns. A 12-part ‘Scott Says’ social media series tackled everyday motorist queries, while the ‘Respect for Retreads’ campaign worked to dispel common misconceptions surrounding remanufactured tyres.

Internally, workforce engagement remained a key priority. Senior leaders conducted a three-week roadshow across 10 UK sites to connect directly with personnel, backed by structured wellbeing and safety initiatives and staff social events.

Reflecting on the manufacturer’s holistic progress, Tracey Mortimer, managing director of Continental in the UK and Ireland, noted: “This is a huge achievement for Continental and reflective of the time, energy and commitment that our teams invest at all of our sites around the country. Together, we strive to provide people with the safety and performance they deserve for their vehicles, while also standing alongside our customers with help, guidance and support to ensure we are adding value to their business.”
The award joined personal recognition of Mortimer with the Chairman’s Award and technical services general manager Steve Howat’s induction as NTDA Honorary Life Member.

Vaculug was formally presented with The King’s Award for Enterprise during a ceremony at its head office in Grantham. The honour was bestowed by the Lord-Lieutenant of Lincolnshire. Considered the highest official award for British businesses, The King’s Award highlights Vaculug’s commitment to sustainable manufacturing and circular economy practices within the commercial vehicle sector.

“Receiving the King’s Award for Enterprise is a proud moment for everyone at Vaculug,” said Jorge Crespo, managing director. “This honour is a testament to the dedication, hard work and technical innovation of our entire team in Grantham. It highlights our commitment to delivering sustainable solution for the commercial vehicle market while keeping manufacturing thriving in Lincolnshire.”
Local press, company leadership, and staff gathered to witness the presentation of the official Grant of Appointment scroll.

The King’s Award for Enterprise programme, which is in its 58th year, celebrates outstanding achievements by UK businesses, with winners authorised to fly the official King’s Award flag and display the emblem for five years.

Proposed changes to in-use vehicle emissions regulations represent a crucial step forward in tackling emissions tampering and enhancing the environmental performance of the UK vehicle parc. As the Department for Transport consults on strengthened controls, industry bodies like the Independent Automotive Aftermarket Federation (IAAF) are calling for more robust testing methods to identify compromised systems across the country.

For Cataclean, these legislative proposals underscore the vital role of regular vehicle maintenance in managing emissions from existing vehicles. Independent garages remain central to helping motorists identify potential issues early and restore proper engine performance through effective servicing. To support this ecosystem, Cataclean continues to champion preventative care with its flagship 8-in-1 fuel and exhaust system cleaning solution, expertly engineered to combat harmful carbon build-up across critical engine components.

Maddie Bamber, key account manager at Cataclean, commented: “The discussion around in-use vehicle emissions highlights the importance of looking after the vehicles already on our roads, as well as addressing emissions tampering. At Cataclean, we’re committed to providing solutions that help motorists and workshops tackle carbon build-up as part of ongoing vehicle care.”

With more than three decades of experience supporting vehicle efficiency, Cataclean believes preventative maintenance will remain an essential pillar for the automotive sector as it adapts to tighter environmental standards and increased regulatory scrutiny steadily moving forward.

Universal Components Group (UPG) is celebrating major career milestones for two key members of its procurement department, highlighting the expertise and dedication underpinning its automotive aftermarket operations. Procurement manager Ant Pickering marks 15 years since returning to the business, having originally joined in 2000 before progressing through warehouse and internal sales roles. After returning in 2011, Pickering advanced into procurement management, navigating increased automation and a rapidly expanding supplier network.

“I truly believe I have the best procurement team any company could have,” said Pickering. “While I support them, they also support me… There are always new challenges ahead, so here’s to the next 15 years at UPG.”

Senior procurement assistant Sarah Pugh is celebrating two decades with the company, having joined in 2006. Over 20 years, Pugh has seen shipping and logistics grow increasingly complex while supporting the business through key depot developments and brand transitions. Beyond her day-to-day role, she has actively represented UPG in community initiatives, including ten years of volunteering for charity partner Barretstown.
“I am proud to have been here for 20 years. It is a big achievement, and I hope to be here for many more,” Pugh commented, noting the strong team culture as a key factor in her longevity.

Recognising their contributions, alongside colleague Jimmy Oldfield, who also reaches the 15-year mark, UPG director Martin Butterworth praised the trio: “Ant and Sarah’s stories show what long service brings to a business: knowledge built over many years, strong relationships and a willingness to support others… In an aftermarket that continues to evolve, their experience helps us adapt while maintaining the service our customers rely on.”
Putin releases American Stephen Hubbard from Russian prison
Russian President Vladimir Putin has freed another American, 74-year-old Michigan native Stephen Hubbard, from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has freed another American from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump. Stephen Hubbard, who's a 74-year-old native of Michigan, had been serving a prison sentence in Russia after being convicted of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. His release came as White House Envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in Russia to discuss the latest U.S. efforts to end the war in Ukraine. NPR's Charles Maynes is on the line from Moscow. Hi there.
SUMMERS: Charles, if you could, just tell us more about Hubbard and how he ended up in a Russian prison.

MAYNES: Yeah. You know, Hubbard is a former school teacher who was detained by Russian forces in Eastern Ukraine in 2022. He'd moved there after marrying a Ukrainian woman. And after his capture, he was later sentenced in a closed trial to nearly seven years in prison, as you know, for fighting on behalf of Ukraine while in his 70s. The U.S. formally designated him wrongfully detained under the Biden administration. And amid concerns over his health and safety, the Trump White House made gaining his release a priority.
SUMMERS: Was this release a surprise, though?

MAYNES: Not really. President Trump had signaled negotiations for Hubbard's freedom were in the works in comments to journalists this week. But the reveal came during a visit today by White House Envoy Steve Witkoff to Saint Petersburg, Russia's former imperial capital, where he met with President Vladimir Putin. The reason was to discuss new proposals from the U.S. aimed at trying to find an end to the war in Ukraine. And yet, with cameras rolling during introductory remarks, Hubbard's case took center stage. Witkoff thanked Putin for arranging Hubbard's release. Putin confirmed the American was already at the airport, and then Witkoff added this.
STEVE WITKOFF: You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir. And I salute that. I commend you, and I thank you again.
SUMMERS: I got to say, Charles, hearing Steve Witkoff describe Putin as a humanitarian - that is pretty striking.
MAYNES: Yeah. It's not the first time Witkoff has been publicly flattering Putin, but you can imagine how well that went over in Ukraine, given 4 1/2 years of war.
SUMMERS: And sticking with Hubbard for a minute here, do we know anything about his condition, how he's doing?

MAYNES: Well, state media issued footage of a smiling Hubbard shaking hands with Witkoff as the Kremlin's White House envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, looked on. Hubbard will, of course, need the full medical examination, but he seemed to look reasonably well. And Hubbard's family is happy. His son, who's an Orthodox priest named Father Joseph Coleman, thanked President Trump, as well as President Putin, for securing his father's release. And Hubbard's already on his way home.
SUMMERS: And, Charles, did the United States give up anything for Hubbard's return?

MAYNES: Well, President Trump, in a social media post celebrating the news of Hubbard's release, insisted, no. He said the U.S. hadn't given, quote, "anything in return." But, of course, Hubbard's release took place against this really extraordinary last two weeks during which Trump has made a series of gestures towards Russia and against Ukraine. He's agreed to buy previously sanctioned Russian diesel fuel. He's placed a waiver on a congressional sanctions package that he himself had signed into law. He's pressed Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil facilities and even called for Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy's ouster.
SUMMERS: And the Trump administration, how do they explain those moves?

MAYNES: Well, Trump argues this engagement with Russia, you know, these deals are part of a wider plan to keep Moscow involved in the peace negotiations and that they're in the interest of American consumers as well. You know, and there's something to show for that. Putin announced that the first shipments of Russian diesel - 60,000 tons - would be heading to the U.S. in the next few days. And a Kremlin aide said Putin had agreed to resuscitate trilateral peace talks with the U.S. and Ukraine, something he'd been refusing to do. The question is whether that's just optics or there's something really new to discuss here.
SUMMERS: NPR's Charles Maynes in Moscow, thank you.

Meet the people moving north to escape increasingly hot summers
LONDON – Mike Coe never thought he would leave his dream home in rural Worcestershire, not far from Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare's birthplace.

That was until Coe started researching the warming temperatures in the region. Coe had a job making videos for environmental activists, and ten years ago, when he spoke to his colleagues about the effects of climate change – and read the scientific papers himself – he started to get concerned.

"I realized that it was likely to get very, very hot in the British Midlands, even during my lifetime," Coe, 69, told NPR. "I said… I think we need to move to Scotland." A decade later, now Coe and his partner Lizzie Stoodley live on the Isle of Skye off Scotland's west coast.

There they have built a "Passivhaus" — a highly energy-efficient home — the second they have built. And they are glad they built their new home where they did. "Our decision to move seems to have been confirmed as being the right one, particularly this year," Coe told NPR.

Friends who still live further south have told the couple that the weather was "unbelievably hot" and "incredibly uncomfortable" this summer, as the United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record, with five successive heat waves and widespread drought.

But while southern regions warmed up, the weather on the Isle of Skye remained temperate. "I think there are quite a few more very hot summers I might escape by living here rather than remaining where we did," Coe said.
Susan Chinnery and her partner Steve Lewis, used to live near Milton Keynes, 50 miles north of London. But they began finding the summer months increasingly uncomfortable.

"I hate the hot weather," Chinnery told NPR. "I remember 2022 when Steve and I… we were actually sleeping outside on the patio because it was just too hot to sleep indoors." Like many British homes, their Victorian-era house was designed to keep in the warmth, and doesn't have air conditioning.

Lewis said that 2022 reminded him of the famously hot British summer of 1976, and he realised it was only going to get warmer. "I thought to myself, it's arrived," he told NPR. "This is the slow and inexorable decline into some new state."
Last year, Chinnery and Lewis moved to Westray, one of the Orkney Islands off northern Scotland, largely because of rising temperatures.

Melissa Terras also moved to Scotland, partly because of climate change. "When I mentioned climate change to people as one of the reasons why we were going to move north, people laughed," Terras told NPR. "They were like, 'What are you talking about?'"

In 2017, Terras moved her family from Letchworth Garden City, a town 40 miles north of London, to Edinburgh. A professor at the University of Edinburgh, Terras chose a house "up a hill," mindful of rising sea levels. She says more people are now thinking as she did several years ago.

The trend is also emerging in the housing market. Real estate agents in the Scottish Highlands told NPR that more buyers are citing cooler summers as a factor in their home-buying decisions. Recent figures show that house prices in Scotland rose year over year, while they fell in southeastern England and Greater London.
All over Europe, there are signs that climate is beginning to influence where many people are choosing to live, alongside factors including jobs, housing and the economy.

Scientists say Europe is the world's fastest warming continent. Large areas of Europe saw scorching temperatures this summer, with widespread wildfires, and at least 35,000 excess deaths thought to have been linked to the heat.

As climate change intensifies, countries around the world are grappling with more extreme impacts. At this year's U.N. General Assembly, Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, called recent flash floods in his country "a warning to the world," urging a "culture of preparedness" for future climate crises.
Gaia Vince, a London-based journalist and author of Nomad Century, predicts climate change will drive hundreds of millions of people from hotter regions to more temperate areas this century.

The U.K. has felt the effects, too. "We've had five almost consecutive heat waves this year alone, and our infrastructure is built for a completely different climate — everything is built for a climate which no longer exists," Vince told NPR.

Britain will also see migration, Vince said, as people adapt their lifestyles and infrastructure. Wealthier individuals are already moving toward places such as Ireland and Scotland in search of a more livable climate, she said.
Vince expects a similar trend in the United States, with the Great Lakes region and Alaska potentially attracting people from farther south.
Some Americans are already making the move to Scotland. Jason Sorensen, a California native, moved with his wife, Christine, last year to Golspie in the Scottish Highlands.
After experiencing wildfires in Los Angeles and hot summers while working in London, Sorensen said "something broke" inside him, and he decided he wanted to live somewhere cooler.

"Between now and 2100, there really are only a few places that you could categorize as 'best of the worst' oases if things really go to hell," Sorensen told NPR. "Certain parts of Norway, the South Island of New Zealand, maybe southern Chile down near the Lake District, maybe certain parts of Alaska — and northern Scotland."
Not so long ago, people who said they wanted to live in Scotland for the weather would have been laughed at.
But for many living farther south, it seems the joke isn't quite so funny anymore.
United States GP: McLaren with upgrades for Austin race as reigning F1 champions bid to ward off Red Bull threat

McLaren bidding to hit back with stronger results across the next triple header after seeing Red Bull close right up on them in Constructors' Championship in fight for third; watch every session of the United States GP in Austin from Friday evening, live on Sky Sports F1

McLaren will introduce further upgrades at the United States Grand Prix as they bid to improve their car's performance and stave off a resurgent Red Bull in the standings over the remainder of the season.

The reigning world champions continue to sit third in the Constructors' Championship with six rounds to go but fell into the clutches of fourth-placed Red Bull over the first of the end-of-season triple headers.

While McLaren failed to score a podium across that run of races, Red Bull claimed four top-three finishes - including two wins for Max Verstappen - to cut what had been a 76-point deficit to their rivals to just seven points.

McLaren's official pre-Austin preview described the team's results over the last three events as falling "significantly short of expectations" and that their 33-point haul in that run was "significantly lower than anticipated".
McLaren now head to a Circuit of the Americas track in Austin this weekend that they are hoping will be more suited to the strengths of their car, which will be boosted by some further revisions.

Rob Marshall, McLaren's chief technical officer, said: "We're bringing a modest selection of upgrades for this event, aimed at improving some braking reliability and performance issues. We also have some small floor changes to test.
"We have all seen how difficult it is to predict the relative performance of the top teams over the last five or six races.

"Obviously, there are many factors in play here: cars being upgraded, cars suiting and drivers liking certain circuits among other factors. The last few races have not been great for us, but I think we're getting stronger again and Austin is probably a better circuit for our car.
"Practice will be important for correlating what we've seen in our development tools with the track.
"We are still learning how best to extract performance from this car. We have the full range of corner types here so getting the best balance for the whole lap will be our main focus."

McLaren's cause in Singapore was not helped by them losing eight points on the final lap of the Sprint when their cars collided after Lando Norris attempted an overtake on Oscar Piastri. Norris later apologised for the accident, admitting it was ill-advised move on his team-mate at such a late stage of the short-form race.
The world champion said in the team's Austin preview that "I take responsibility for my mistakes, and I learn from them".

McLaren now return to the scene of a previous high-profile incident in Austin from 2025, when both their drivers crashed out on the first lap of the Sprint in a chain reaction set off by Piastri colliding with Nico Hulkenberg, and have little room for any similar missed opportunities 12 months on.
Speaking on the post-Singapore GP edition of The F1 Show podcast, Sky Sports F1's Bernie Collins said: "McLaren have had a few incidents through the year where they have not maximised their points.

"[In Singapore] Max Verstappen maximised the result, McLaren did not and there have been several weekends where McLaren did not maximise the result. This accident [in the Sprint] was a silly example of it.

"Arguably, I think if Hadjar hadn't missed three races when Liam Lawson was in that car Red Bull would be ahead of McLaren. And that's what McLaren know, that they have been saved I think, at this stage, because Hadjar wasn't in that car for three races and [Red Bull] weren't scoring the points that they could have done.
"But now Red Bull are on the up and they need to up their game if they are going to survive in that P3 position because it doesn't look like it at the moment."

Karun Chandhok added: "I think they probably know they now have the fourth-fastest car, which is a bit of a concern, and Red Bull are probably now the fastest if not second-fastest car for most tracks."

After losing at Atletico Madrid last time out in the Champions League, Lisandro Martinez hit out at the club's hierarchy, calling out technical director Jason Wilcox for failings in the transfer window.
This time captain Fernandes took aim at the club's coaching staff in a stinging take-down of their pressing plan.
Asked by TNT Sports about a lack of cohesion in United's work out of possession, Fernandes defended his team-mates and put the blame on Carrick and his coaches.
"It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave a little space in behind and try to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball," he said.

"But sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confident, they have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball the legs are, and the brain, much more difficult to make it work."
Was that tactical idea what cost Man Utd in Como? "That's on the manager and on the staff to see it, it's not on me," said Fernandes.
"I just said, I think sometimes we have to be more brave on the pressure, trying to take a risk of getting that press very high and making them uncomfortable - as they did to us."

A meeting between Carrick, Martinez and Wilcox repaired relations after the centre-back's comments in Madrid. But Carrick gave a blunt response in his post-match press conference on Wednesday when Fernandes' thoughts were put to him.

For all United did wrong in the game, it was the application of his players which was prominent in his post-match assessment.

"I'll definitely look at what we've done [as a coaching staff] or if it's the motivation and the intention and the purpose and the intensity of a game of football you have to bring," he said. "We didn't bring that today.

New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions, including seasonally dry savannas, tropical rainforests, and lowland swamp forests. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño, fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights, closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks.

"Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems," said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. "It's a horrible situation."

According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 19, more than any other year on record at that point in the year. "Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it's very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997," said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research.

On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons, the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing, vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades.

Unusually dry weather—a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns—has primed ecosystems across the island to burn. The southernmost part of Papua New Guinea, dominated by relatively fire-prone savannas and grasslands of the Trans-Fly region, went more than 90 consecutive days without rain, according to Papua New Guinea's National Weather Service. Since August, parts of the region have seen precipitation of roughly 5 to 10 percent of normal, according to the weather service's data. Local news outlets report that drought is causing crop failures, water shortages, and school disruptions.

In this normally wet part of the world, people ignite the vast majority of fires, researchers say. Crop fires, pasture maintenance, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting are all common reasons people burn in New Guinea. In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island.

"We're seeing an exceptionally high level of fire activity in Papua New Guinea and Eastern Indonesia, particularly Indonesian Papua and Kalimantan, this year compared with Sumatra and other parts of Western Indonesia," said Yang Chen, an associate researcher at the University of California, Irvine. "Papua has emerged as Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier."

Over the past two decades, land in Indonesian Papua has been cleared for industrial oil palm and pulpwood plantations, shifting small-scale cultivation, urban expansion, and mining. According to Global Forest Watch, the region lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double the 2024 total and the most since 2017.

Sumatra's fires are relatively low compared to other drought years partly because many areas are already developed. "Areas with large oil palm, sugarcane, or pulpwood plantations also often have their own private fire brigades to protect their assets," said Field. "It's in unmanaged areas or primary forest edges where we're generally seeing the most fire."
Researchers expect the fires to continue until the heavy rains of the wet season arrive in the southern part of New Guinea, typically in early November.

NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall, from NASA Headquarters, to explain our new Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), and answer your questions.

We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long. It has taken years to move mission concepts through the current two-step process. This has often come with contract management challenges, unpredictability, and not enough funding. NASA is committed to doing better — and I’m excited to share with you how we’re making it happen.

I am so pleased that NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has empowered the Science Mission Directorate to take action and make our mission selection process move more smoothly, efficiently, and effectively. The Administrator has directed us to accelerate the delivery of science, reduce the time and resources spent on long competitive processes, and focus funding on the highest-priority missions across every NASA Science division as quickly and affordably as possible. Predictability in delivering incredible science will be at the forefront of what we do.

We are committed to getting this right. Some of these changes will take time to fully implement. We will roll them out in stages, be thoughtful about them, and refine them with your input along the way. But time is also of the essence. By streamlining how missions are proposed, reviewed, and selected, we can make meaningful change right now. That streamlined approach is Competition Model 2.0, or CM2.0, and it is how we are answering the Administrator's call to get you to science faster.

CM2.0 starts from a simple idea: compete on the science first. Proposals will be science-focused and will not require detailed engineering plans, cost, and implementation work until they are truly needed to make a decision. This frees you to spend more of your time doing science and less of it proposing how to do science.
Here is how we will streamline mission selection across our mission classes:

CM2.0 will not change how we manage our largest missions since that process has already been reformed. After the James Webb Space Telescope, NASA conducted the Large Mission Study which drew lessons from Webb and best practices from our most successful flagships into a single, documented approach for building large missions more efficiently. Flagships will continue to follow that approach, with NASA directing the overall mission to a lead NASA Center and it will then compete the science teams and instruments through targeted solicitations.
Astro-Probes, New Frontiers, and Discovery:
These missions will move to a new, accelerated two-step competition:

- Step 1 asks for just three things: a compelling science case, a science implementation plan, and a proof-of-concept mission design. That removes roughly half of the material currently required in an Announcement of Opportunity (AO) response. This allows the initial selection to focus on what matters most, the science. It also opens the door wider, because a strong idea is judged on its merits rather than on the size of the team behind it. Principal Investigators (PI) without a major university or commercial backing will get a fair consideration, and NASA PIs at any NASA Center remain eligible to respond.

- Step 2 is a Mission Implementation Study carried out with either NASA's two Science Centers of Excellence, the Goddard Space Flight Center, or the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). NASA SMD may award an implementation study (under the management of GSFC) for New Frontiers or Discovery to JHU/APL depending on the science selected. The mission implementation study bridges pre-Phase A and Phase A by evaluating scientific merit, science implementation merit, and mission implementation merit to ensure that risks are surfaced early on rather than hidden. Down-selection to a single mission happens partway through Phase A, and the selected mission completes Phase A and then arrives at KDP-B with a matured mission implementation design. Teams that are not selected are freed from carrying concepts through the rest of Phase A on their own.

These updates in the mission selection process will reduce time from AO to step 2 selection by up to 45 percent. This means that the original 35-months timeline will be reduced to about 19.5 months, all while having a stronger, more mature mission at the time of selection.

These missions follow the same two-step approach with an even broader field of implementing organizations, including universities and industry partners. Implementing organizations and partners will be evaluated on past performance on projects of similar complexity and cost prior to mission selection. PI-led teams can request pairing with either a Goddard or JPL implementation team at Step 1 selection, and NASA can provide Center support where it will help with procurement, contract management, or quick resolution of technical challenges. This will result again in an up to a 45 percent reduction in the selection timeline.
SMEX, Missions of Opportunity, Earth Venture, Hosted Payloads, and Ride Shares

These missions will move to a single-step competition with a smaller review team and virtual site visits. They will also be open to a broad range of implementing organizations. The time to final selection will drop from about 32 months to about 19 months which is a reduction of up to 40 percent. Our smallest missions will be riding the momentum of a maturing commercial space economy and will move even faster. This means more missions, more often, with more incredible science at a lower cost.
Commercial Capabilities for Every Mission Type

The commercial space industry has never been stronger—and it’s only gaining momentum. Mission and implementation teams will be expected to adopt industry best practices and emerging commercial capabilities, including commercial buses, subsystems, and multi-mission operations -- wherever they offer a technical or cost benefit. No mission class is too large or too complex to benefit from the commercial industry. We will keep assessing the commercial landscape at regular intervals, building on our recent Science as a Service Request for Information.
By competing on science first, established teams and first-time teams stand on equal footing. The best idea wins.

Great science deserves great stewardship. Rigorous cost and schedule control remains mandatory across every mission class. Phase A estimates will inform complexity and scope trades. Therefore, breaches of control thresholds will carry real consequences of up to, and including, mission termination. That discipline is how we keep the pipeline flowing for everyone.

Our NASA Centers lead the world in spaceflight experience. Therefore, by appropriately directing work at Goddard and JPL, we will save taxpayer dollars, eliminate unnecessary competition among NASA Centers, encourage collaboration, and keep critical skills thriving across the agency.

This is a moment of real opportunity. We have an administrator who is empowering us to move faster and a commercial market that is ready to help. We have NASA Centers with unmatched expertise, and a science community whose ideas expand and redefine the bounds of human achievement in the cosmos. CM2.0 brings those strengths together so that more great ideas become great missions, all while being faster and returning more science at an affordable price for the benefit of all.

NASA leads the world in discovery and innovation, but none of that happens on its own. It happens because of you. You are the reason the list of what’s "impossible" keeps getting shorter. I am so proud of what this community has achieved, and what incredible science we will continue to discover together
Thank you for your brilliance, your dedication, and your partnership. The best of NASA Science is still ahead of us, and I cannot wait to see where this journey takes us.
Nicola Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters
On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor.

Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.)

It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. The mission ended abruptly 14 months ahead of its planned end date when scientists lost contact with the probe.

The Indian Space Research Organisation, or ISRO, had a lot riding on the success of Chandrayaan-1 moon mission, which marked the first-ever deep space mission by the Indian space agency. It was also the first mission to the moon for India, a country that hopes to launch its own crewed spacecraft and build a space station.

Chandrayaan-1 did more than just demonstrate that India's space program was capable of launching missions to the moon; it also returned some amazing science results, like evidence of water ice on the moon.

"In September 2009, scientists published results of data collected by the American M3 instrument which had detected absorption features on the polar regions of the surface of the Moon usually linked to hydroxyl- and/ or water-bearing molecules," NASA said in a mission overview.
The spacecraft carried 11 instruments to study the moon, five of them built by ISRO. The rest were experiments for the European Space Agnecy and NASA.
"In addition to the five Indian instruments, the spacecraft carried scientific equipment from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Sweden, and Bulgaria," NASA said.
It took until Nov. 8, 2008 for Chandrayaan-1 to enter lunar orbit, where it stayed until contact was lost in August 2009, most likely due to a power supply failure caused by overheating.
"This was short of the spacecraft’s planned two-year lifetime, although ISRO noted that at least 95% of its mission objectives had been accomplished by then," NASA wrote.

India did not stop at the moon with Chandrayaan-1. In 2019, the country launched the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, which carried the Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. Chandrayaan-2 reached lunar orbit successfully, but the Vikram landing failed.

The Chandrayaan-3 misson followed in 2023, which successfully landed a new Vikram lander and Pragyan rover near the moon's south pole. India plans to launch the Chandryaan-4 mission to return moon samples to Earth in 2028.

Few names in the science fiction literary world carry as much weight and respect as author Alan Dean Foster. His award-winning 55-year career as a grandmaster of the genre continues with his latest novel from Blackstone Publishing, "Lost on Paradise", and we have an exclusive excerpt to share with our readers ahead of its release this week.

Foster famously ghost-wrote the first "Star Wars" novelization for George Lucas in 1976 and "Splinter of the Mind’s Eye" in 1978, which was intended to be a low-budget Star Wars sequel should the space opera not become a hit. He’s been a mainstay for go-to fantastic adventures featuring engaging characters, dynamic plotlines, and imaginative worlds for six decades.

In addition to crafting the screen story for "Star Trek: The Motion Picture," Foster also wrote the novelizations for the first three "Alien" films, Disney's "The Black Hole," John Carpenter's "The Thing," "The Last Starfighter," "Star Trek," "Transformers," "Terminator: Salvation", and many more.
New York Times bestselling author Alan Dean Foster, master of both action and emotion, reveals a world where everything is perfect, but nothing is as it seems…

The near-future, off-world escapades of "Lost On Paradise" are the latest addition to Foster’s acclaimed bounty of bestselling standalone novels and series, including the popular "Spellsinger" series.

"Earth is crowded, polluted, and dismal," states the novel's synopsis. "Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina scrape by on her poorly paying job and what little money he gets selling items scavenged from rich people’s trash. Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina dream of Paradise.

"Paradise: a beautiful, clean, verdant world where three races live in harmony—at least, according to the videos sent back to Earth. There are the Eiquan, masters of astonishing technology; the Lusanata, hunters and farmers; and humans, who may be restricted to a few scattered settlements, but still live a life ten times better than those on Earth.
"On the run after a criminal act, Jonos and Liina finally escape to Paradise. It's everything they hoped for. Until tragedy strikes."
The genesis of Foster's "Lost on Paradise" is something that’s been percolating in his fertile mind for many years.

"I had this notion of a planet called Paradise where everything is perfect, and everything on Earth is seriously messed up," Foster tells Space. "There’s this couple who have problems; they’re poor like everybody else.

"And you have a unique male protagonist because he recognizes that his female partner is smarter than him, so she’s the brains of the outfit, and he supplies the muscle. Although he's not stupid. Too often you get a big, hulking guy with no brains. But she has a potentially fatal disease, and they’re trying to get away like a lot of poor people in the world today. So here's a place called Paradise. How do you get there? It’s expensive and difficult. And what happens if they do? Maybe Paradise isn’t always Paradise."
In crafting a deteriorating New York some 150 years or so down the calendar, it was important to stay sharp regarding developments that pop up in the news to avoid any internal logic conflicts.

"You just don’t want to get caught out by a scientific development that you postulate is near future when it's actually contemporary," explains Foster. "So I was very careful with that. But as you’re building out an alien environment and one that’s supposed to be perfect and beautiful, and then there’s maybe some things about it that aren’t, what do you introduce to show that?

"You don’t want to contradict yourself when you’re worldbuilding. That's a large problem that’s unfortunately common in science fiction," notes Foster. "Where somebody is breathing air, and suddenly they’re breathing methane, and it just doesn’t work. There’s a lot of different variables that come together that prove that Paradise is Paradise in some ways and not in others. A good example would be when the first Europeans reached Tahiti. The problem was that the people who entered this Paradise brought venereal disease and smallpox, to which the Polynesians had no resistance. So it's Paradise until you get there, and then maybe you mess it up."
Now enjoy our exclusive chapter excerpt from Alan Dean Foster’s "Lost On Paradise." Published by Blackstone Publishing.

Why shouldn’t a man and a woman in his and Liina’s position try to get to Paradise? Jonos mused as he treaded his way homeward. Though morning continued its ascent, the sun did not. Or so it seemed, when the omnipresent pollution often rendered day as dark as night. The gloom was useful for masking scavenging activities and for concealing one’s identity. It was less suitable for more plebian activities such as breathing and eating. Or living. Life on Earth sucked.

To emigrant humans it went without saying that Paradise was aptly named. Everyone had heard the stories. On Paradise a person could breathe freely. Without a mask, without fear of needing lung implants, without having to worry about inhaling a soupçon of strychnine or similar industrial pollutants. On Paradise food was plentiful and fresh, water devoid of contaminants. There was work, too, for anyone willing to adapt to entirely new surroundings, for those willing to acknowledge the much-talked-about overlordship of the dominant species. For arrivals willing to submit to the experimental, ever-evolving social structure, and to the limitations that were placed on newcomers, the technologically superior Eiquans professed an indifference that amounted to a willing welcome.

Or so the compendium of hugely diverse anecdotes insisted. That’s all they were, Jonos knew. Stories and speculation, rumors and conjecture. Ignoring the spotty rain that had begun to fall, he turned a corner and nearly ran over a couple who scrambled to get out of his way. The man he had accidentally jostled started to say something, quickly realized the size of the individual he was about to chastise, and mumbled on his way, dragging a woman—likely his wife—with him. Jonos paid them no mind. Half of him was engaged in navigating his way home, the other half in dreaming of what Paradise might actually be like.

In truth, he had never met anyone who had actually been to Paradise. He had never met anyone who knew anyone who had been to Paradise. That did not make the distant world any less real. The media periodically released vits and images of the place. These showed an Earth-like planet swathed in an atmosphere perfectly suitable for humans. The indigenous wildlife was fascinating, the few but thriving, improvised communities intriguing, and the rarely seen Eiquans themselves tall, gracile, and sophisticated. So what if they weren’t humanoid? They were bisymmetrical, anyway, highly intelligent, and by all accounts no worse than indifferent to the interests of other species. So beautiful and graceful was their slender physicality, so mellifluous their speech, that even though they were quite alien the idea of living among them held no fear for Jonos.
Anything, he knew, would be a step up from Earth.

Don't miss the Orionid meteor shower peak tonight (Oct. 21-22) as tiny shards of Halley's Comet collide with Earth's atmosphere to carve fiery streaks through the Autumn sky! But will the light cast by the waxing gibbous moon spoil the show?

The Orionid meteor shower activity peaks when Earth travels through the densest section of the debris trail left by Comet 1P/Halley. The comet is currently racing back towards the sun ahead of its next visit to the inner solar system in 2061.

Under perfect dark sky conditions 10 to 20 shooting stars could brighten the night sky each hour as the peak unfolds, according to NASA. However, the light cast by the waxing moon — just four days from being full — will likely reduce the number of visible meteors by hiding fainter Orionids from sight.

Orionid shooting stars will appear to travel away from a point of origin, close to the red star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion, rising above the eastern horizon an hour before midnight for viewers in the U.S.
When and where to see Orionid shooting stars this October

Your best chance at spotting the fast-moving meteors will come in the hours before dawn on Oct. 22, after the moon has set and the radiant approaches its highest point in the night sky. It's best not to stare directly at the radiant, where the glowing meteor trails will be relatively short compared to those left by shooting stars that appear 45-90 degrees away from the bright star Betelgeuse, thanks to an effect known as foreshortening.

Try to travel away from city lights and allow 20-30 minutes for your eyes to adapt to the dark. Always make sure someone knows where you're going if you head somewhere remote to catch the shower and be sure to take a red light to ensure that you can find your way while also preserving your night vision!

Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells

- Scientists have turned blood cells from an 80-year-old into neural stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20, effectively reversing more than 60 years of cellular aging in the laboratory. The discovery offers a new way to investigate how cells become younger and could help researchers better understand age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's.

Scientists in Germany have found a way to dramatically reverse the molecular age of human cells, transforming blood cells from an 80-year-old person into stem cells with an age signature of less than 20 years.

Researchers at the University Hospital of Bonn and the University of Bonn achieved this remarkable transformation by reprogramming immature red blood cells into neural stem cells, which can eventually develop into brain cells. During the process, molecular markers associated with aging were effectively reset, making the cells more than 60 years younger at the molecular level.

Unlike earlier approaches, the rejuvenation happened gradually, allowing scientists to follow the changes over an extended period. This slower process could provide important clues about how cellular aging can be reversed and potentially help researchers investigate treatments for diseases associated with aging.
The findings were published in the journal Aging Cell.
How Scientists Turn Blood Cells Into Brain Stem Cells

The human body contains hundreds of specialized cell types, all of which originate from a single fertilized egg and carry essentially the same genetic instructions. As cells develop, however, they take on specific roles. Under normal circumstances, a skin cell cannot transform into a liver cell, and a blood cell cannot become a nerve cell.

Modern laboratory techniques have made it possible to overcome these biological restrictions. Scientists can now reprogram certain mature cells to adopt entirely different identities. For example, skin cells can be converted into cells capable of producing nerve tissue, an approach that could eventually contribute to treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.

The process relies on a combination of proteins called transcription factors, which regulate how genes are activated. By changing which genetic instructions a cell follows, these proteins can redirect its development and give it a new cellular identity.

"Using this method, we have directly converted red blood cell precursors into neural stem cells," explains Prof. Dr. Oliver Brüstle, director of the Institute of Reconstructive Neurobiology at the University Hospital of Bonn.

Earlier experiments by the Bonn team had already demonstrated that nerve cells generated through this approach could successfully connect with existing neurons after being transplanted into the brains of mice.
Scientists Reverse More Than 60 Years of Cellular Aging
The latest investigation focused on an especially intriguing consequence of cellular reprogramming: the dramatic reversal of molecular aging.

"In our current study, however, we focused on a different phenomenon: namely, the observation that cells become significantly rejuvenated during reprogramming," emphasizes Brüstle, who is also a member of the Transdisciplinary Research Area (TRA) Life & Health at the University of Bonn.

To determine how much the cells had rejuvenated, the researchers examined their molecular clocks, particularly biological markers known as epigenetic clocks. These clocks estimate a cell's biological age by analyzing chemical modifications to DNA that tend to accumulate or change as organisms grow older.

Importantly, these modifications do not alter the DNA sequence itself. Instead, they affect how frequently certain genetic instructions are used (epigenetics). Because these patterns change predictably with age, scientists can use them to estimate how old a cell appears at the molecular level.

The results were striking. After reprogramming, cells taken from an 80-year-old individual displayed molecular age signatures corresponding to someone younger than 20. In other words, the process had reversed more than six decades of cellular aging.
"We also know that this epigenetic rejuvenation ensures that the cells actually behave like young cells," says the scientist.
A Slower Rejuvenation Process Reveals New Clues

Scientists have previously observed that reprogramming cells can reset their biological age. However, earlier demonstrations of this effect involved a more complicated process requiring two distinct stages.

First, researchers would convert an existing cell, such as a blood cell, into a pluripotent stem cell. These versatile cells have nearly unlimited developmental "career paths" because they can give rise to many different cell types throughout the body.
The pluripotent stem cell would then be guided into becoming a neural stem cell, which is more specialized and can produce cells found in the nervous system.
This conventional approach produces rejuvenation relatively quickly, making it difficult to examine all the changes taking place.
The Bonn researchers instead bypassed the pluripotent stage entirely.

"In contrast, we converted blood cells directly into neural stem cells -- that is, without first passing through the pluripotent cell stage," said Brüstle. "In our approach, rejuvenation occurred gradually and could be tracked for over 100 days."

The researchers observed a dramatic reduction in molecular age, with the study highlighting rejuvenation of approximately 60 years after 50 days. Because the process continued over a much longer period, scientists could examine the biological changes as they unfolded rather than observing only the final result.
What Cellular Rejuvenation Could Mean for Alzheimer's Research
The ability to watch cells gradually become younger could be particularly valuable for scientists trying to understand the mechanisms that control biological aging.
By studying this extended transformation, researchers can investigate which molecular pathways are involved and test whether particular substances can speed up or slow down the rejuvenation process.

"Rejuvenation that extends over such a long period of time is ideal as an experimental model: Since the epigenetic clocks are slowly reset over several weeks, we can use this model to investigate which factors and active substances accelerate or slow down the rejuvenation process."

The findings could be especially relevant to neuroscience, where aging is closely connected to the development of serious neurological conditions. Although the work does not establish a treatment capable of reversing aging in people, it offers a laboratory model for investigating how cells regain youthful characteristics.
This could eventually help scientists better understand the cellular changes associated with conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.
"After all, age is the most important risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's!"

The research involved teams from the University Hospital of Bonn, the University of Bonn, and RWTH Aachen University. Funding was provided by the EU's Horizon 2020 program, the German Research Foundation (DFG), and the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space (BMFRT).

Just 4 minutes a day can dramatically improve strength after 65

- A new Penn State study suggests that just four minutes of daily strength training can significantly improve mobility and physical function in older adults. After 12 weeks, participants showed meaningful gains in balance, leg strength, and their ability to stand up from a chair, all important factors for maintaining independence and reducing fall risk.

A daily strength training routine lasting just four minutes can significantly improve strength, balance, and mobility in older adults, according to new research led by Penn State College of Medicine. The findings suggest that maintaining physical independence with age may require much less exercise than many people assume.

Published in the journal PLOS One, the study found that adults aged 65 and older experienced meaningful improvements in physical performance after only 12 weeks. These gains are especially important because muscle strength and mobility influence the risk of falling, the ability to live independently, and overall health and longevity.

For older adults, being able to move comfortably and perform everyday activities is essential for maintaining quality of life. Simple tasks such as standing up from a chair, climbing stairs, and walking can become more difficult as strength and balance decline.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, unintentional injuries, including those caused by falls, are among the leading causes of death in adults aged 65 and older.

Despite the importance of physical fitness, many older adults believe that meaningful improvements require long, demanding workouts. Christopher Sciamanna, professor of medicine and public health at Penn State College of Medicine and lead author of the study, says the new findings challenge that assumption. Even a brief daily routine can improve important measures of mobility and physical function.

"The human body is designed to improve very quickly," Sciamanna said. "And just a few repetitions of an exercise performed regularly can lead to huge improvements. Exercise is about forward thinking -- think about what you want to be able to do and train for it."
Why Shorter Workouts Could Make Exercise Easier

Strength training, also known as resistance training, involves making muscles work against some form of resistance, such as body weight or elastic bands. Research has shown that it can substantially improve muscle strength within a few months.

However, fewer than one in five older adults meet the recommendation to perform muscle strengthening activities at least twice a week. Common obstacles include discomfort, limited time, and the physical demands of conventional exercise programs.
Another challenge is that planning an effective workout can feel overwhelming, particularly for people who are unfamiliar with exercise.

"Exercise is actually really complicated, because you have to decide how many repetitions, how far, how many sets, how much rest, and how many times per week," said co-author Smita Dandekar, associate professor of pediatrics at Penn State College of Medicine. "It's hard work, so there's huge problems with people wanting to do exercise. If we can make it short, we're part way there."

The researchers had already seen encouraging results from an earlier experiment called FAST (Functional Activity Strength Training)-1. In that smaller study, 24 older adults performed just 30 seconds of push-ups and squats each day. After six months, their ability to perform squats had improved.
Other research has similarly suggested that performing only a few sets of exercises each week can produce strength improvements approaching those achieved with considerably longer workouts.
These findings led Sciamanna and his colleagues to investigate whether an especially brief exercise program could produce measurable improvements in older adults.
Testing a Simple Four-Minute Exercise Routine
For the new study, the Penn State researchers developed a program called FAST-2 to evaluate whether a short daily workout could improve mobility and physical ability in adults older than 65.
The trial included 97 participants whose average age was 74. They were randomly divided into two groups, with one following the exercise program and the other receiving no intervention.

Before the study began, participants reported exercising for an average of only about 18 minutes per week. That was far below the general recommendation of at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity each week, Sciamanna explained.
The FAST-2 routine consisted of four simple movements:
- Push-ups: To strengthen muscles in the upper body.
- Chair stands: Repeatedly standing up from a seated position to work the legs.
- Two-arm rows: Pulling against resistance to strengthen the upper body.
- Stair stepping: Stepping up and down to challenge the legs and support functional mobility.
Each exercise lasted 30 seconds, followed by 30 seconds of rest, bringing the complete routine to four minutes.

Participants received four elastic resistance bands and an adjustable-height stepper, along with written instructions explaining how to perform each movement. The researchers also provided easier variations to accommodate different physical abilities.

For example, participants could perform push-ups against a wall or countertop rather than on the floor. Those who found chair stands challenging could use their hands on their knees for additional support.

As their strength improved, participants were encouraged to make the exercises progressively more difficult. Someone performing modified push-ups might advance to the standard movement, while another participant might increase the height of the stepper.

To evaluate the program, researchers measured how quickly and effectively participants could rise from a chair and how long they could balance on one leg. These assessments were conducted at the beginning, midpoint, and end of the 12-week study.

Such tests are valuable because they reflect movements people rely on throughout the day. Performance on these assessments can also help predict future mobility problems, fall risk, and the potential need for additional care.
Significant Strength and Balance Improvements in Just 12 Weeks
The results showed that the brief exercise program produced significant gains in physical function, even though it involved only 60 seconds of lower body resistance training per session.
Participants demonstrated several measurable improvements:
- 4.2 additional chair stands: An increase in the number of times participants could stand up from a chair within 30 seconds.
- 3.6 more seconds of balance: An improvement in how long participants could remain standing on one leg.
- 2.3 seconds faster: A reduction in the time needed to complete the sit-to-stand assessment.

These changes may seem modest, but they reflect physical abilities that are essential for everyday independence. Stronger legs and better balance can make activities such as getting out of a chair, climbing stairs, and walking easier to perform.
Sciamanna emphasized that these simple physical tests can reveal important information about a person's future health and independence.

"These indicators predict your future ability to go into a nursing home, your future likelihood of falling and of developing difficulty walking," Sciamanna said. "They give you a sense of whether or not you're going to be able to be active in the future."

Although the study measured improvements in physical performance rather than directly testing whether participants experienced fewer falls or avoided nursing home care, the findings suggest that short workouts could help preserve abilities closely tied to independent living.
A Workout Older Adults Can Actually Stick With
Beyond the improvements in strength and mobility, the researchers identified another major advantage of the four-minute routine: participants were able to follow it consistently.
Throughout the study, they completed their exercises on 81% of days.

That level of participation suggests that a short, straightforward workout may be easier to incorporate into daily life than a longer exercise program. It could also help people overcome obstacles such as limited time, discomfort, or difficulty maintaining a regular fitness routine.
For older adults who are largely inactive, even a small amount of consistent resistance training could therefore provide a practical starting point for improving physical function.

The researchers say their results reinforce the idea that exercise sessions do not need to be lengthy to produce meaningful benefits. By focusing on movements that support everyday activities, a few minutes of daily effort may help older adults maintain strength, mobility, and independence.

For Sciamanna, the ultimate purpose of exercise extends beyond simply becoming physically stronger. It is about preserving the ability to participate in life and continue doing the things that matter most.

"Exercise is the key to freedom," he said. "Freedom is the ability to be able to do what you want to do, and I would say that if you can't do what you want to do, you're not free. I approach exercise by thinking of what I want to be able to do in 20 years, and then I train to do that."

The fossil record shows that our Homo erectus ancestors were the first hominins to show signs of adapting to life on the ground, with longer legs and shorter arms emerging (the name translates to 'upright human').

It's therefore important that anthropologists can date the species correctly – and a new fossil analysis from an international team of researchers, published in the Annals of Human Biology, pushes back the emergence of these proto-people by about 200,000 years.

Imagine archaeologists of the distant future digging up the first iPhone and finding it wasn't invented in 2007, as previously assumed, but appeared in the time of Neanderthals and woolly mammoths. That's the sort of timescale we're talking about.

The discovery comes from the Drimolen Main Quarry near Johannesburg in South Africa, a hugely significant site for early humans known as the 'Cradle of Humankind'. What's more, the study includes additional findings for a more distant ancient human relative.

"This paper publishes a new adult fossil attributed to Homo erectus, DNH 127, providing further confirmation that this species first appeared in southern Africa 2 million years ago," says archaeologist Jesse Martin, from La Trobe University in Australia.
The adjusted timeline isn't completely new, because a skull fragment designated as DNH 134 had already been dated to the same period.
However, DNH 134 belonged to a young child, making comparisons with adults tricky.

A total of 18 fossils were analyzed in this latest research, with the physical characteristics of the bones used to identify each species, and geological techniques, including radioactive dating, used to determine the age of the fossils.

Besides the single DNH 127 fossil for H. erectus, the team also linked 14 fossils to another hominin, Paranthropus robustus. This ancient relative is farther from us than H. erectus on the family tree, and had heavy jaws and big teeth for processing food that was hard and tough.
At the same time as H. erectus was evolving larger brains and smaller teeth, the teeth of P. robustus were getting bigger, and their chewing muscles were getting stronger (shown by jaw shapes).
Ultimately, it would be the H. erectus lineage that survived.
"These two human species shared the same landscape and are both preserved in the Drimolen cave," says Martin.
"While we know that Homo erectus and the lineage leading to us was ultimately the successful one, 2 million years ago P. robustus outnumbered Homo erectus at Drimolen by more than 10 to one."

The P. robustus discoveries back up the idea that the species was evolving over time. Other fossils from the same species found in other locations suggested larger, stronger hominins, a sign of the species changing.
Overall, the new P. robustus fossils revealed some characteristics in jaw structure that hadn't been seen before, and several areas of variation.
"The large number of fossils from Drimolen, some of which are published in this paper, allow an unprecedented insight into the micro-evolutionary changes that shaped human ancestors," says Martin.

We already knew ancient human ancestry was complicated, with multiple species overlapping in different places rather than following along one after another. This latest study adds some clarity for two species in the Drimolen region.

It's worth bearing in mind that the fossils here are relatively small fragments, and further investigation will be required to confirm the presence of H. erectus and P. robustus this far back in time. The good news is there are a lot of discovered fossils to study at this site, and most likely more to be dug up.
There may well be more to find here to help understand why the P. robustus evolutionary line eventually died out, and ultimately, H. erectus likely led to modern-day humans.
"During this time period it was our [H. erectus] ancestors that looked like the outside long-odds chance to survive," says Martin.
The research has been published in The Annals of Human Biology.

Data centers need water to stay cool and functional, and lots of it: The larger facilities can consume as much water a day as a town of 50,000 people, and because much of the cooling involves evaporation, freshwater is often preferred.

That raises serious questions about the environmental impact of the cloud compute we use to run AI queries, host photos and videos, stream music, and all the rest. Researchers are trying to get a handle on what the impacts on water usage actually are.

In a new study published in Environmental Science & Technology, researchers led by a team from the Carnegie Institution for Science in the US mapped the location of the 9,347 currently identified data centers worldwide.

When the local water conditions of all these sites were analyzed, the team found that around 25 percent of data centers are in areas where there's a water gap during at least one month of the year – that's when water demand outstrips supply.

Based on climate models and 3 °C (5.4 °F) of average global temperature rise from 1900 levels, the number of water-stressed data center locations would rise to 33 percent within as little as 10 years, the researchers found.

"These facilities are not landing in empty landscapes," says environmental scientist Lorenzo Rosa, from the Carnegie Institution for Science. "They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms."

While electricity can be spread across long distances through a power grid, the same can't be said for water. It typically needs to be sourced locally, which means the local conditions at sites chosen for data centers really do matter.
Water typically gets pulled from lakes, rivers, and aquifers – which can all vary seasonally in terms of the water they supply.

"The energy footprint of data centers has been quantified in detail because electricity is metered and reported," says Rosa. "Water scarcity is measured locally, inconsistently, and often not at all."
"So, we built the map because it did not exist."

The map showed that 41 percent of global data centers are competing directly with cities and municipalities for their water, while for another 28 percent of sites the primary water use is for agriculture.
For 523 facilities – that's a little over 5 percent of the total – there are already water gaps for at least 9 months of the year.

There were differences in terms of climate change impact too. Most data centers pushed beyond the water gap threshold by temperature rises would be in the US, the modeling showed, while in countries such as the UK and Germany there wouldn't be much change.
"Data centers typically have the financial capacity and institutional priority to secure water supplies whenever water is available," write the researchers in their published paper.
"As a result, the primary risk may not be to data center operations themselves but to other water users within the same basins."

The researchers note that information on data center water usage remains limited – the giant tech companies involved are reticent to share the exact level of demand these facilities are putting on our natural resources.
More accountable reporting would definitely help, which might require intervention from regulators and governments.

There is some positivity from the researchers at the end of their paper, though, pointing to efforts to use wastewater and treated seawater in place of freshwater, as well as improvements in data center heat management. What's clear is that changes are needed before the data center water drain gets worse.

"The extent to which water-stress exposure translates into operational impacts for data centers themselves or into measurable consequences for other water users remains an open question to address," write the researchers.
"Ensuring data center long-term viability will require siting and governance choices that account for local hydrological limits."
The research has been published in Environmental Science & Technology.

The minute Gabriela Farfan stepped into a small natural history museum in Madison, Wis., where she grew up, she knew she wanted to work with minerals. Farfan remembers seeing all different shapes and colors and being enthralled. “From that point forward, I knew I wanted to become a geologist someday,” she says.

Farfan is now living her teenage dream as the curator of gems and minerals at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C. Her specialty is biomineralization — how organisms build skeletons, corals, pearls and shells. Farfan hopes to answer questions about how they form and what stories they tell by studying crystal structures and the chemistry of minerals.

These days, she investigates signals trapped within minerals. Corals, for example, build layers of calcium carbonate mineral over time, trapping chemical signatures from the ocean. The data tell all kinds of stories — about stress, disease outbreaks and changes to ocean temperature and sea level. Farfan unlocks those tales using X-ray and Raman spectroscopies, bouncing beams off samples to see what they can tell us.

She hopes museum visitors will remember that the sparkly gemstones, the ones that first enamored her, are just as natural as the plants and bones in other exhibits. “Minerals are actual natural history objects,” Farfan says. “Those are actually formed by Mother Nature and it’s spectacular.”

The interim head of the National Science Foundation (NSF), Brian Stone, is set to retire as soon as the end of this year, according to reports. There is no clear plan for a successor to steer the agency because President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the NSF, James O'Neill, has yet to have a confirmation hearing in the Senate.

Stone, who has led the agency since the spring of last year, will resign effective December 31, according to a memo that was sent to NSF staff on Tuesday and was obtained by journalist Dan Garisto. In the note, Stone reportedly wrote that he would be “working closely with the White House to identify who will perform the duties of the NSF Director as of January 1, 2027, should Mr. O’Neill’s nomination still be pending at that time.”
In a statement to Scientific American, NSF spokesperson Mike England appeared to confirm Stone’s upcoming retirement but did not confirm whether he would be leaving at the end of 2026.

Stone had “served the U.S. National Science Foundation and the American people with distinction for 26 years, including over the past 18 months while performing the duties of NSF Director,” England said in the statement. “His leadership has been instrumental in advancing NSF's mission, and we thank him for his decades of dedicated public service. Brian will continue to perform the duties of the Director until his retirement and NSF will announce any future leadership updates as they are available.”
The reported memo also indicated that acting NSF chief of staff Rebecca Keiser will depart as well. England did not confirm or deny this reporting.

Stone has led the NSF on an interim basis since April 2025, after the resignation of the agency’s previous director, Sethuraman Panchanathan, who was appointed during the first Trump presidency in 2019. Panchanathan’s departure came amid Elon Musk’s U.S. DOGE Service cuts, which saw mass staff firings, resignations and axes to grant funding. A staff member of the NSF for more than 25 years, Stone had previously spent 10 years as the agency’s chief of staff.

Stone’s imminent departure comes at a moment of turbulence at the top of the NSF. This past April the Trump administration fired all 22 members of the agency’s science advisory board—these positions are appointed by the president and serve staggered six-year terms. The advisers play a critical role in determining how the NSF disperses the roughly $9 billion in funding it doles out annually. The firings were widely criticized by the scientific community, with thousands of researchers signing an open letter that said it constituted an “alarming attack” on U.S. science. No new board members have since been named .
