A cyclone in the Philippine Sea reached wind speeds of about 185 miles per hour (around 290 kilometers per hour) on Tuesday afternoon EST. Those wind speeds are the strongest of any storm this year, forecasters say.

As of Wednesday morning EST, Super Typhoon Champi had winds of 175 miles per hour; it is expected to weaken in the next day or so, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The storm is currently about 430 nautical miles south of Kadena Air Base in Japan and is heading northwest, according to the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.

You’re more likely to see strong storms in the western Pacific than anywhere else on the planet. But the typhoon underscores how tumultuous Pacific storm activity has been in comparison with activity in the Atlantic. In the North Atlantic, 2026’s strongest storm so far was Hurricane Isaias, which had maximum winds of about 120 mph (193 kph), according to Colorado State University’s (CSU’s) cyclone database. By contrast, in the northeastern Pacific, September’s Hurricane Polo hit wind speeds of about 178 mph (286 kph), while in the northwestern Pacific, April’s Typhoon Sinlaku and July’s Typhoon Bavi also reached around the same strength. Champi is the 25th northwestern Pacific storm this year, according to CSU’s tracker.

To be considered a typhoon or a hurricane, a cyclone must achieve wind speeds of at least 74 mph (119 kph). The designation of hurricane or typhoon depends on where the cyclone occurs. In the Northern Hemisphere, Pacific cyclones that occur west of the international date line are considered typhoons, while those occurring east of that border are categorized as hurricanes.

It’s been a historic year for cyclones. As Scientific American previously reported, the Atlantic has been unusually quiet: Hurricane Isaias was the first storm of its kind for the season, setting a record for the latest-forming first Atlantic hurricane since reliable record-keeping began. Meanwhile the Hawaiian Islands in the Pacific Ocean have seen an unusually high number of hurricanes this season.

Those trends are driven in part by El Niño, a climate pattern that influences weather across the globe. During El Niño years, hurricanes activity tends to slow in the Atlantic and pick up in parts of the Pacific.
The biggest “land rush” of the 21st century is underway—but not on Earth.

Together with multiple international partners, the U.S. and China are racing each other to build crewed outposts around the moon’s south pole, a region rich with water ice and other resources that could be used to kick-start an otherworldly economy and strengthen humanity’s expansion deeper into space. NASA’s Artemis IV mission seeks to send astronauts to the lunar south pole in 2028, and China is targeting human landings there by 2030.

But the clamor to capitalize on that prized patch of lunar real estate shouldn’t overlook other areas on the moon that could be even more valuable for science, according to an authoritative new report. Convened by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, a blue-ribbon panel of experts contends that human sorties to nonpolar regions of the moon hold great promise for resolving long-standing mysteries about Earth’s nearest celestial neighbor, the solar system and the universe at large.
Better yet, the report offers a short list of destinations to prioritize.

The NASA-sponsored report comes from the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) Committee on Key Nonpolar Destinations across the Moon, and it flags four places to send future human missions: Bhabha Crater, Mons Hadley, the Orientale Basin and the Aristarchus Plateau.

“Returning to the moon will be a great achievement for humanity—and setting foot where we never have before will be a major moment for science,” says James Day, co-chair of the committee and a professor at the University of California, San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

Visiting these four sites would add immense scientific value to whatever will be learned from any sequence of U.S. and Chinese crewed missions to the lunar south pole, adds committee co-chair Daniel Dumbacher, a professor of engineering practice in the School of Aeronautics and Astronautics at Purdue University.
Dumbacher and Day both discussed their findings in-depth during a webinar shortly after the report’s release.

Bhabha Crater, the report notes, is on the lunar farside and would give astronaut expeditions the ability to access material from the moon’s oldest known preserved impact basin and to deploy ultrasensitive radio and optical astronomy experiments shielded from Earth’s noisy emissions.

The Mons Hadley region, part of which was previously explored by Apollo 15 moonwalkers, is a prime location for a space weather observatory. This site, the report says, could also host experiments to assess how piled-up regolith—impact-pulverized rocks that make up the lunar “soil”—could shield against radiation hazards.

The moon’s Orientale Basin is one of the largest and best-preserved multiringed impact crater in the solar system; going there would give unprecedented looks into the deep structure and origin of our natural satellite. Mission crews, the report adds, should return samples from the basin to Earth to reveal exactly how the basin was formed; while they’re there, they could also deploy a gravitational-wave observatory.

Lastly, the moon’s Aristarchus Plateau is a geologically rich volcanic landscape. Collecting samples there would help researchers understand volcanic processes that have shaped the moon and identify potentially important resources that could support future exploration.

The NAS panel also notes that the moon’s accessibility and sterility make it “an excellent testbed” for refining “planetary protection” procedures—that is, for finding ways to avoid Earth life contaminating other potentially habitable places in the solar system (and ensuring any alien biology doesn’t catastrophically contaminate Earth). Crewed dry runs at lunar test beds could help establish the rules of the road before sending humans to more biologically sensitive environments.

“Practicing planetary protection protocols on the moon will lead to greater confidence in the successful execution of these on other planetary bodies, such as Mars, where life may exist or may once have existed and the stakes are significantly higher,” the report states.

Adding a whole swath of extra proposed crewed lunar landing sites in addition to already planned human forays to the moon’s south pole may seem like overkill, says committee member Clive Neal, a professor of civil and environmental engineering and Earth Sciences at the University of Notre Dame. But the exercise is meant “to be enabling for Artemis and not a distraction.”

“There are four examples given for different missions, but it comes back and feeds into [NASA’s] developing moon base,” he says. One overlooked concept that the report seeks to highlight, Neal adds, is “the idea of a ‘distributed’ moon base”—a network of interlinked sites that can be more than the sum of their parts, providing far more value overall than any solitary outpost.

That’s because the moon probably has much more to offer than just the resources at its shadowy south pole—and figuring out the specifics is a long-term project with far-reaching implications. “There’s both science that enables exploration as well as exploration-driven science that enables a long-term human presence on the moon,” Neal says. “Achieving a permanent human presence on the moon is akin to now having a permanent human presence in low-Earth orbit,” he adds, and the lessons learned will feed forward for future crewed voyages to Mars.
A “History Book” for the Entire Universe

Jack Burns, a professor emeritus of astrophysics at the University of Colorado Boulder, is delighted by the report’s recommendations. He briefed the specially convened panel regarding a proposed array of low-frequency radio telescopes on the lunar farside.

Called FarView, this facility makes use of the moon’s radio-quiet environment to open the last unexplored electromagnetic window for astrophysics, delivering breakthrough science across astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, heliophysics and planetary science, he tells Scientific American.

“Astronauts could play a crucial role in the early stages of that array, helping in site surveys, as well as setting up power stations and communications and the basic electronics to get started,” Burns says. The primary science driver for FarView, he adds, is the exploration of the cosmic dark ages, a mysterious era shortly after the big bang and before the formation of the first stars.
As for astronauts conducting such duties versus robots, “the modern way of looking at it is not either; it’s both,” Burns observes.

The NAS report underscores the need to explore the whole moon, not just its south pole, he adds. “The moon is our history book. With Apollo, we just thumbed through the first few pages. But there’s much more to delve into, as the moon is a unique learning tool, not only to understand that body but also to help unwrap the history of our Earth.”

Erica Jawin, a research scientist at the Planetary Science Institute, who was not part of the NAS panel, agrees. Answering questions such as why the moon’s nearside looks so different from its farside, when the giant lunar impact basins formed, and how much water and other “volatile” materials may lurk in the lunar interior would help reveal otherwise-hidden chapters of our planet’s and our solar system’s deepest history.

“These questions, among many others, can be addressed by exploring nonpolar locations,” Jawin says. “The scientific community has repeatedly discussed locations of high scientific value for surface exploration.” The Aristarchus Plateau has been of particular interest.

“The Aristarchus Plateau has been consistently recognized for its scientific value in the form of diverse volcanism and the young, bright Aristarchus Crater, as well as its exploration potential for everything from resource prospecting for water to manufacturing building materials using the thick pyroclastic deposit,” Jawin says.

A robust and successful lunar exploration program, Jawin continues, should leverage the unique role humans can play in conjunction with robotic assets. In particular, it is critical to understand specific locations where scientific exploration would benefit from having a human-crewed component, she said.

“Humans have unique skills for exploration and observation that differ from robotic surface or orbital assets. Particularly, humans excel in visual analyses such as assessing geologic setting and diversity across a landing site, as well as in complex decision-making and confronting unexpected obstacles,” Jawin notes.

With proper investment into scientific and technological capabilities, Jawin concludes, “the coming years could be a renaissance for human exploration of the moon, allowing us to answer scientific questions that have persisted for decades.”
Oil prices climbed Thursday on worries over a possible escalation in the Middle East conflict as the U.S. reportedly plans to resume strikes against Iran.
Brent crude futures rose 1.71% to $110.67 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude gained 1.42% to $98.53.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, The New York Times reported, citing unnamed U.S. officials. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.
The U.S. has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets, after reports said that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave.

The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.
"$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs.

He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs.
"I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.
The U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate.

The move comes as the U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, according to The New York Times, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.
The developments point to a possible widening of the nearly eight-month war, while U.S. and Iranian negotiators continue talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets. Meanwhile, Reuters reported Washington also plans to withdraw family members from other missions in the region.

A strike Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least one person and injured eight. Two people died in a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field, the Saudi Press Agency reported, adding that operations were not affected.

In recent days, the U.S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up military exercises, including flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers, according to The New York Times. The Times also reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel this week to discuss potential new strikes.

The renewed military strikes would likely target Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal, according to The Times, noting that President Donald Trump has yet to approve the fresh strikes and has repeatedly vetoed plans for a return to major combat this year.
Iranian officials have vowed to widen their attacks to target data centers and undersea internet cables, while refusing concessions on their nuclear program.
Despite the persistent shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Middle East oil flows through the vital strait have recovered to near pre‑war levels according to Kpler.
As Brent crude topped $110 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate gained 1% to $98.12, recovering appetite for crude from China could drive oil prices higher, according to the commodity research firm.

"China's crude import demand is expected to continue recovering, driven by rising refinery throughput and rapidly declining crude inventories," said Muyu Xu, senior crude oil analyst at Kpler. The war has cut China's oil stockpiles, with the fastest drawndown on record at 1.6 million barrels a day in September, Xu estimated.

China still holds 1.1 billion barrels in reserves, about 80 days of refinery needs, Xu said. She added that with virtually all Iranian cargoes outside the U.S. blockade discharged, substantial new crude arrivals in China appear unlikely.

Chinese state-owned refiners are likely to have a stronger appetite and greater urgency to secure prompt Middle Eastern barrels as they face higher throughput and inventory-replenishment needs. Independent refiners are also seeking alternatives to Iranian crude, a shift that could limit further downside in the Dubai structure, Xu said.
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.

The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.

Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.

"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.

Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.

The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.

Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.

Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.

"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.

Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.
David Krumholtz is sharing why he missed the 10 Things I Hate About You reunion during Julia Stiles‘ tribute to Heath Ledger on Dancing With the Stars Tuesday night.
In a video posted on Instagram Wednesday, the actor explained that he’s currently in the Catskill Mountains in upstate New York filming a movie.

“I could not be in L.A. for Dancing With the Stars last night. I would have loved loved loved to have been there,” he said. “Everyone looked so amazing. Julia’s tribute to my dear friend, who I miss every single day, was amazing and stunning, and I’m so proud of her.”

“I thought the cast looked amazing. They all look so young still,” Krumholtz added before taking off his hat to show his newly bald head. He quipped that “it would have been weird” to join his former co-stars in the ballroom after shaving “what’s left of my hair” because it would have become “internet fodder.”
“I didn’t want that, but that’s not why I wasn’t there. I would have dealt with it. Anyway, love them all, love you all,” he concluded.

During the latest DWTS episode, Stiles and her pro partner Ezra Sosa dedicated their dance to Ledger, who starred opposite Stiles in the beloved 1999 rom-com. He died in 2008 at the age of 28 from an accidental overdose.

The pair danced to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You” by Frankie Valli, which was the song Ledger’s Patrick Verona serenaded Stiles’ Kat Stratford with during her soccer practice at the high school stadium. In the scene, he runs and dances across the stands as the marching band plays to try and win her over after Joey Donner (Andrew Keegan) pays him to take Kat out.

Following Stiles and Sosa’s emotional dance, which featured some of Ledger’s iconic moves, the poem her character reads in the film about Patrick starts playing in the ballroom. After the actress lays a flower on the ground in honor of Ledger, she is joined by her fellow 10 Things I Hate About You co-stars, including Keegan, Joseph Gordon-Levitt (Cameron James), Larisa Oleynik (Bianca Stratford), Gabrielle Union (Chastity) and Susan May Pratt (Mandella).

10 Things I Hate About You, directed by Gil Junger, follows teen Joey who wants to date Bianca, but she can’t date until her antisocial older sister, Kat, has a boyfriend, per her strict father’s rules. That’s when Joey pays a mysterious boy, Patrick, to ask Kat out. In the film, Krumholtz played Michael Eckman, a friend of new student Cameron who also has a crush on Bianca.

MELBOURNE, Australia — Live Nation’s Australian portfolio of live music venues continues to grow with the addition of a new 5,000-capacity space in North Melbourne.

The concerts giant will deliver and operate the purpose-built venue at Arden Central, a major multi-billion-dollar, government-backed urban renewal and innovation precinct, about one mile from the city’s CBD.

Once completed, the site is expected to host more than 100 events each year, creating “new performance opportunities for Australian artists and local talent, attract international touring acts and give fans another place to experience live music,” reads a statement from LN.
Announced Thursday, Oct. 22, the venue is part of the first stage of Arden Central, a cultural and parkland neighborhood being developed by Hamton and Hostplus and serviced by train.

“Melbourne is one of the world’s great live music cities, and continued investment in venues is essential to attracting international artists and keeping Melbourne relevant in an increasingly competitive global environment,” comments Alex Klos, president, Australia & New Zealand at Live Nation. “This purpose-built venue will add a significant new stage to Melbourne’s live music ecosystem, while helping establish Arden Central as a vibrant new destination for live entertainment.”
The wider precinct, budgeted at A$7 billion, should provide more than 5,400 homes for over 10,000 people, alongside retail, hospitality, community facilities and 5.5 hectares of open space.

There, LN joins new precinct partners Melbourne Victory Football Club and the University of Melbourne, plus the North Melbourne Football Club, the four-time VFL/AFL premiers which has called Arden Street home for more than 125 years.

With a 5,000-capacity, LN’s newest venue is one of its biggest in these parts. Currently, the live entertainment juggernaut operates The Palais Theatre (2,900 capacity) and Festival Hall in Melbourne, Fortitude Music Hall (3,000) and The Triffid (800) in Brisbane, Hindley Street Music Hall in Adelaide (1,800), Anita’s Theatre in Wollongong (1,200), and the Northbridge Music Hall in Perth, which is expected to open to the public in the summer of 2026-27. LN also operates the 13,000-capacity Spark Arena in Auckland, New Zealand.

“This venue is being designed around the live experience, creating an intimate connection between artists and fans while delivering everything expected of a best-in-class touring venue,” comments Guy Ngata, senior VP, venue development at Live Nation, on the announcement of the North Melbourne project.
A range of premium experiences, artist amenities and efficient production access “have been embedded into the venue’s design,” he continues.
An opening date has yet to be floated for the new venue, which is designed by Blueprint Studio, LN’s in-house design and development group, in collaboration with Populous.

John Anderson, the Country Music Hall of Fame inductee with a distinctive voice and a weighty songbook that included “Swingin’,” “Straight Tequila Night,” and “Seminole Wind,” died today (Oct. 21) at the age of 71.
“It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend,” reads a statement from his family.

Anderson, who attended the Country Music Hall of Fame induction ceremony to herald this year’s honorees on Sunday (Oct. 18), died peacefully in his sleep, reads the statement from his family, roughly seven weeks before his 72nd birthday. “His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever. Please keep our family in your thoughts and prayers as we grieve this unimaginable loss.”

“To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special. We are completely heartbroken.”

His fellow country artists were remembering him as a singular talent. “There is too much for me to say about John Anderson in just a statement,” posted Blake Shelton on X. “I am sick and I am stunned. But I am a very lucky man. I got the opportunity to find out that my hero wasn’t just the guy I hoped he’d be. He was so much more than that. John was my friend.”
John Rich called Anderson “my favorite country artist of all time…He was a massive influence on me in more ways that I can count. I love you, Uncle John.”
A native of Apopka, Fla., Anderson relocated to Nashville in 1971. An early job saw him nailing shingles onto the roof of the Grand Ole Opry House ahead of that iconic building’s 1974 opening.

“I was just wanting to play and sing pretty much at any level that I could,” he told Billboard in 2024. “Thankfully, I was blessed that one little job led to another one, and most of the time it was kind of a little upgrade.”

That upgrade came when he signed with Warner Bros. Records and went about constructing a lofty career in music with such works as “I’m Just an Old Chunk of Coal (But I’m Gonna Be a Diamond Someday),” “Wild and Blue,” “I Just Came Home to Count the Memories,” “1959,” “Black Sheep,” and his signature song “Swingin’, which would scoop both the CMA Horizon Award and single of the year in 1983.

Anderson’s hot start cooled for a time, but his career took off once again when he signed with BNA in 1991 and landed a comeback hit with the Country Airplay chart-topping “Straight Tequila Night,” housed on his album Seminole Wind.

A neo-traditional pioneer, Anderson was both a critical and commercial success. He landed five No. 1s, among 20 top 10s, on Billboard‘s Hot Country Songs chart, with those top 10s spanning 1981-95. On Top Country Albums, he notched five top 10s, from the years 1982-92. Respect came from his peers, too, with Academy of Country Music’s career achievement award in 1993, induction into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2014, and entry into the Country Music Hall of Fame a decade later, in 2024.

Anderson battled health issues in recent years, but pushed through the pain. “Through all of 2017 and all the way up until May of 2018, I had spent most of my time in the hospital and had been very, very ill,” he told Billboard in 2020. “I had almost 100% hearing loss. I did OK being sick, but when I lost my hearing and couldn’t play and sing, that really almost put an end to me. I just started praying and praying harder than I’ve ever prayed in my life and you know what? My hearing started coming back.”

During one procedure, he says he almost died on the operating room table. Anderson, however, was a hard man to stop. During the peak of the pandemic, he released an album of new material, Years, produced by The Black Keys’ Dan Auerbach and David “Fergie” Ferguson.

“John Anderson was a one-of-a-kind song stylist who proved that fresh innovations were best born from time-honored traditions,” recounts Kyle Young, CEO of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum. “Whether he borrowed inspiration from Lefty Frizzell’s vocal bends or the Florida swamp land, he brought dynamic distinction and creative soul to a world that needed to hear his voice. In 1981, John famously gave life to Billy Joe Shaver’s lyric, ‘I’m just an old chunk of coal, but I’ll be a diamond someday.’ He was already a diamond then, and a diamond he always will be.”

Colombian Nobel Prize in Literature winner Gabriel García Márquez considered himself more of a writer than a singer, says Rubén Blades. But the legendary Panamanian singer/songwriter sees himself more as a “journalist” who “tries to be as objective as possible within the subjectivity of creating a song.”

“What I wrote was honest and I still feel that way,” Blades said on Wednesday (Oct. 21) during the Icon Q&A With Rubén Blades panel, moderated by Billboard‘s co-chief content officer Leila Cobo at Billboard Latin Music Week.

Entire generations across Latin America and the U.S. have grown up listening to Blades, one of salsa’s most influential voices, who helped redefine the genre with a unique combination of musical innovation and powerful storytelling. A central figure in New York City’s salsa revolution of the 70s, Blades expanded the horizons of classic Afro-Cuban salsa by incorporating influences from rock, jazz, Pan-Latin music and sounds from various parts of the world.

“Music offers many varieties; not everything has to be political or critical — it’s also for having fun and dancing,” he noted. “My contribution was believing that music didn’t necessarily have to talk about the same themes — betrayal by a woman or a friend — but could go beyond that.”

This is how his songs have stood out, not only for their unforgettable melodies but also for their socially conscious lyrics and memorable characters. He turned stories of everyday life into timeless music, with classics such as “Pedro Navaja,” “Decisiones” and “El Padre Antonio y Su Monaguillo Andrés.”

At 78, Blades remains very active in music, touring across the region and working on various acting projects. These include his recent appearance in the movie Campeón Gabacho by Mexican filmmaker Jonás Cuarón and his upcoming role in Porto Rico, the first fiction feature film directed by René Pérez (Residente), which also marks Latin music superstar Bad Bunny’s debut as a lead actor.

“What [Residente] is doing is extremely interesting,” Blades said without revealing details about his role in the film. “We both share the same curiosity — I learn from him, he learns from Bad Bunny, and from Viggo Mortensen too. We’re learning from everyone, and René is learning from them now.”

During the talk, Blades also reminisced about the last time he spoke with his former collaborator Willie Colón, who passed away on February 21, 2023. The two had a long-standing dispute over the Siembra 25 Años concert (2003) and the master rights related to it. Blades shared that the last time they met was in 2023 at the wake of musician Jorge “Georgie” González.

“It was a cordial meeting,” recalled Blades, who is also a lawyer and Panama’s former Minister of Tourism. “The last photos we took together were that afternoon. My respect and recognition for him will never disappear.”

This Thursday (Oct. 22), Blades will be honored with the Billboard Icon Award at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards, which will be broadcast live on Telemundo from Miami. The award recognizes an artist whose career has not only remained relevant over time but has also established them as one of the most distinguished artists in their genre, celebrated worldwide for achieving both musical and commercial success.

Blades, whose career spans more than five decades, said he still feels energized to continue touring — even performing five-and-a-half-hour shows, as he did during a concert in Puerto Rico. “I think the only surprise is that I don’t know how to drive,” he confessed, adding that it’s not something he plans to learn at this stage of his life.

The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.

Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.

But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.

AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.

“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.

Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
The PHP Foundation did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.

Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.

“The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons,” Moses wrote. “In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.”

Waste tyre treatment operators face an April 2027 permitting deadline, subject to parliamentary approval

The Environment Agency of England and Wales (EA) has published detailed plans to significantly alter the waste management landscape, including a relatively short phasing out period for the T8 exemption for mechanically treating end-of-life tyres (ELTs). The withdrawal of the exemption will require operators to transition to full environmental permits. The withdrawal of the T8 exemption represents a hard-won victory for the UK’s Tyre Recovery Association and its members, who have campaigned for around a decade for the exemption’s removal. The EA discussed this impending regulatory change at the TRA’s Briefing Day 2026 in August.

According to the guidance, which was updated on 21 October 2026, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) and the EA have outlined a strict timeline for the upcoming regulatory changes, which are subject to parliamentary approval expected before 17 December 2026:
- 6 January 2027: The new waste exemption rules officially come into force.

- 6 April 2027: The three-month transition period for the T8 exemption expires. From this date, the T8 exemption will be officially withdrawn, and operators can no longer rely on it to carry out mechanical treatment of end-of-life tyres unless formal steps have been taken.
Conditions and requirements for operators
To successfully navigate the transition away from the T8 exemption and continue business legally, tyre treatment facilities must meet specific conditions set out by the Environment Agency:
Mandatory Permit Application: Operators currently utilizing the T8 exemption must apply for a waste environmental permit before the 6 April 2027 deadline.

Interim Continuity: Businesses are permitted to continue their current operations under the existing exemption while their formal permit application is actively being processed by the Environment Agency, provided the application is submitted before the April deadline.

Cease Operations if Non-Compliant: If an operator cannot or chooses not to apply for a full environmental permit by 6 April 2027, they are legally required to completely cease all mechanical end-of-life tyre treatment activities previously covered by the T8 exemption.

Site-Specific Rules & Multi-Exemption Limits: Operators must also review whether they hold multiple exemptions at the same site. Under the broader reforms, from 6 July 2027, combined storage limits across multiple exemptions will be capped at the lowest limit among them. Furthermore, if the site has a “technical connection” to an existing permitted facility that increases overall environmental risk, businesses may need to integrate their operations into a single permit structure.

Industry stakeholders are urged to review their current registrations on the public register immediately and liaise with the Environment Agency to ensure timely permit applications before the April cut-off.
For full details of the planned waste exemption transition, refer to the EA’s Guidance page.

Long before satellite navigation and GPS, explorers were already setting their sights toward space. Since we first saw the night sky, humanity has been fascinated by the stars. Over thousands of years, astronomers have tracked the positions of stars and other objects (such as planets, which were described as planetes, or wanderers, by the ancient Greeks). They used the stars to tell stories, make predictions, and even find their way. All of which depended on having an accurate map, mental or otherwise, of the heavens above.

This stunning map by Florian Winkler catalogs the stars of the night sky in the Northern Hemisphere. It’s built using information from Stellarium, the HYG Database, and W. H. Finlay’s Concise Catalog of Deep-sky Objects.

The map shows the accurate position and brightness of stars, Messier objects (such as nebulae or spiral galaxies), and constellations. Winkler’s meticulous symbology differentiates stars by their brightness and variability. Labels identify stars and constellations, as well as their Bayer designation.

In the center of the map, you’ll find Polaris, or the North Star. The map’s stereographic projection reflects what you would see if you were to stand at the North Pole and look skyward. Polaris would be directly above you in the center of the sky. The rest of the stars are charted by their celestial coordinates, which function similarly to longitude and latitude. Known as declination and right ascension, the radial grid on the map shows these coordinate lines, reminiscent of meridians and parallels on a terrestrial map. A dashed circle cutting through the center of the map is the ecliptic, which shows the path of the Sun and planets through the sky.

While it’s easy to get lost in the details of the map, it never overwhelms. The map evokes the feeling of gazing at the infinite night sky. Yet it includes enough context to orient yourself and feel like a seasoned astronomer. Winkler’s work blends millennia of celestial knowledge with modern cartographic techniques to create a dazzling map that parallels the wonder of the stars themselves.

During Meta’s earnings call on Wednesday, the company revealed its board had approved a new class of non-voting stock, called Class C common stock. The shares give the holder an ownership stake but no vote on company decisions. This class takes effect in January. Meta says it will use the stock for capital raising, employee pay, and acquisitions — including its expensive push into AI — while maintaining the current voting structure that favors its founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, who controls around 60% of the vote.

Now, however, the New York Times has reported there’s another reason for the new class: helping Zuckerberg pay for California’s proposed “billionaire tax,” if voters approve it. Because the new shares carry no votes, he could sell some of them to cover the tax without giving up voting control.

Proposition 40, which was drafted by Berkeley tax law professors and is being sponsored by California’s largest healthcare union (SEIU United Healthcare Workers West), would level a one-time 5% wealth tax on the net worth of several hundred California billionaires who primarily live in the state. Backers say the policy could generate as much as $100 billion over five years, the bulk of which would be used to pay for the state’s healthcare needs, with the rest for food assistance and education.

The Times also reports that Zuckerberg pressed Meta’s board to come up with a plan to protect him from the tax. According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm. Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes.
The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing made by Meta, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class.

The filing says that as far back as July, Zuckerberg was discussing the billionaire tax with board members. The topic came up again in additional meetings and communications throughout that month and August.

The filing also describes how the plan would work. Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own. The company calls this a one-time stock dividend and says it should work out to a two-for-one stock split. The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says.

That is where Prop 40 comes in. The filing says the dividend “will allow Mr. Zuckerberg to immediately sell or transfer up to 20% of the shares of Class C common stock that he receives in the Dividend, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the Company, for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control.” Because the dividend is one-for-one, half of his post-dividend shares will be Class C, so the 20% cap equals 10% of his total economic stake.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr. Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr. Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.”
It’s been estimated that Zuckerberg would have to pay as much as $11 billion as part of the tax.

Prop 40 has notably riled many of Silicon Valley’s most prominent businesspeople. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it. Other business leaders and critics of the proposal have criticized it online, with many claiming that it amounts to economic suicide for California, driving a capital flight from the state. However, as Meta’s new policy would appear to show, the state’s mega-companies and the people who run them have creative ways of dealing with the tax, should it materialize.

“Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S. Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added.
The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it.

That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?”

Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management, scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability.
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.
There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem.

A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures.
The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture.

That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic.

A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application's latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn't.

The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn't worth the cost.

Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.

Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.

GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.

The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize. Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.

Don't think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn't to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application's business requirements.

For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value.

Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today's leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances.
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy.

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset.

EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable.
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes.
The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale.

Tom Kean Jr. needed to vanish to become interesting. He’d been in public office for 25 years — first as a New Jersey state assemblyman, then a state senator, then a congressman — without making much of an impression. The only federal bill he’d written that became law, signed by President Joe Biden, increased funding for firefighters. It was worthy but not especially noteworthy.

House members of both parties desperately try to attract attention and stand out from their 434 colleagues. Yet Kean, after unseating a Democratic incumbent in 2022, went in the opposite direction: He generally shunned the press and seemed to prefer video town halls to in-person gatherings. If the wider civilian public recognized his name, it was because Kean was the eldest child and namesake of a widely respected former New Jersey governor.

Then, late on the afternoon of March 5, Kean voted “yes” on a bill to fund the Department of Homeland Security, helping end a partial shutdown of the agency in the wake of a string of ICE shootings. After which the congressman went … well, almost no one knew where. For nearly four months.

Kean, 58, attracted more press coverage during his absence than he’d probably accumulated in the previous quarter century. Reporters checked out a Kean family-owned ten-acre estate on Fishers Island in Long Island Sound and another on the Jersey shore that’s registered under the name Rendezvous LLC. They quizzed the neighbors of Kean’s primary residence in Westfield, New Jersey, and noted that the house’s mailbox was full. No signs of the congressman.

Social-media posts and press releases kept flowing, keeping up an eerie appearance that Kean was still on the job, even as most of the staffers preparing these dispatches had no idea where their boss had gone. “They were worried about him and frustrated with the lack of information,” a New Jersey political insider says. About six weeks into the mystery, a post appeared bearing Kean’s signature, saying only that he was addressing “a personal medical issue.”

When Kean did resurface in late June, he took to the House floor in a largely empty chamber. There, he read a five-minute statement disclosing that he had been hospitalized for the treatment of depression. “There is no timeline for healing,” he said. “There is no timeline for recovery. Only the work of getting better one day at a time.”

This explanation for Kean’s absence from Congress generated considerable and justifiable sympathy — mixed with criticism that, unlike other lawmakers who have received treatment for serious depression, Kean kept his whereabouts unknown.

After his D.C. speech, Kean mostly went dark again. Over the past few months, he has launched a kind of political science experiment: Can you win a tough reelection fight in a key House district against a formidable opponent by largely staying out of view?

Carlos Santos is the chairman of the Republican committee in Union County, a crucial population center at the eastern end of Kean’s congressional district. He has nothing but praise to offer. “The congressman delivers for the people of CD 7. For instance, he brought back some tax cuts with SALT,” Santos says, referencing the federal deduction for state and local taxes. Last year, Kean successfully pushed to raise the limit by $30,000, partially restoring the cut made during President Donald Trump’s first term — a decrease that hit hardest in blue states, including California, New York, and New Jersey.

Does it bother Santos that Kean was off the radar for months? “Hey, we’ve elected Democrats that have been dead,” he says. (Well, Pennsylvania has, anyway.) “The congressman has been in our office for door-knocking launches. And I’m going to be with him tonight.”
“Um,” Santos says. “Local events around the county.”

He can’t divulge where Kean will be because the campaign doesn’t publicly release its schedule and many of Kean’s appearances are invitation-only. My interview requests to the campaign and to Kean’s Capitol Hill office went unreturned. It’s a different way to run a campaign, I say. “Yes,” Santos replies, tightly.

Mike DuHaime has been the political director of the Republican National Committee, and he ran Chris Christie’s first winning bid for New Jersey governor. He has known the Kean family for decades. “On the trail, Tom is hearing from people who are sharing personal stories with him and they’re appreciative of him being forthright about his depression,” DuHaime says. “Will that add up to some votes? I don’t know.”

Regardless, Kean is running up against an electoral force stronger than anything related to his personal story: the president’s deep unpopularity. Kean, in his single debate with Democrat Rebecca Bennett, refused to distance himself from Trump on the Iran war or tariffs. “When the president’s numbers are where they are nationally, and even worse in New Jersey, that’s going to make it really difficult for any Republican in this district,” DuHaime says — even in a district where Republicans have a registration edge of about 19,000 voters and even though Kean retains a financial advantage over his opponent. Polls have been sparse, but in mid-October, two of the biggest Republican super-PACs seemed to take a dire view of Kean’s prospects, pulling all ad money from New Jersey and redeploying it in more winnable races. (A Democratic strategist, evaluating both Bennett’s prospects and the wider midterm outlook but determined not to sound overoptimistic, says, “Things are looking less shit.”)

The Trump drag and the strangeness of Kean’s absence aren’t the only factors shaping this race, however. The Democratic primary yielded in Bennett a nominee who is both engaging and a good ideological fit for the general-election audience. She is a classic centrist in the mold of fellow military veterans like New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill, in contrast to some of her party’s more left-leaning candidates. “The Navy pilot thing kind of screams moderate,” DuHaime says. “Nobody thinks communists are going to the Naval Academy.”

When I meet her, Bennett is wearing white sneakers, sensible blue jeans, and a jacket that is — what exactly is that color? She consults with an aide, and they decide on fuchsia. “I spent 15 years wearing a flight suit every day,” she says with a laugh. “When I got out, I didn’t know how to dress. I was looking at regular clothes and saying, ‘Where are all the pockets?’”

She has just finished speaking to a group of about 100 mostly Democratic voters in Califon, New Jersey, a bucolic town set amid rolling hills, horse ranches, and insurance-company office parks. It’s in the western part of a district that borders Staten Island, then fans out toward Pennsylvania. The Seventh Congressional District contains wildly different demographics. On balance, the district is wealthy, highly educated, and predominantly white, but it includes some gritty industrial locales such as Rahway and parts of Linden.

Bennett, 40, grew up in a small town slightly southwest of Fort Worth, Texas, before winning an ROTC scholarship to attend Cornell University. After flying the Navy’s version of a Black Hawk helicopter, including in missions over the Middle East, Bennett moved to New Jersey to take a job in middle management at Johnson & Johnson. When it comes to public disgust, big pharma rivals Trump, so Kean’s ads have been hammering Bennett for the roughly seven years she spent employed in the industry. She claims the experience prepared her to push for patient-friendly legislation should she get to Washington, including for a public-health insurance option.

The fact that Bennett was a registered Republican until 2016 may well help her against Kean, given the district’s swingy history, as may the fact that Trump was the reason she switched parties. In 2016, she says, “I looked at it and realized my values aligned with the Democratic Party.” Ask about whether the party nationally has embraced too many cultural-identity issues and Bennett tacks rapidly back to her pragmatic message. “What I hear every day on the campaign trail when I’m talking with voters is things are not working for them — whether it’s ‘Prices are too high’ or their kids can’t find jobs … We gotta go, we gotta try, we gotta iterate. It’s not about spending the next 20 years talking.”

Bennett’s sense of urgency kicked in two days after Trump beat Kamala Harris: “My whole life, I have just run at whatever the biggest, hardest problem is. I told my husband, ‘I have to run for office now.’” She has proved a fast learner as a first-time candidate, shedding much of her initial stiffness. Bennett weaves in endearing anecdotes about her two young daughters — “The other day, my older one didn’t want to do something and she goes, ‘It is my body, my choice.’ And I was like, ‘That’s great, but you gotta brush your teeth’”— while not hesitating to knock out some teeth. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is “an absolute disgrace.” Her opponent, Kean, is ”a coward.” How? “Why is he continuing to do what Mike Johnson and Trump tell him to do? He’s a rubber stamp. He’s not willing to face voters; he’s not willing to talk to them.”

How to discuss Kean’s treatment for depression while not appearing callous has been tricky. Bennett regularly expresses her hope that the congressman’s recovery is going well before pivoting to how she believes Kean’s absence hurt the district. “He seems like a nice guy,” she says. “But we need someone who is going to show up and represent. I think that he has failed this district. I think he voted to take health care away from tens of thousands of people.”

She’s referring to her opponent’s 2025 vote in favor of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut more than $1 trillion in Medicaid and Obamacare spending. Bennett stops short of spelling out the contrast she’s drawing. In a moment of crisis, Tom Kean Jr. deserved to get health care. But he didn’t need to worry about his insurance coverage.

U.S. Northern Command and multiple research organizations just wrapped up a joint, three-year experiment to test new radar technology that could enable the Northern Warning System to detect incoming threats at longer ranges across Alaska and northern Canada.

The Sept. 7-14 test event marked the conclusion of live-fly testing in the experiment series, which explored how existing radar infrastructure and emerging technology could complement current surveillance capabilities, according to an Oct. 19 release from Alaskan Command, a subordinate command under NORTHCOM. The Arctic air domain awareness experiment series focused on closing surveillance gaps across a region where vast distances, harsh weather and limited infrastructure present challenges for air surveillance.

The Air Force Research Laboratory and Defense Research and Development Canada also participated in the exercise alongside scientific organizations in the region. The Air Force and NORAD have relied on the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77 radar systems to detect and track incoming threats out to 250 miles throughout the region.
The experiment paired an existing high-frequency transmitter, paired with a newly developed, low-cost receiver array, according to the release.

Initial results show the system was “successfully able to achieve full skywave (beyond line of sight) detections” of an E-3 Sentry from the 962nd Airborne Air Control Squadron, HC-130J Combat King IIs from the 211th Rescue Squadron, and KC-135 Stratotankers from the 168th Air Refueling Wing—aircraft that served as cooperative targets, providing known positions against which researchers could compare the experimental data, the release states.

Researchers used the University of Alaska Fairbanks’ High Frequency Active Auroral Research Program, or HAARP, facility and a receiver array in Cold Bay developed by MITRE to collect data on participating aircraft over the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea.

The effort supported a broader focus of Alaskan Command to improve how units detect and track aircraft across Alaska and its approaches and help commanders assess potential threats for homeland defense, the release states.

“Understanding what this technology can do in the Arctic starts with collecting data under real operating conditions,” Dr. Carolyn Stwertka, chief scientist for Alaskan Command, said in the release. “Working with operational units allows us to compare the experimental observations with known aircraft positions and assess where this approach could help address gaps in air surveillance.”

The experiment occurred as NORAD is building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network.

The Homeland Defense OTHR, which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031.

Meanwhile, the Air Force is looking to replace its Air Route Surveillance Radar-4, a three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations.

The ARSR-4 system, which was built in the 1990s, was designed to help operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. The system has been very effective, but Air Force officials maintain that newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly, according to a recent Air Force Life Cycle Management Center sources sought notice.

With a successful Mars gravity assist in its rearview mirror, NASA’s Psyche spacecraft has fired up its thrusters and is accelerating to the metal-rich asteroid of the same name. During the first leg of its journey, following an October 2023 launch, the mission used its electric propulsion system intermittently to maneuver to the right place for harnessing Mars’ gravity for a propellant-saving speed boost and a slight trajectory change.

On Sept. 28, the spacecraft began to use its propulsion system nearly continuously, pausing just once each week to check in with mission controllers on Earth. This keeps the mission on track for its rendezvous with the asteroid Psyche in the main asteroid belt by the summer of 2029.

“It’s now ‘pedal to the metal’ to the asteroid Psyche,” said Don Han, the Psyche mission’s navigation lead at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, which is managed for the agency by Caltech. “We will be running our propulsion system at every available opportunity, pausing only for necessary engineering activities. The thrusters will be operating nearly 90% of the time from now until we reach the asteroid.”

Where conventional spacecraft thrusters rely on large quantities of fuel to provide powerful bursts of thrust for relatively short periods of time, the Psyche spacecraft’s solar-powered propulsion system uses electromagnetic fields to steadily deliver up to 250 millinewtons of force — about the amount of force that you would feel from the weight of holding one AA battery.
The highly efficient system relies on a mechanism known as the Hall effect, in which charged atoms, or ions, of the inert gas xenon are expelled to create thrust — and a bright blue glow.

Each of the four thrusters operates one at a time. Though the thrust is tiny, it builds up over the course of the journey, enabling the spacecraft to gain speed as it travels through interplanetary space. At its maximum speed during cruise, the Psyche spacecraft will be traveling more than 100,000 mph (160,900 kph) relative to an observer on Earth.

The spacecraft uses its two five-panel, cross-shaped solar arrays — with a sunlight-collecting area of 800 square feet (75 square meters) — to generate electricity to charge its batteries and power its systems, including the propulsion system. The spacecraft launched with nearly 2,400 pounds (1,090 kilograms) of xenon in seven fuel tanks. In the three years since launch, it has used about one third of that supply, leaving plenty to reach its target and assist the spacecraft as it orbits the asteroid Psyche during a two-year prime science mission.

“There are some unique things that mission designers need to consider with a propulsion system that is powered by the Sun,” said Steve Snyder, the Psyche mission’s lead engineer for propulsion operations at JPL. “For the next three months, we’ll be thrusting at full power before we begin slowly throttling down to approximately half power as the spacecraft moves farther away and its solar arrays receive less sunlight and generate less power.”

Another consideration for mission designers: Despite how gentle the Hall-effect thrusters are, using them requires consistent management throughout cruise. As the thrusters expel xenon ions, the magnetic field generated causes the ions to swirl. These swirling ions can create a slight torque, or twisting force, that if left unchecked would interfere with the spacecraft’s pointing.

To compensate for the torque and absorb the excess angular momentum it generates, the Psyche spacecraft relies on reaction wheels to change their spin rate. After several hours, engineers command the spacecraft to turn off its thruster, rotate, and then run a different thruster at low power in a different direction for several minutes to remove the momentum that built up in the reaction wheels.

“For a propulsion engineer, it’s a fun thing that you can only measure this torque in space and not on Earth, as it’s so small,” said Snyder. “In fact, this is the first time anyone has been able to measure this effect on a Hall thruster as a function of power level and of operating time, and for such a long duration in space. The Psyche spacecraft is an excellent laboratory to test it.”

When it arrives in 2029, the spacecraft will insert itself into orbit around the asteroid Psyche, which is thought to be the partial core of a planetesimal, a building block of an early planet. The spacecraft will map the asteroid and gather science data during a series of orbits that go lower and then higher in altitude around Psyche, which is about 173 miles (280 kilometers) across at its widest point.
If the asteroid proves to be an ancient planetesimal’s metallic core, it could offer a one-of-a-kind window into the interior of rocky planets like Earth.

“The Mars flyby was an incredible opportunity for the team to calibrate instruments and practice procedures for a planetary encounter ahead of arriving at the asteroid Psyche,” said Lindy Elkins-Tanton, principal investigator for the Psyche mission at the University of California, Berkeley. “Now we are cruising with confidence deeper into the solar system, powered by sunlight, ready to explore a mysterious new world in the asteroid belt.”

The isolated nation of Bhutan was the last country on Earth without access to television – until 1999. This short documentary from the PBS investigative series Frontline, first aired in 2002, captures the small Buddhist kingdom as the impact of TV began to reverberate. Beaming in images from around the globe, the medium introduced not just a novel form of distraction, but, as one government official puts it, new desires for things the Bhutanese previously didn’t even know existed. As the film explores, this includes everything from emulating professional wrestlers to buying branded clothing. Throughout, the interviewees – including small children, businesspeople and Buddhist monks – seem, at some level, to be aware that this development is at once culturally corrosive, irresistible and, perhaps, inevitable.
