These are also widely customizable; you can adjust the ANC and transparency level in the app, and the controls themselves offer plenty of customization options. Sound quality is solid, too; these don’t have show-stopping audio, but the profile is engaging and enjoyable, with some emphasis on the low-end.

There’s nothing that makes these headphones necessarily remarkable. There are cheaper options, better-sounding ones, and more effective noise-cancelers. But they do a lot of things well, with only a handful of tradeoffs.
Quick Summary: Cambridge Audio’s Melomania P100 SE are a low-key hit from a storied audio brand, with great comfort and sound quality.
- Pros: Great audio for the price, easy tactile controls
- Cons: Bulky design and case, others have better ANC

Cambridge’s headphones may have a passing resemblance to another English headphone brand, Bowers & Wilkins, but the key difference is the price. At $300, the P100 SE significantly undercut rivals like B&W, Bose, and Sony, while still delivering great sound quality, solid ANC, and superb comfort.

If Cambridge has flown under your radar, it might be because the brand is best known for its HiFi home audio equipment, including its well-regarded speakers and amplifiers. But the brand has lately found success with portable audio, including its Melomania earbuds and headphones.

Where the P100 SE headphones make their mark is in battery life; these boast a whopping 100 hours of playtime, far outstripping the competition. The catch is that all that battery makes these some seriously bulky headphones. While they’re comfortable and surprisingly lightweight, they protrude significantly from the head when worn, and the case is very large.

Otherwise, the headphones have intuitive physical controls, with playback and volume on the right earcup and ANC and power on the left. There’s no 3.5mm headphone jack, but a USB-C to 3.5mm cable is included for wired listening.
Overall, the P100 SE is a sleeper hit for headphone value, with rich sound quality and ANC, great comfort, and jaw-dropping battery life.
How We Picked the Best Noise-Canceling Headphones

All of the options on our list were hand-tested. We prioritized factors that are hard to evaluate without hands-on testing, such as comfort, fit, and sound quality, while also looking at the spec sheet for factors like battery life, Bluetooth codecs, and more.

While it would be tough to test every option on a plane without burning through some serious miles, we tested the noise-canceling in real-world (flights, busy streets) and simulated (table fans, loud TVs) settings, all to see how well they handle a variety of distractions.

20 years after retiring Ali G, Sacha Baron Cohen has dusted off his tracksuit collection and reprised the character for “Ali G: Who Iz I?,” now open in theaters before coming to Amazon Prime Oct. 30. The comedian first brought Ali G to audiences at the turn of the century with “Da Ali G Show,” where he interviewed some of the world’s most powerful figures (and, more often than not, made fools of them in the process).

“As Ali G, I had the privilege of sitting with some of the smartest and most powerful people in the world, and all of them were punctual,” Baron Cohen told Josh Horowitz Wednesday night during a live taping of “Happy Sad Confused” at New York’s 92nd Street Y. After a lengthy pause, he turned his attention to the one exception: “Donald Trump kept us waiting for about 40 minutes.”

Baron Cohen recalled feeling “intimidated” upon entering Trump Tower with director James Bobin, where they waited in a room while Trump shouted a string of expletives “not for the likes of delicate Jewish ears” at Rudy Giuliani over the phone.
“Later on, I heard that he used to do that with other people,” Baron Cohen said. “It really was a power move.”

Trump appeared taken with Bobin, who Baron Cohen described as a “very handsome, blond, Oxford-educated” Englishman. But when he realized he’d be sitting down with Ali G instead, his demeanor “immediately” changed.

“I actually met a woman who was in the car with him after that interview, and he was apparently furious,” Baron Cohen said. “He actually went out publicly a couple of times to criticize me. And in the end, we used all those clips and used them to advertise another show that I did.”

Baron Cohen’s interview with Trump aired in 2003, back when the future president was best known as a New York real estate mogul, before going on to host NBC’s “The Apprentice.” Looking back at their encounter, Baron Cohen said he could understand how Trump won a second term in the White House, pointing to the president’s “elements of brilliance.”

“I mean, how has he survived a second term? People underestimated him,” Baron Cohen said. “We were too easy to dismiss him as a nincompoop. There are elements of brilliance to him, otherwise. And that explains his appeal with the fact that he’s there for a second term, the fact that he’s transforming this country. I won’t say positively or negatively.”

This was not the only time Baron Cohen reflected on Trump’s one-of-a-kind characteristics on his latest press tour. He told Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway on the Pivot podcast that the president is “amusing” and that there’s “a huge amount of comedy in the way he speaks.”
“He’s intentionally being funny,” Baron Cohen explained. “And if you have a look on the far right, they use comedy and sarcasm as an engaging way to dismiss criticisms.”

Baron Cohen suggests that Trump’s popularity, perhaps, reflects a broader theme explored through his own collection of provocative characters: “In the black and white, the world is a little bit complicated.”

In medieval Italy, it was accepted wisdom that anyone walking near a swamp risked falling ill from “bad air” — mala aria. Victims were struck with fever, headache, nausea, and chills, and occasionally the illness escalated to vomiting, jaundice, and death. Today, we still call this affliction malaria. For much of human history, it has ravaged populations in humid tropical and subtropical regions, killing untold numbers. In the 20th century, it was responsible for up to 5% of deaths worldwide; it still kills approximately 600,000 people each year.

What malaria was and how it infected humans was deeply mysterious until barely 150 years ago. In 1880, the French physician Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran peered at a sample of a soldier’s blood through a crude microscope and discovered the true cause of the disease: not miasma, but a genus of shape-shifting single-celled protists called Plasmodium. Since then, scientists and doctors have described in precise detail the parasites’ life cycle, hosts, and disease progression, and even the nuances of various Plasmodium species, which present slightly different forms of the disease. But some crucial aspects have remained a mystery.

For example, Plasmodium invades human red blood cells as part of its life cycle. To get in, the microbe creates a ring-shaped structure called the moving junction, which briefly creates a gap in the cell membrane it can slip through. The gap then disappears without a trace. It opens and closes so rapidly, at such a small scale, that imaging technologies couldn’t capture it. Researchers had no clue what the portal structure actually looked like. “Because of that,” said Chi-Min Ho, a microbiologist and structural biologist at Columbia University, “we didn’t really know anything about how it works.”

Now, Ho’s lab has imaged the moving junction right at the moment of invasion, in unprecedented detail. Her team found that when the Plasmodium parasite installs molecular gaskets in the host cell, it radically remodels the cell membrane to slip through without a trace. This knowledge could help inform the next generation of malaria treatments and influence the drug-discovery process for other parasitic diseases, such as cyclosporiasis and toxoplasmosis.

“It’s a totally mind-blowing paper,” said Jake Baum, a parasitologist at the University of New South Wales, who was not involved in the research. “At the end of the day, this is not molecular biology. This is biophysics.”

The history of malaria research has paralleled advances in microscopy, from the development of simple light microscopes like the one Laveran used to the cutting-edge cryo-electron techniques of Ho’s lab. This is because the cells the microbes invade are extremely tiny — and the parasites are even smaller. At about 8 micrometers across, red blood cells are among the smallest cells in the human body, and all species of Plasmodium are a fraction of that size during the invasion stage.

Attempts to image the parasites in the act of breaking and entering got off the ground in the 1970s, when pioneering microbiologists first applied electron microscopy. These scientists observed a distinct thickening of the cellular membrane near the parasite’s access point. Then the tiny, round Plasmodium seemed to simply merge with the cell, like a water droplet coalescing into a larger pool. It would be decades before techniques developed enough to isolate the proteins that make this possible, much less image them.

Another hurdle is that malaria parasites have a very complicated life cycle. They are most at home in the gut of a mosquito where they can reproduce sexually. Humans are what’s known as a reservoir host — a place for the parasite to live while it waits to be taken up by an insect.
“The food supply happens to be our red blood cells,” said Kirk Deitsch, a microbiologist and immunologist at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York. “That’s why they’re invading us.”

To this end, the Plasmodium parasite assumes a variety of shapes and sizes as it moves through its life stages: Sometimes it’s shaped like an egg, sometimes a spindly thread, sometimes a gangly starfish. It can move through this cycle in rapid succession or hang out in one stage (the hypnozoite phase in the human liver) for years. When it enters its tiny, round merozoite stage, the parasite is ready to invade a red blood cell.

Plasmodium pulls up to the scene of the crime with all the proteins and other biological equipment it needs. The entry procedure is more delicate than simply punching a hole in the host cell. “If you’re trying to push an orange into a balloon, the balloon mustn’t pop, right?” Baum said.

Based on previous research, scientists knew the broad strokes of this process. The parasite approaches a host red blood cell and inserts a ring of protein anchors into the cell’s membrane. Collectively these anchors are known as the moving junction. Plasmodium locks into them with proteins expressed on its surface — and then pushes forward. The moving junction forms a continuous portal in the host cell membrane for the parasite to travel through. Once the parasite is fully inside, the cell membrane seals up behind it. The whole process takes less than a minute.

Ho and the other authors of the new paper used cryo-electron microscopy to probe the four individual protein units in each anchor. What they learned allowed them to propose a more detailed model for how the moving junction actively remodels the host cell’s membrane. The parasite injects into the red blood cell three proteins, which form a dense wedge beneath the membrane surface; a fourth protein connects this structure to the invader. Plasmodium places many of these anchors on the red blood cell surface. The proteins produce electrostatic forces and pressure in the cell membrane, which crowd and displace its lipid molecules. This deforms the membrane and reverses its curvature. It bows slightly inward around the parasite — in fact, some lipids slough off and reassemble into a protective membrane for the invader — before re-forming and sealing behind it.
“It’s a really nice example of how a field has built step by step by step toward a really powerful observation,” Baum said.

Once inside, Plasmodium approaches its remodeling work more comprehensively. Red blood cells are essentially bags of hemoglobin; they have no nucleus or organelles to speak of. So Plasmodium builds from the ground up. It secretes proteins that allow it to feed on hemoglobin, remove waste, and stretch the cell’s cytoplasm. Ho compared it to the conversion of an empty warehouse floor into a stylish lofted apartment.
“It’s putting in plumbing,” she said. “It’s putting in the floors. It’s literally building everything for itself.”

In this process, the parasite also redecorates the cell’s exterior. It is equipped with genes that allow it to make a series of distinct but closely related adhesive proteins that it can express on the red blood cell’s surface. These proteins cause the cells to stick to the walls of the blood vessels around them — one of the main causes of malaria’s painful symptoms. In 2025, research from Deitsch’s lab found that by periodically switching between proteins, the parasite can avoid tipping off the immune system to its presence for days or weeks at a time. Such extensive exterior cellular remodeling serves a purpose: It helps Plasmodium avoid a trip to the spleen, an organ that filters out dead, defective, or broken red blood cells as well as any undercover parasites.
Rick Fairhurst and Jordan Zuspann, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health

The parasite itself undergoes a radical change inside the cell. It transforms from a roundish merozoite into an amoebalike trophozoite. It grows several cytoplasm “arms” and flattens out, said Christiaan van Ooij, a molecular parasitologist at Keele University in the United Kingdom. This also helps it evade the immune system. The trophozoite shape is more flexible than that of the spherical merozoite, and the immune system clocks supple cells as healthy and stiff cells as dead.

The parasite then replicates asexually for about 48 hours, dividing inside the red blood cell until it’s so full of Plasmodium that it bursts. Like house flippers, the parasites move on to other blood cells. Within days, millions could be lurking in the bloodstream.

In this way, malaria can quickly overwhelm a human host. It is all enabled by the moving junction that allows the parasites to set up shop without tipping off the authorities. The structure of the moving junction could help researchers intervene, with drugs to block the parasite from invading a host blood cell in the first place.

Malaria treatment has long been something of a hit-or-miss proposition. Without a granular view of how Plasmodium interacts with host cells, researchers had to test various compounds by trial and error. If a given drug seemed to fight the illness, they had little idea what part of the infection process it had disrupted. “All that work was done essentially blind,” Deitsch said.

This has made developing new malaria treatments notoriously difficult. The former workhorse antimalarial drugs, such as chloroquine, sulfadoxine, and pyrimethamine, are now known to target the parasites in the bloodstream. But the Plasmodium species that infect humans are rapidly evolving resistance to these compounds.

Invasion offers a tantalizing choke point for new medicines. “If you block invasion, then you stop the parasite in its tracks,” Ho said. To make her point, her team used an AI-powered protein-design platform to craft an inhibitory protein that could block the moving junction. In test tubes, it prevented Plasmodium from entering red blood cells. But its safety and efficacy haven’t been tested in animal models.

It’s possible that the moving junction could be something of a skeleton key that could be used to treat other parasitic diseases. Plasmodium is a member of the apicomplexans, a large phylum of parasitic protists that also includes Toxoplasma gondii, a cat parasite, and Cyclospora, which causes explosive diarrhea. These single-celled organisms appear to enter using the same biochemical equipment as Plasmodium. “All of these are parasites that have this invasion machinery,” Deitsch said. The study of those conditions could in turn inform malaria treatment. A 2026 paper described the mechanism by which Toxoplasma senses the right moment to deploy its moving junction, and malaria may operate the same way.

But the moving junction may prove to be too much of a moving target. “Some people have always argued that invasion is a really bad drug target because it’s a very short process,” van Ooij said. Any drug with the ability to stop invasion would have a roughly 60-second window in which to do so, which means it would need to remain stable in the body for a long time or act extremely quickly, or both.

Ho’s team already has their sights set on another target. They plan to use similar cryo-electron microscopy techniques to solve the structure of other protein complexes involved in malaria infection, such as those adhesive proteins that keep infected blood cells from journeying to the spleen.
“We’ve caught one white whale,” Ho said. “So we want to go after the other remaining white whales.”

Gunmen open fire at a church during a funeral in Jordan, killing 7 and wounding 40
JERUSALEM — Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.
The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90 kilometers (55 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.
Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. "It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire," Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan's security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was "carried out by unknown assailants," but didn't say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that "investigations are underway at full speed."
Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom's Petra News Agency.
Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.
Jordan's Health Minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan "will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties" and offered his "deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded."

Jordan's Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.
Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world's foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday's shooting, calling it a "heinous terrorist attack."
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and "affirmed Iraq's solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism," Hussein's office said in a statement.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as "especially heinous," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. "The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account."
Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels

Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.

The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.

Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.
"We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily," al-Shahid said in a phone interview.
Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.

The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.
Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."
Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents' access to wells

Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.

War-related damage to Taiz's aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.

By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.
As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents' access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.
The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.
As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.
The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food

Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.

Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.

Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.
These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.

"The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises," Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.
Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.

Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.
"We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food," he said in a phone interview.

Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.

While the Yemeni government still controls the center of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city.
Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south toward Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that won't be easy.

"Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters," said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to brief the media, but Yemen's foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group's tightening grip on the city.
The Houthis' fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials said.
Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians.

Abdel Gaber said he can hear loud explosions every day from fighting that is happening roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away. The family isn't returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety.
Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive.
"Staying in our home is inevitable — whether it be a matter of life or death," al-Shahid said.
Israeli PM pledges massive military operation after West Bank checkpoint attack

The Israeli military is demolishing homes and forcibly removing hundreds of Palestinians from a neighborhood in the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank following an attack by Palestinian gunmen on an Israeli checkpoint that killed two soldiers and wounded three others.

In response to that attack yesterday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces a tough election on Tuesday, vowed to launch a military operation in the West Bank "on a scale not seen since the Six Day War," when Israel first occupied the West Bank almost 60 years ago.
"We will act to demolish this place, to change it completely," Netanyahu said in a televised speech from the location of the attack, close to the Palestinian city of Hebron.

He likened the plan to an Israeli military assault against two long-standing Palestinian refugee camps in the northern West Bank last year in which the Israeli army displaced tens of thousands of Palestinians. Human Rights Watch said those expulsions amounted to war crimes, a charge that Israel rejects.

On Friday afternoon, the Israeli military had already begun bulldozing homes close to the site of the shooting. The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem is calling on foreign governments to act to prevent "another wave of ethnic cleansing and war crimes."

Commenting on the attack, the Israeli military told NPR that soldiers were positioned behind concrete barriers at the checkpoint when two gunmen opened fire on them. A firefight continued for about 20 minutes before Israeli soldiers killed the attackers.

This comes amid a surge of violence and land seizures by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. The United Nations Human Rights Office for the occupied Palestinian territory has described it as a "new level of dehumanization of Palestinians."

Israel imposed widespread closures in Hebron on Saturday, making movement difficult in and around the most populous city of the occupied West Bank. Israel regularly imposes restrictions on movement across the Palestinian occupied territory with some 925 checkpoints, roadblocks, earth mounds and other barriers.

Analysts tie the wide-scale Israeli response to Friday's attack to the Israeli national elections on October 27, claiming this is an effort by Netanyahu to appear strong to voters. According to polls, Netanyahu and his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, are neck and neck in the race. Neither candidate currently has enough support to form a government.

"For Netanyahu, his ticket before the election is, 'I'm Mr. Security,'" Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, told NPR. "In order to show that he is the protector of Israel, he will take harsh measures in order to show the Israeli public that he supports them and he's defending them."

This is a view shared by other analysts, who see this latest military action more as an effort by Netanyahu to remain in power than a closely thought-out strategy to improve Israel's long-term security. Citrinowicz called Netanyahu's response — to evict families from their homes in the neighborhood the attackers came from, without evidence of a connection to the gunmen — "collective punishment."

"The way to prevent [more attacks by Palestinians] is not collective punishment. It's by giving hope," Citrinowicz said. "Distinguish between those who want to commit terrorist attacks and arrest them and those who just want to live peacefully and help them to live peacefully, with an economy that works, with everything they need for stability.
Daniel Estrin in Tel Aviv and James Hider in Washington, D.C., contributed reporting. This story was edited by Samantha Balaban.

West Ham 2-3 Southampton: Saints claim thrilling win at the London Stadium

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between West Ham United and Southampton at the London Stadium on Saturday; Saints record a thrilling win at the home of their promotion rivals.
Southampton announced themselves in the Sky Bet Championship promotion race with a statement 3-2 win at pre-season title-favourites West Ham.
Kuryu Matsuki, James Bree and Lewis Dobbin were all on target in a chaotic first half, while Kyle Walker-Peters and Tomas Soucek replied for the Hammers.
Nuno Espirito Santo's side, relegated on the final day of last term, would have gone top with a win but instead saw their nine-match unbeaten run grind to a halt.
There were thousands of empty seats by the end at the London Stadium, with those who stayed booing the Hammers off.
For anyone who thought promotion would be achieved at a canter in east London, this was a wake-up call.
The Hammers now have a Southampton side, who were deducted four points at the start of the season, in their rear-view mirror, lying just two points behind.
Saints took the lead inside two minutes after Konstantinos Mavropanos and Divine Mukasa stood back and admired as Leo Scienza danced into the penalty area.
Scienza blasted his shot straight at Hammers goalkeeper Mads Hermansen, who made a fine point-blank save, but the rebound rolled to Matsuki who tucked it into the opposite corner.
West Ham tried to hit straight back with Walker-Peters finding Jarrod Bowen, who cut inside but dragged his shot wide.

However, the hosts were two down after 10 minutes when Casper Jander's cross was tipped away by Hermansen as far as Bree, who without breaking stride lashed a spectacular volley into the roof of the net.
Mukasa almost made amends for his earlier error when he won the ball off Ryan Manning and jinked inside Scienza only to see his shot deflected wide.
West Ham did claw one back when former Saint Walker-Peters skipped past Jander on the edge of the box and launched a rocket into the top corner.

The Hammers were pressing incessantly for an equaliser but then promptly shot themselves in the foot as more lacklustre defending allowed Finn Azaz to shoot straight at Hermansen, with Dobbin this time snaffling the rebound.

The unlikely figure of Mavropanos almost pulled one back after the break but his rasping drive was well saved by Daniel Peretz, before fellow centre-half Max Kilman trotted forward and crashed a shot against the crossbar.
Arne Engels then took aim from the edge of the box but Peretz saved with his legs, which was the cue for scores of West Ham fans to make their way towards the exits with 10 minutes still remaining.
Those who left missed substitute Soucek curling in a consolation in stoppage time, before Peretz kept out a header from Taty Castellanos to preserve three points for Saints.

Cardiff 1-0 Birmingham: Yousef Salech steers Bluebirds to victory

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Cardiff City and Birmingham City at the Cardiff City Stadium on Saturday; Yousef Salech misses penalty but then scores winner.
Cardiff halted Birmingham's winning run as Yousef Salech secured a 1-0 victory to continue the Bluebirds' climb up the Championship.
Salech was named among the home substitutes initially, but defender Krystian Bielik suffered an injury in the warm-up and had to drop out on an afternoon of relentless rain in the Welsh capital.
The late change saw Cardiff reshuffle their resources and Salech plunder a first-half winner, his sixth goal of the season coming 10 minutes after James Beadle had saved his spot-kick.
Cardiff have now recorded three straight home wins as they continue to show real signs of adapting to life in the second tier following promotion from League One.
Birmingham had arrived on the back of three successive wins without conceding, and remain in the play-off places after suffering their first defeat since September 9.
Cardiff manager Brian Barry-Murphy was serving a touchline ban after receiving his third yellow card of the season.

Both sets of players wore black armbands to mark the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster, in which 116 children were among the 144 who died in the Welsh mining village, and a minute's silence before kick-off was impeccably observed.
Salech featured for the first time in five weeks after a shoulder injury, but could not pull down a Joel Bagan pass that would have taken him through on goal.
Luis Vazquez's wait for a first Birmingham goal went on as the Argentinian striker was unable to connect with Jay Stansfield's cross.

Cardiff were awarded a spot-kick after 21 minutes when Tomoki Iwata dragged down Perry Ng at a corner. Salech sent the penalty low to Beadle's right, but the effort lacked power and the Birmingham goalkeeper pushed the ball to safety.
It was the second successive spot-kick Cardiff had missed following Chris Willock's failure to convert against Watford.
But Salech quickly made amends by holding off Phil Neumann from Ollie Tanner's cross and producing a tidy turn and finish past Beadle.
Some Birmingham players held their arms aloft believing Neumann had been sent to the floor by a foul, but referee Tim Robinson clearly saw it as a case of Salech being stronger.
Beadle came to Birmingham's rescue at the start of the second half, denying Cian Ashford with his legs after Tanner and Salech had opened up the visitors.
Salech fired just past the base of a post as Cardiff increased intensity in the search for a second goal and Beadle fielded Ashford's attempt from distance.
Birmingham had not tested Nathan Trott until Stansfield met Alex Cochrane's cross, but it was a routine stop to say the least and Cardiff were untroubled until the closing stages.
Marvin Ducksch headed Max Bird's cross wide and Birmingham's best chance came two minutes from time when Trott superbly kept out Demarai Gray from point-blank range.

On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space.
While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before.

The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth.

Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film. When they saw the images for the first time, the scientists were literally jumping up and down with joy.

The ability to photograph Earth from space drove both an expanded interest to continue pushing into space and led to unexpected societal changes with regards to how humanity considered its home planet.

For military and intelligence agencies, the potential now existed for reconnaissance at a far larger scale than what was possible with high-altitude aircraft. That capability expanded to agriculture and meteorological purposes, eventually making Earth observation one of the most common reasons satellites and space stations are deployed into orbit today.

Earth photography from space also gave birth to the environmental movement, as people began to see the planet differently. The fragility of this orb became more apparent, as now Earth appeared a "blue marble" set against an endless black void.

It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of "Star Trek" before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.

You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say.
That should trouble any Trekkie. "Star Trek" — a show built on progressive ideals, thoughtful characters, and boundary-breaking television — was completely and totally afraid to say anything at all.

To be clear, "Star Trek" is no stranger to genre mashups, and they're not inherently a bad thing. Trek has been running for nearly 1,000 total episodes, and they've been doing mashups since the very first season of "Star Trek: The Original Series", which featured gangster, historical fiction, and war-themed episodes.

The holodeck took things further, giving the writers an excuse to set the action anywhere they could dream up. No more alien planets that look suspiciously like Earth were necessary to completely flip the series’ genre; just work up a hologram malfunction and suddenly "Trek" is a Sherlock Holmes-esque mystery or a noir thriller. And even without the holodeck, genres are fluid things that often take from each other to tell stories within each other’s realms.

But while "Trek" has always dabbled, it's never done an entire season of genre episodes… in fact, that might be unprecedented in all of science fiction TV itself, let alone "Star Trek". This season of "SNW" didn’t use occasional gimmicks to take a break from space fare; it was all gimmick, all the time.
- Episode 1: Dinosaur adventure/western (Land of the Lost)
- Episode 2: Space horror (Event Horizon)
- Episode 3: Raunchy comedy (The Hangover)
- Episode 4: Wartime drama (Casablanca)*
- Episode 6: Disaster movie/real-time story (The Poseidon Adventure)
- Episode 7: Soap opera (Days of Our Lives)
- Episode 8: Cold War film/submarine movie (The Hunt for Red October)
- Episode 9: Fairytale fantasy (Anything with a dragon)
- Episode 10: Star Trek (Yes, this episode was basically SNW mashing up with TOS, and we're counting that).
* Some of you are screaming that Episode 4 was a noir. It was not. Not everything in black and white with fedoras is noir.
"Strange New Worlds" season 4 was genre-blending at scale. This wasn’t a hint of another genre influencing the episode; it was full-blown immersion into each and every one.

In the past, when other genres have come into "Trek", the series still felt tonally consistent; the characters never bent to the will of the genre, and its direction stayed the same. That was not true of this season. Characters, directorial style, and tone all bent to the will of the selected genre instead of fitting into the already established universe. There were multiple episodes this season that felt nothing like a "Star Trek" episode.

Also — and I may be in the minority here — there were only two episodes this season that I’d argue were executed well (Episode 6 and Episode 8), meaning that the relentless gimmicks paraded out each week felt not just detrimental to the show itself, but they weren’t much fun to watch either.

The real question that crops up from this season is why they did it at all. If you listen to the show’s producers, it’s because they love "Trek" so much and they thought it would help move the characters along.

"I really do respect and hear the criticism that: 'When you have 10 episodes [per season], should they be more homogeneous?’”, co-showrunner and executive producer Akiva Goldsman told TV Line when addressing the criticisms for the season. “For us, the answer was no, because the original series always jumped around in genre … Part of what 'Star Trek' did well was use genre for storytelling, and that was what we wanted to explore in this series.”

He is, of course, absolutely correct; that is exactly what "Trek" has traditionally used genre episodes for. When "The Original Series" went to the Nazi planet, it was one of the first and earliest examples of directly confronting fascism and Nazism on American television. When the show played with Greek gods, it took the moment to have a groundbreaking interracial kiss. Even when it went broad comedy in “The Trouble with Tribbles,” it at least kept its characters consistent and its universe coherent.
For the most part, that practice continued throughout classic "Trek" and even into the modern era, with genre being used to aid storytelling, not overwhelm it.

Season 4 of "Strange New Worlds" does none of this. It isn’t using genre as elevation; it’s using it as a distraction: a shiny gloss over a collection of episodes too afraid to say anything that will get the series accused of being “woke” or progressive. Later in the interview, Goldman claims that they can’t please everyone, but that seems like exactly what they were trying to do this season-- resulting, of course, in pleasing no one.

This season is running scared from the current moment, and it’s doing so by hiding behind gimmicks. Any previous series of "Trek" (or any great science fiction) would be tackling subjects such as immigration, fascism, war, or any other societal issue that is overwhelming us right now, but "SNW" is doing none of that, instead presenting farcical genre fare
Fear exists for one purpose; to be conquered

It’s hard not to draw a direct line from this approach to the purchase of Paramount by Skydance last year and the company’s new leadership, who are more than cozy with President Donald Trump. There seems to be little other reason that a franchise and series that were being bashed for being “too woke” and overly progressive would veer so hard into gimmickry that barely hides the hollow shell this show has become.

Rewatching the first three seasons of "SNW" shows how hard a turn this series has taken since the re-election of Trump and the steady march of companies trying to kowtow to a government that wants to squash progressive ideology.

The show has gone from telling powerful stories for both its characters and society to a series of running gags that do little more than slap the Federation delta onto people’s chests so people think it's still "Star Trek".

It isn’t. This season of nothingness is exactly what you get when you ask "Trek" not to push boundaries, not to be hopeful, not to be bold, and not to progress forward. When a show founded on speaking out and saying something spends an entire season running away from doing just that, it’s not just a condemnation of the show itself; it’s a condemnation of the creative process behind it.
The real issue with this season isn’t the attempt to play in genre for ten episodes straight; it’s that the reason they did it was fear, not hope.

Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?

- A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.

A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.

Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication.

The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best.
How Ear Nerve Stimulation Could Lower Blood Pressure

The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure.
By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure.

The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic.
Clinical Trial Tests the Device in 63 Patients

The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels.

Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself.
Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week.

The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home.

However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device.
Promising Results in Patients With Severe Hypertension
Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension.

A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment.

This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness.
Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:

"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.

"As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."
A Potential New Option for Hard-to-Control Blood Pressure

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time.
Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment.
This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies.

Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients.

For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach.

A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science

- A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.

Researchers at the University of Vermont have discovered a surprising pattern in human language that challenges a scientific theory widely accepted for more than 70 years. Their findings suggest that the meaning of words is shaped by something more fundamental than emotion: our understanding of power, danger, and order.

The study, published in Science Advances, introduces a new approach called "ousiometrics," which uses mathematical methods to measure the essential meaning of language. Its most striking finding is that the words people use show a consistent and widespread preference for safety over danger.
This hidden safety bias could transform how researchers study language, understand human behavior, and develop artificial intelligence systems that interpret what people say and write.
Scientists Discover a Hidden Safety Bias in Human Language

Since the 1950s, much of the scientific understanding of word meaning has relied on a framework developed through pioneering research by psychologist Charles Osgood and others. Known as the VAD model, it describes meaning through three emotional dimensions: valence (positive vs. negative), arousal (excited vs. calm), and dominance (controlling vs. submissive).
This approach became influential in psychology, linguistics, and artificial intelligence, particularly in systems designed to identify the emotional tone of written language.
However, the University of Vermont researchers found evidence that this long-established model overlooks important aspects of how meaning is organized.

Their analysis examined billions of individual uses of more than 20,000 words across a wide range of real-world texts. Using advanced computational techniques, the team identified a different underlying structure. They found that the three dimensions in the traditional VAD model are not independent of one another, as previously assumed.

Instead, their results indicate that word meaning can be more effectively described through three separate dimensions: power (weak vs. powerful), danger (safe vs. dangerous), and structure (ordered vs. chaotic).

The research, supported by the US National Science Foundation, Google, MassMutual, and other funders, found that this new framework accounted for more than 90% of the variation in measured word meaning. The traditional VAD approach explained approximately 72%.
That improvement could be especially important as large language models, automated content moderation, and other AI technologies increasingly depend on understanding human communication.
Why Human Language Favors Safety Over Danger
One of the study's most unexpected discoveries emerged when the researchers examined how words actually appear in everyday communication.
Across books, news reporting, social media, and spoken language, words associated with safety appeared much more frequently than those associated with danger.
This finding offers a new explanation for a familiar phenomenon called the Pollyanna principle, which describes the tendency for human language to lean toward positive rather than negative words.
For decades, researchers generally interpreted this pattern as evidence that people favor positive emotional expressions. The new analysis suggests that something more fundamental may be responsible.
According to the researchers, the apparent preference for positivity largely reflects an underlying preference for safety.
"The Pollyanna principle's positivity bias," the study concludes. "is, in fact, a one-dimensional projection of an underlying safety bias."

"This is a big observation that comes out of this work," said Peter Dodds, director of the UVM's Complex Systems Institute and senior author of the study. "Expressions of safety are crucial to all language."
Could Human Language Be Shaped by Survival?
The discovery raises an intriguing possibility: the structure of human language may reflect evolutionary pressures associated with staying alive.
From this perspective, words do more than communicate feelings. They also help people recognize threats, evaluate uncertainty, establish trust, and coordinate actions with others.
Being able to distinguish between safety and danger is essential to survival. The researchers suggest that this basic human priority may also influence how meaning is organized in language.

Throughout daily life, people constantly exchange information about whether individuals, places, situations, and behaviors are threatening or safe. The new findings suggest that these distinctions may be more central to communication than previously recognized.

They also offer a different interpretation of why positive language is so common. Rather than simply expressing happiness or approval, many positive words may convey a sense of security, stability, or predictability.

Julia Zimmerman, a postdoctoral researcher in UVM's Computational Story Lab and a co-author of the study, said the three newly identified dimensions reflect experiences that are fundamental to human life.
"Power, danger, and structure," she said, "are relevant to every person that's ever lived."

Researchers have also long recognized that people tend to favor language associated with goodness and low aggression. The team argues that these familiar tendencies may arise from the same deeper pattern.
"We now understand," the team writes, that these are "shadows of an underlying linguistic safety bias."
Although the results are consistent with a possible connection between language and survival, they do not establish that evolutionary pressures directly caused the safety bias.
A Discovery That Could Change How AI Understands Language
The findings have implications that extend well beyond linguistics.

Many artificial intelligence systems use sentiment analysis to determine whether language expresses positive, negative, or neutral feelings. Some approaches also draw on the traditional VAD framework to measure emotional meaning.
If that framework does not fully capture the underlying structure of language, systems built around it could overlook important distinctions in what people communicate.

The researchers suggest that incorporating power, danger, and structure could eventually help AI models interpret language more accurately and explain their assessments more clearly. This may be particularly useful when analyzing trust, risk, and decision-making.

In linguistics, the findings offer a different way to understand the foundations of meaning. Instead of treating emotional tone as the primary organizing principle, the new framework emphasizes distinctions related to strength, safety, and predictability.

Psychology could also be affected. Decades of studies have used the VAD model to investigate emotions, perception, and behavior. A different set of fundamental dimensions could encourage researchers to reconsider how some of those findings are interpreted.

The discovery may also interest neuroscientists. The human brain is highly sensitive to threats and signals of safety, and the newly identified linguistic bias suggests that these biological priorities may be reflected in language. This potential connection could help researchers explore relationships between brain activity and symbolic communication, although further research would be needed to establish them.
A New Tool Measures the Hidden Meaning of Words
To investigate these patterns, the researchers created analytical methods designed to measure meaning across enormous collections of written and spoken language.
One of their central innovations is the "ousiometer," a tool that rapidly evaluates the essential meaning of large bodies of text and produces an average meaning score.
(The word "ouisa" comes from Ancient Greek and is a root for the English word "essence.")

The ousiometer builds on an earlier tool developed by the research team called the "hedonometer" (a happiness meter). While that instrument measures the overall emotional tone of language, the new approach examines broader patterns of meaning.

The researchers demonstrated that the ousiometer can analyze material from remarkably different sources, including Jane Austen's novels, Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories, the New York Times, Wikipedia, Twitter, and transcripts of talk radio programs.
The tool can also track how meaning shifts as a story unfolds.
For example, the researchers analyzed an English translation of Victor Hugo's Les Misérables and mapped its changing meaning throughout the novel.

They called this changing pattern an "ousiometric trajectory." The visualization resembles the twisting shape of a multicolored protein, with the narrative moving across a grid based on four contrasting pairs: dangerous/safe, weak/powerful, gentle/aggressive, and bad/good.
By following this path, researchers can observe how the underlying meaning of the text changes from one section of the story to another.
Why Counting Word Frequency Changes the Results
Another important innovation involved distinguishing between words themselves and how often people actually use them.
In linguistics, researchers describe individual words as categories called "types," while each appearance of a word in text is known as a "token."
(For example, as a category "apple" is a type and every time the word "apple" is used in a sentence is a token.)
This distinction matters because a word that appears millions of times contributes much more to everyday communication than one that is rarely used.

Earlier research often gave each word equal importance, regardless of its frequency. The Vermont team instead incorporated how often words appear in real communication, allowing patterns to emerge that might otherwise remain hidden.
This approach was particularly important for identifying the widespread preference for safety-related language.

The ten-member research team was led by Peter Dodds and Chris Danforth, professors in UVM's College of Engineering and Mathematical Sciences. Their collaborators included researchers from the Santa Fe Institute, the Complexity Science Hub in Austria, Howard Hughes Medical Center, the University of California, Berkeley, the University of Adelaide, and MassMutual Data Science.
Rethinking What Human Language Reveals About Us
Understanding this hidden safety bias could have consequences for how researchers study communication across society.
If words consistently reflect a preference for safety, that tendency may influence how stories are told, how information spreads, and how people interpret events and experiences.
The findings could eventually inform research into political communication, mental health messaging, and AI systems designed to interact with people.
More broadly, the study challenges the idea that human language can be understood primarily through emotions such as happiness, fear, and excitement.

Instead, the researchers propose that meaning has a deeper structure connected to power, danger, and order. Their findings suggest that language may reflect the challenges humans face when navigating uncertain environments, maintaining relationships, and identifying threats.

By revealing this previously overlooked structure, the team offers a new way to understand what words communicate and why certain kinds of meaning dominate everyday conversation. Human language, their research suggests, may be more closely connected to our fundamental need for safety than scientists have traditionally recognized.

- Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation.

Samples collected from asteroid Bennu by NASA are revealing surprising new details about how our Solar System formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago. A new chemical analysis challenges earlier theories about the asteroid's birthplace and suggests that Jupiter played an important role in shaping the materials from which Bennu and other ancient objects formed.

Bennu completes one orbit around the Sun every 1.2 years and makes a relatively close approach to Earth about every six years, coming within roughly 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles). NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission traveled to the asteroid, collected material from its surface, and successfully delivered the samples to Earth in 2023.

On September 23, 2023, a capsule carrying approximately 120 grams of asteroid material landed in the Utah desert. Scientists around the world subsequently received small portions of the precious cargo for detailed study.

Among them was Maria Schönbächler, Professor of Isotope Geochemistry at ETH Zurich, whose laboratory received half a gram of Bennu material. Her team immediately began examining the samples for clues about the asteroid's history.

The research, now published in Science Advances, has uncovered a distinctive chemical signature that not only helps identify Bennu's origins but also provides new evidence about the processes that shaped the early Solar System.
Bennu's Chemical Fingerprint Reveals Its Cosmic Relatives
To investigate Bennu's origins, the ETH Zurich researchers examined isotopes of three elements: iron, titanium, and chromium.

Isotopes are different forms of the same chemical element that contain varying numbers of neutrons, giving them slightly different masses. By measuring the relative amounts of these isotopes, scientists can identify a material's chemical fingerprint. These patterns provide clues about where an asteroid's ingredients originated and, in some cases, when they formed.

The analysis revealed that iron and titanium are distributed remarkably evenly throughout Bennu's material. It also uncovered a close chemical relationship between Bennu, the asteroid Ryugu, and a rare group of primitive meteorites known as CI meteorites.

CI meteorites are carbon-rich remnants of the early Solar System that have undergone relatively little alteration over billions of years. They are exceptionally uncommon among meteorites recovered on Earth.

Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites share strikingly similar isotopic fingerprints, suggesting that their original materials came from the same reservoir of ancient cosmic dust. Their chemical signatures also differ substantially from those of other known asteroids, meteorite groups, and planets.
These similarities offer an important clue about where these objects formed and what conditions existed during the Solar System's earliest stages.
Scientists Discover Bennu's Unexpected Birthplace

For years, researchers generally believed that primitive asteroids like Bennu originated in the outer Solar System, perhaps in the same distant regions where comets formed. They also suspected that Bennu's original material came together relatively late in the Solar System's development.
The new findings challenge both assumptions.
Instead, the researchers propose that the material that became Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites accumulated near a boundary known as the water-ice line.

This boundary marks the region in the disk surrounding the young Sun where temperatures were low enough for water vapor to freeze into ice. Around 4.5 billion years ago, it may have been a particularly important meeting place for material traveling from different parts of the developing Solar System.
Dust originating in both the inner and outer regions mixed near this boundary. Water ice helped the smallest particles stick together, allowing them to gradually accumulate into larger bodies.
"Bennu is a hybrid: the material does not clearly match either the inner or the outer Solar System," says Schönbächler.
Its unusual chemical composition suggests that Bennu formed from a combination of materials originating in both regions rather than from a single, isolated source.
Jupiter May Have Played a Crucial Role in Bennu's Formation
The researchers also developed a scenario explaining how this mixing could have occurred, with Jupiter emerging as a key player.

Jupiter began forming extraordinarily early in Solar System history, within approximately one million years of the Sun's birth. At that time, the young Sun was surrounded by a rotating disk of gas, dust, and ice.

Within this disk, countless small particles gradually collided and stuck together, building larger objects through a process called accretion. Over time, some of these growing bodies became asteroids and planets.
As Jupiter rapidly increased in mass, its immense gravitational influence began reshaping the distribution of material throughout the disk.

The researchers suggest that the growing gas giant acted somewhat like a structural barrier, preventing most larger particles from crossing its orbital region while still allowing finer dust to move around it.
This fine material, originating from different parts of the disk, could then mix extensively near the water-ice line.
According to the proposed scenario, the parent bodies of Bennu and Ryugu, along with the objects that produced CI meteorites, formed from this thoroughly mixed material.
Jupiter may therefore have helped determine not only where these ancient asteroids formed but also which ingredients became incorporated into them.
Ancient Dust and Ice Reveal the Ingredients That Built Earth
The proposed formation scenario could also explain two of Bennu's most intriguing characteristics: its abundance of water-bearing material and its chemical resemblance to the Sun.

Near the water-ice boundary, ice could evaporate as temperatures changed, releasing water vapor that later condensed again in cooler regions. This process would have helped concentrate water in the material from which Bennu formed.
Meanwhile, Jupiter's influence may have limited the movement of larger particles, leaving the asteroid's parent material dominated by fine dust.
Because these tiny particles could circulate and mix efficiently throughout the disk, they preserved a chemical composition that closely resembles the overall elemental mixture found in the Sun.
The process is somewhat similar to the way fine household dust spreads and settles across many different surfaces rather than remaining in one location.
This extensive mixing could explain why Bennu's material retains such a representative sample of the ingredients present during the Solar System's earliest history.
"Bennu may offer our best glimpse of the original mix of chemical elements from which the terrestrial planets were ultimately built," as Schönbächler states.
Bennu is considered an exceptionally primitive asteroid because its material formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago and has experienced relatively little chemical alteration since then.
That makes its samples particularly valuable for reconstructing the conditions that existed before Earth and the other rocky planets finished forming.
By studying the asteroid's chemistry, scientists can better understand how the Solar System developed and which processes determined the composition of its planets.
Bennu's water-bearing minerals and organic compounds also make it important for investigating how early Earth obtained some of the chemical ingredients necessary for life.

Although these findings do not establish exactly how those materials reached our planet, they provide valuable evidence about where such ingredients originated and how they were distributed throughout the young Solar System.
A New Mission to Mars' Moon Could Reveal More
Despite the new discoveries, several questions remain unanswered.
"We are now wondering whether other asteroids have the same isotopic signature as Bennu and Ryugu," Schönbächler goes on to state.

Researchers also want to determine more precisely how Jupiter influenced the movement of dust and whether its gravitational effects were responsible for favoring the accumulation of particularly fine particles.
Additional asteroid samples could help scientists test the proposed formation scenario and establish whether Bennu's chemical signature is shared by other ancient bodies.
With the Bennu analysis now complete, Schönbächler is looking ahead to another opportunity to examine material from the early Solar System.

Japan's space agency, JAXA, is preparing a sample-return mission to Phobos, one of Mars' two moons. The mission is scheduled to launch at the end of October 2026, with the goal of collecting material from the Martian moon and bringing it back to Earth.
"It would be exciting to also obtain this material to analyse it in my laboratory," she says.

Schönbächler plans to apply to JAXA for access to the samples. However, the scientific community will need to be patient. The capsule carrying material from Phobos is not expected to return to Earth until 2031.

Those future samples could provide another important piece of the puzzle, helping researchers determine how different regions of the early Solar System exchanged material and ultimately produced the planets, moons, and asteroids we observe today.
