The Southwestern US is in an ongoing megadrought that began in 2000, largely driven by overconsumption of water and climate change.
Water scarcity in the region is immediately visible in the Colorado River and the reservoirs of Lake Mead and Lake Powell.

As the region's agricultural industries and human populations grow, water levels continue to fall. Currently, surface reservoirs contain just 15 months' worth of water, based on average current consumption rates.
Farmlands use up the majority of the Basin's water supply: about 52 percent of water from the Colorado River goes to agricultural irrigation.
When those rivers, lakes and reservoirs dry up, those industries – and the ~40 million people who live in the Colorado River Basin – rely on another, hidden source of water below ground.
But researchers from Virginia Tech and Indiana University Bloomington show those groundwater supplies are also rapidly declining, in ways they didn't expect.
Their results are presented in a new paper published in Water Resources Research.
Vast quantities of water are stored in aquifers underground, in both the Upper and Lower regions of the Colorado River Basin.
The Upper Basin's groundwater has historically been considered more resilient, because it usually receives a top-up from snowmelt thanks to the Rockies and other mountains in the area.
But since at least the start of the 20th century, the amount of water landing on those mountains in the form of snow has been on a steady decline.
The snowpack across Utah and Colorado in March of 2026 was below 2001-2025 averages, and peaked about four weeks earlier than usual.
Scientists at the USGS have already linked the ongoing decline of snowfall to the Colorado River's ever-worsening stagnancy.
But the new analysis of data from 2004 to 2023 reveals that those once-reliable Upper Basin groundwater supplies are drying up even faster than those in the lower Basin.
During a recent period of severe drought, from October 2019 to the end of September 2022, the Upper Basin lost roughly 4.6 trillion gallons of groundwater.
The Lower Basin, once considered the more vulnerable of the two, lost around 2.5 trillion gallons in that period.
"We generally think of the Upper Basin as more resilient because of its snowmelt-driven recharge," says Esther Oyedele, a geoscientist at Virginia Tech and lead author of the paper.
"I did not expect to see so much groundwater loss there during the recent drought."
It's unlikely the basins have been replenished, since snow has been so scarce in the years since.
"What surprised me even more was that groundwater did not track surface-water shortages in the same way in the Upper and Lower Basins," Oyedele says.
In the Upper Basin, their analysis showed surface water deficits were strongly coupled with the probability of groundwater drought.
But in the Lower Basin, there was less of a link.
This might be because surface water availability in the Lower Basin is already chronically limited, so groundwater extraction there is less dependent on how much water is flowing above ground.

"Continued groundwater depletion, especially in the Upper Basin, could further reduce groundwater contributions to rivers and intensify the feedback between groundwater loss and surface-water shortages," says hydrologist Susanna Werth, an expert in remote sensing at Virginia Tech.
"Looking at surface water alone is no longer enough. Protecting the Colorado River Basin requires managing the water above and below ground."
The research has been published in Water Resources Research.
Raising a low hormone level might seem like a straightforward way to restore balance, but for testosterone, health improvements could depend on how far that level rises.
Testosterone helps support sexual desire, muscles, and bones. Some men with a deficiency receive replacement treatment. Could the hormone's level also affect how regularly the heart beats?

A review in the Journal of the Endocrine Society, led by cardiovascular researcher Anand Reddy Maligireddy at the University of Kansas Medical Center, explores that question. The team examined existing human studies and laboratory research.

Their conclusion is that both low and high testosterone levels are linked to a higher risk of a heart rhythm disorder, though it's not yet clear whether the hormone itself is to blame. The researchers suggest that risk may be lowest around the middle of the normal hormone range.
For men who need testosterone treatment, this could help inform the hormone level doctors aim for and how they monitor patients.

The disorder occurs when the heart's upper chambers lose their coordinated rhythm. Called atrial fibrillation, it can cause a fluttering heartbeat, fatigue, and dizziness, although some people have no symptoms. It also raises stroke risk, and some patients need long-term blood-thinning medication.

"Both too little and too much testosterone appear to raise the risk of atrial fibrillation, through separate biological mechanisms," says study co-author and cardiologist Rajat Barua of Kansas City Veterans Affairs Medical Center.

Earlier population studies had linked low testosterone to a higher risk of the rhythm disorder. Among them, the Framingham Heart Study found that lower hormone levels were associated with a higher risk of developing atrial fibrillation in some age groups.
Evidence concerning higher levels includes an analysis of 4,570 older men without previous cardiovascular disease.

Over a median 4.4 years, men in the highest two testosterone groups had roughly twice the risk of atrial fibrillation as those in the middle group. Overall, 286 of the men developed the condition during the study. The same study found no statistically significant increase in risk at the low end.

The 2023 TRAVERSE trial examined testosterone treatment. It randomly assigned 5,246 men with low testosterone and existing cardiovascular disease or increased cardiovascular risk to receive either testosterone gel or a gel containing no testosterone.

Atrial fibrillation occurred in 3.5 percent of the testosterone group and 2.4 percent of the comparison group. However, the trial did not find an increase in its main combined measure of cardiovascular death, nonfatal heart attack, or nonfatal stroke.

Laboratory research suggests that low and high testosterone could affect the heart through different pathways. Low levels may disrupt calcium regulation inside heart cells, while higher levels may alter potassium currents. These processes help control the electrical signals coordinating heartbeats.

The researchers recommend assessing a patient's heart health and other risks before treatment begins. Obesity, high blood pressure, alcohol use, and sleep apnea – in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep – should also be considered. Excess body fat is itself linked to lower testosterone.

It's worth noting that not all studies agree, however. A 2024 analysis of 106 randomized trials did not find a statistically significant increase in atrial fibrillation when trials other than TRAVERSE were considered together.
Observational studies also cannot establish that hormone levels caused the disorder, only show correlations in the data.
Aiming for the middle of the normal range has not yet been shown to reduce atrial fibrillation, but the findings could help guide us toward more individualized testosterone treatment and monitoring.
For now, further trials are needed to establish whether doing so leads to fewer heart rhythm problems.
The research has been published in Journal of the Endocrine Society.
When you picture lightning, it tends to be fairly straightforward – a jagged gash of light that splits the sky, disappearing in less time than it takes to blink.
But for centuries, a strange picture of a more eerie form has emerged.
Thousands of records and eyewitness accounts have told of balls of lightning hovering above the ground before disappearing in a pop like soap bubbles.

This fleeting phenomenon is all but impossible to study – and reports vary wildly in descriptions of its size, its hue, and even its behavior, making it one of the most peculiar mysteries in atmospheric science.

But if you can't catch ball lightning in a field, physicist Chuliang Zhou and colleagues at the Chinese Academy of Sciences have reasoned, maybe we can learn more by reproducing something like it in a lab.

"Here we report the first controlled generation of a macroscopic, long-lived soliton driven by relativistic terahertz electromagnetic fields," the researchers write in a paper published in Nature Photonics.
"This work establishes a laboratory-accessible platform for investigating optical soliton physics, advanced energy storage mechanisms, and the long-standing scientific puzzle of ball lightning."
A soliton is essentially a single, self-contained wave that keeps its shape and structural integrity through a delicate balance of physical forces.
They can form in plasma, water, light, potentially even some biological membranes – basically any medium where competing physical effects can balance to sustain a stable wave.
Some theories suggest that ball lightning is a kind of electromagnetic soliton, trapping energy in a shell of plasma.
To find out whether they could make this kind of soliton, the researchers turned to a very, very pointy piece of tungsten.

OK, it was a little more complicated than that – but the tungsten needle, with a tip just 100 nanometers across, was instrumental. A human hair, for context, measures between 80,000 and 100,000 nanometers across.
The researchers fired an ultrashort laser pulse at the needle, generating a powerful electromagnetic wave that traveled along its length.

When the wave reached the tip, its energy became concentrated into an extraordinarily intense electric field that stripped electrons from atoms in a waiting cloud of argon gas, creating a superheated bubble of ionized argon – plasma.
It flickered into existence as a tiny ball of light.
The fragile, luminous sphere started as a pinprick around 80 micrometers across, then expanded to a larger pinprick several hundred micrometers over the next 100 nanoseconds.

That might not sound like a long time, but it's vastly longer than the electromagnetic pulse from which it was born. And rather than simply dissipating like an ordinary cloud of hot plasma, the sphere maintained its structure as it expanded.
The researchers tracked this expansion and analyzed the wavelengths of light the sphere emitted as it cooled, comparing their observations with theoretical models and computer simulations.
This expansion, the researchers found, matched the theoretical predictions for an electromagnetic soliton.
This suggests that electromagnetic energy remained trapped within the plasma, helping sustain the glowing orb even as it expanded.
By contrast, their simulations of the thermal expansion in ordinary plasma produced a much faster, more diffuse process.
But a tiny dot of light in a carefully controlled laboratory experiment is far from the wild atmospheric conditions where ball lightning is typically reported.
So, the researchers used their theoretical models to see how the phenomenon might behave at larger scales, driven by lower-frequency electromagnetic radiation.
Their calculations suggested that electromagnetic solitons driven by microwaves, rather than terahertz radiation, could theoretically grow to meters across and persist for seconds.
That's much closer to some of the eyewitness reports of how mysterious balls of lightning behave.
It's far from a definitive explanation for ball lightning – but solving meteorological mysteries isn't the only potential application for these tiny fireballs.

The ability to trap electromagnetic energy in a stable, localized structure could also open new avenues for energy-storage technologies and studying how light interacts with matter under extreme conditions.

"Our controlled laboratory approach to spatiotemporal characterization under tunable conditions provides a systematic pathway to decode the century-old enigma of ball lightning formation," the researchers write.

"By unifying extreme field photonics, plasma science, and atmospheric geophysics, our findings redefine terahertz-driven platforms as discovery engines for both applied technologies and unresolved natural phenomena."
The research has been published in Nature Photonics.

Our voices have superpowers. From a coach firing up a soccer team before a big game to a mother soothing a cranky baby in the middle of the night, the human voice is key to expressing feelings and forging connections. The tone of a person’s voice might even communicate feelings to loved ones better than facial expressions. So what happens to a person when their voice disappears?

People who have lost the ability to speak due to neurodegenerative disease or brain injury are talking again thanks to groundbreaking technologies that can decode the instructions the brain sends to speech muscles. For this issue’s cover story, senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders interviewed Casey Harrell, a man who regained his voice — lost to ALS — through a brain-computer interface.

You can listen to Harrell in his own words in Season Two of The Deep End, our award-winning podcast. Harrell told Sanders: “It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”

In the podcast, Sanders digs into other innovations, including AI voice cloning, as well as the sinister potential of such technology to hijack people’s voices. “It might be used in a way people don’t want to have happen,” she says. Hear more wherever you get your podcasts.

In this issue, we also report on the progress in developing an effective treatment for stiff person syndrome, a rare autoimmune disorder that makes the body’s muscles freeze without warning. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration hasn’t yet approved any treatments for the disorder, which occurs in roughly 2 in 100,000 people. But that could some day change. Researchers are testing new CAR T cell therapies, senior writer Meghan Rosen reports. The process involves modifying a patient’s white blood cells so they wipe out harmful immune cells. Scientists hope a single treatment could cure the disease.

And there’s more controversy about using AI in mathematics, senior physics writer Emily Conover reports. OpenAI made waves when the company announced that it had solved one of the most famous puzzles in math — a day after mathematicians reported advances on a similar problem. The development is among a flood of AI-fueled achievements this year and raises big questions about who gets credit when the algorithms are doing the work.

About 1671, parson Symonds, who officiated at Garsdon church in north Wiltshire in south west England, was riding home late one night when a specter leapt up behind him. The specter rode parallel to him until they came to the parsonage, where it jumped off. The apparition then turned to face Symonds, and “gap’d at him”. Symonds identified the ghost as that of John Estcourt, a gentleman who had died about two years earlier.

Halloween is all about witches and ghosts. In English scientific circles in the second half of the 17th century, there was a discussion about whether such things existed and how their existence could be proved.

The Royal Society, founded in 1660, was the country’s principal scientific institution. Joseph Glanvill, a Royal Society fellow, investigated spirits and witches. His Saducismus Triumphatus(1681) aimed to prove their existence by cataloguing cases in detail. He argued that denying them was to deny God’s existence.

Symonds’ haunting was recorded by that of another of the society’s fellows, John Aubrey, in a survey of Wiltshire’s natural world. Aubrey agreed with Glanvill that the supernatural deserved serious study and directed his readers to Saducismus, but he thought Glanvill somewhat gullible.
Aubrey was born in 1626 at Easton Piercy, a few miles from Garsdon. I have edited John Aubrey’s Natural History to mark his 400th anniversary.

This natural history of Wiltshire was begun in 1656 and was the first English county survey of nature to be attempted – although by the time he finished it, decades later, other surveys had already been published. It was an important scientific work, and in 1691, acknowledging that, the Royal Society had the Natural History copied and added to its library.

Its subject matter is highly idiosyncratic, and Aubrey sometimes goes off on tangents. He covers swan-sized dragons in north Africa in a chapter on birds and the existence of giants in a section called “Men and Women”. Almost at the end of the text is a chapter titled “Accidents” that records extraordinary events, including supernatural ones, like the haunting of Symonds.
Aubrey has long been seen as naive, partly because of Miscellanies (1696), the only book he published, which recorded tales of the unexplained. In the Natural History, he was clear:

Though I myselfe never saw any such things, yet I will not conclude that there is no truth at all in these reports. I believe that extraordinarily there have been such apparitions: but where one is true, a hundred are figments.

He also documented exposed frauds, such as Katherine Waldron, who pretended to be bewitched and endured pins being driven into her flesh to prove it. As the objective of natural history at this time was to gather evidence from which new scientific theories could be developed, Aubrey’s method in chronicling cases was entirely in keeping with the aims of scientific enterprise.

So, Aubrey was neither uncritical nor dismissive about Symonds’ story. Symonds was “a lusty strong fellow”, presumably not someone nervous or hysterical and prone to flights of imagination. His position as a churchman also gave authority to his testimony. Yet Aubrey noted a French saying that drunk men saw devils, a skeptical observation that cast doubt on the account. But he concluded with a strange detail: it was corroborated by the parson’s horse, “that trembled and sweat, when he came home and continued to do so the next day, and would not eat his oates”. The horse could not lie or get drunk; its fear, manifest in the trembling and sweat, was genuine.

Aubrey recorded another anecdote about a night ride. It concerned Sir Ralph Bankes’ valet:“a briske young fellow”, who, riding late over Badbury Warren, Dorset, discerned something that looked black, which, as he approached, became bigger.
Feare came upon him, and he protested his haire stood on end: but thought he, I have but a life to lose and I will see it, be it spirit or not.
The valet spurred his horse and came to the place, only to find the apparition was “a heap of horse dung”.

In Symonds’ haunting, the truth of the specter could not be tested; but witnesses were recorded, and their testimony weighed. In the valet’s case, the witness tested the truth of the ghost himself and found it was a pile of dung.

Aubrey applied the same empirical method throughout his Natural History to both natural and supernatural phenomena. He assembled evidence with care, tested it if he could and resisted easy conclusions. It’s an approach worth remembering this Halloween when fantastical tales hit your social media feed. A phantom may prove to be a load of poo.

The Pentagon has granted the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a controversial and little-used “heat ray” weapon at the U.S.-Mexico border, prompting questions over how safe it is and how it works.

The weapon is called the Active Denial System, and it is considered a nonlethal weapon: it causes pain but is not supposed to damage tissue. It works using millimeter waves, which—true to their name—have wavelengths between one and 10 millimeters. Millimeter waves are also used in full-body scanners, such as those in airports—but the military weapon puts out its 95-gigahertz waves at a higher intensity for just a few seconds at a time, says Kenneth Foster, a professor emeritus of bioengineering at the University of Pennsylvania.

This energy penetrates about 0.4 mm, the thickness of about four sheets of standard printer paper, of the skin, where it excites water molecules in cells and heats them up. The feeling is reportedly similar to standing in front of a hot oven. “It causes intense pain, but the exposure is not long enough to do damage,” Foster says.

If the weapon is used at the border, it will mark one of the few uses of this technology ever since its development in the early 2000s, as CNN reported on Wednesday. According to the nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights (PHR), the system was used briefly in Afghanistan in 2010 but has not been employed in warfare since then. Prison officials in Los Angeles considered testing the device for riot control in 2010, yet pushback from civil rights groups and the Federal Communications Commission led to the program being scrapped.
“The weapon is politically toxic,” Foster says.

The system is bulky and temperamental; it doesn’t work well in rain, fog or mist because the moisture attenuates the heating effect on the targeted person. Foster suspects that the system’s cost, expense and bulk have a lot to do with why it hasn’t been used more; other nonlethal methods such as sound cannons are cheaper and more available, he says.

Persistent concerns about the safety of something that sounds suspiciously like a microwave oven are also a barrier. Microwaves, with their longer wavelengths, penetrate farther into skin and can cause more damage. Military testing suggests that exposure to millimeter-wave nonlethal weapons does not cause skin damage. Tests on volunteers in 2005 and 2006 did lead to a handful of people getting skin blisters and rashes, however. An incident in 2007 in which the weapon was set at the incorrect power and pulse duration led to one airman receiving second-degree blistering burns on 8 percent of his body. So it is possible that improper usage could cause injury.

“There is very, very little published on these weapons,” says Rohini Haar, an emergency physician at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Public Health and a medical adviser at PHR. Without published research, she says, there is little information on their safety in general or on potential differences in safety in real-world usage versus experimental or training exercises.
John Erath, Senior Policy Director for the Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation, a nonprofit, points out that testing such weapons in human trials for safety is “an ethical dead-end.”

PHR has also documented numerous cases of crowd-control weapons being used against people with no easy way to escape. Indiscriminate use of the system could cause injury not just from the heat itself but also from the reaction of those targeted, says Michael Crowley. He is a senior researcher at the U.K.-based nonprofit Omega Research Foundation, which tracks the use of military and police weapons and human rights abuses.

“Given its silent and invisible nature, the ‘pain ray’ makes avoidance of the weapon difficult, which could prevent people from dispersing safely, lead to panic-driven stampedes and consequent serious injuries,” Crowley says.

“Furthermore, those subsequently injured or crowd members who have existing mobility difficulties, including the elderly and very young, may not be able to leave the area and then be subject to repeated or prolonged exposure of this weapon, potentially leading to further intolerable pain and serious injuries,” he adds.

In August Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., took the stage at the Department of Health and Human Services headquarters in Washington, D.C., and announced what would be a first for the U.S. government: an upcoming formal definition of “ultraprocessed foods.” The reason for defining the term, Kennedy said, was to help bring healthier food options to Americans. But Kennedy held back sharing what, exactly, the definition would be.

Processed foods have been a target for Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” agenda. Some scientists and health organizations, including the American Heart Association, support a federal definition, too. But a consensus definition on ultraprocessed foods has been notoriously difficult to reach.

The lack of a clear definition can create “ambiguity” in how to enforce or monitor food regulations, says Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutrition science professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. “It can leave manufacturers and retailers confused,” in addition to consumers.

Now, more than two months later, the federal effort to define ultraprocessed foods has reportedly stalled. According to Bloomberg Law and the Wall Street Journal, Kennedy’s plan was met with a wave of pushback from the food industry and the White House because of concerns about the legal ramifications of such a definition.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, ultraprocessed foods make up some 55 percent of the average American’s daily calories—the percentage is even higher among young people aged one to 18. Researchers say defining these foods would make it easier for the government to limit ultraprocessed foods in school lunches, for example, or to put labels on food packaging to better inform consumers about what they are eating.

That matters, because evidence suggests ultraprocessed foods are bad for us: they are linked to the risk of chronic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, as well as worse mental health outcomes. But it’s unclear whether these ill effects are entirely linked to the foods’ ingredients or nutritional value, the way in which they were processed or something else.
Ultraprocessed foods may also be addictive and tend to be convenient, portable and heavily marketed to children, Taillie says.

We asked the experts what they consider to be ultraprocessed foods, why these foods are often considered “unhealthy” and why it’s so hard to agree on a definition—on the federal level and in the field.
How do scientists define ultraprocessed foods?
Imagine an ultraprocessed food: whatever you are thinking of, you are probably right on the money, says Marion Nestle, a nutrition expert and a professor emerita at New York University.
“In my experience, consumers ‘get’ the concept easily, so easily that they start avoiding them,” Nestle says.

To Nestle, ultraprocessed foods are those that are “industrially produced, designed to be irresistible, if not addictive, and are usually formulated with lots of sugar, salt, and flavor, color and texture additives.”
“An operating definition is ‘you can’t make them in your home kitchen,’” she adds.

“If you think about what a lot of these ultraprocessed foods are, they are designed for consumption,” says Matthew Landry, an assistant professor of global health and biobehavioral sciences at the University of California, Irvine. They might come in textures and flavors designed to keep us snacking.
Some scientists have sought to categorize processed foods with tools, such as the NOVA food classification system.

Under this system, foods are sorted into four categories: Group 1 includes unprocessed and minimally processed food, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, nuts, legumes and meat. Group 2 includes “culinary ingredients,” such as salt, sugar and fats. Group 3 includes processed foods that are canned or fermented, such as cheese. The fourth group represents ultraprocessed foods and is comprised of items that have undergone “extensive chemical or physical processing,” Taillie says.

Foods in this fourth category are typically high in added sugar, sodium, and saturated fats and may include artificial ingredients such as flavors, colors or emulsifiers, Taillie says. Chips, candies and frozen meals might fall under Group 4.
Where things get tricky are the edge cases: What category should a flavored yogurt fall under? What about granola bars or tofu?

NOVA only classifies foods based on processing levels, not nutritional value. Other classification systems, such as one called FPro, attempt to take nutritional information into account. But scientists haven’t agreed on one shared system.
Why is it so hard to come up with a consensus definition?

There are several reasons. For one, companies aren’t required to disclose how a food product was processed on its label, Taillie says. Using other sources of information—such as ingredients lists—can serve somewhat as a proxy, she says. For example, if a product’s ingredients include added colors, sweeteners, thickeners or chemical names that you don’t recognize, then it’s probably ultraprocessed.
Complicating matters further is that, as with any food classification system, drawing a line between what is “processed” and what is not is somewhat arbitrary, Taillie says.

“You have to set a threshold somewhere, which means that there are going to be some products that are captured that people will look at and inherently feel that should not be captured, or vice versa,” she says.

Under systems such as the NOVA scale, foods that experts might consider beneficial to our health, such as some yogurt, could be categorized alongside less healthy ones. In a July journal article, for instance, Landry and a co-author argued that ultraprocessed, plant-based meat alternatives such as soy burgers can act as a “gateway” to eating whole, plant proteins, such as beans or lentils. In turn, making a clear definition for foods that are processed but have other “redeeming nutritional qualities” is challenging, Landry says.

There’s also a layer of complexity when considering how a definition may be used. Not everyone has access to whole foods—people who are food-insecure, for instance, might rely on shelf-stable foods, such as frozen meals. Landry argues that any federal action to define ultraprocessed foods should take that into account.

And then there’s opposition from the food industry, which has “absolutely” been a roadblock, Nestle says. Food companies’ antagonism toward reaching a consensus definition has been “strong and well coordinated,” Taillie agrees, with actions that have included lobbying at the state and federal level.
“These are among the most profitable products on the market,” Nestle adds.
If you’re interested in cutting down on ultraprocessed foods, there are benefits to doing so. But there’s no need to sweat over a single cupcake or cup of instant noodles, experts say.

“As a consumer, I’m not too worried about whether this slice of bread that I have in the morning is ultraprocessed or not,” Taillie says. “I’m really looking at the course of the entire day. How many foods am I consuming that might fit into that criteria?”

GOODYEAR, Ariz. — An Airbus A320neo, one of the world's most popular planes, rolled off the Mobile, Alabama, factory line in July 2022, painted bright yellow for its next destination: Spirit Airlines.

It was built to fly for decades. But this May, less than four years later, it was stripped for parts worth millions and crushed, the steel teeth of an excavator tearing through its fuselage at a facility on the outskirts of Phoenix.

More aircraft are getting dismantled years, if not decades, earlier than expected, industry executives told CNBC. It is the result of a shortage of parts, none more precious and expensive than aircraft engines, that has exasperated airlines and driven up costs for years.
Even after the engines are removed, firms are looking for parts as varied as landing gear and antennae to sell.

"It's the first time in my career that involved purchasing an aircraft that's less than five years since date of manufacture," said Bill Thompson, vice president who leads aircraft and engine acquisition for the Americas at aviation asset management and trading firm EirTrade Aviation, which bought the less than 4-year-old Airbus A320neo earlier this year.

He said the company paid "single-digit" millions each for that airplane and a similarly aged one, and it expects to make a profit from selling the more than 1,000 parts it took off them before they were crushed.
"I don't know if you're going to sell the coffee makers but you never know. Sometimes you do," he said.

Twenty-one newest-generation aircraft were torn down from June 2025 through this past August, according to aviation data and advisory firm IBA Group. The scrapped planes were 6.4 years old on average, and included mostly Airbus but also some Boeing planes. That compares with an average retirement age for narrow-body airplanes of 21.7 years, IBA said.

"Anytime that you end up with any period of market softness in aircraft availability, engine availability, it's going to cause investors to look at other options," said Simon Goodson, CEO of AerFin, a company that buys, sells, repairs and leases aircraft and parts. "We always say to our aircraft and engine traders, 'Please don't fall in love with the metal.'"
Hundreds of aircraft are retired each year as manufacturers ramp up production for airlines, so older planes are swapped out for newer, more fuel-efficient models.
But aside from retiring aging planes, some owners don't want to wait around for replacement parts or repairs on younger jets.

"A year might not sound that long, but does three or four years?" said Dave Querio, CEO of Ascent Aviation Services, a company that repairs, modifies, stores and disassembles aircraft, based in Marana, Arizona, outside of Tucson. "That's the issue for the aircraft that came in in '23, '24 and '25."
In some cases, owners can reap more for the parts than they can selling the plane or paying storage costs and waiting for it to get back in the air again.
Querio said he hasn't seen "the volume of younger aircraft being torn down as I'm seeing today."
A major reason for the young retirements is the long wait and rising prices for jet engines.
One problem is that cutting-edge engines that burn hotter and use less fuel are coming up for maintenance far earlier than airlines expected.

The maintenance requests have kept engine repair and overhaul facilities backed up, from those owned by manufacturing giants GE Aerospace and RTX unit Pratt & Whitney to smaller, independent ones. Airlines and leasing firms have been hunting for spare parts and engines anywhere they can find them, like here in Goodyear, Arizona.

The trend has added more fuel to the already hot secondhand parts market. An engine fan blade could cost $50,000 or even more than $100,000 for bigger jets, Goodson said. Engines that power some Airbus A320neo aircraft have 20 of those blades. A disc for the engine, meanwhile, could cost between $1 million and $2 million.

An engine recall because of a manufacturing defect has backed up repair shops and grounded hundreds of Airbus planes around the world. Spirit Airlines bore the brunt of that problem in the United States, years before the airline collapsed.

The engine is made by Pratt & Whitney, which issued the recall in 2023 after discovering contaminated powdered metal used in making some parts. Those engines are worth close to $17 million this year at the high end, up 60% from the upper end of the range in 2019, according to IBA.
Airlines are removing some engines off retired planes to keep current aircraft flying while they wait for engines to come back from the shop.
"So you're just playing Legos and moving engines on and off aircraft," said Mike Stengel, a partner at AeroDynamic Advisory, an aerospace consulting firm.
The problems are driving up the cost to buy or rent one of the popular engines to record levels.

Renting one is ranging from about $160,000 to $180,000 a month, according to IBA data. A competing engine for the A320neo family made by CFM International, a joint venture of GE Aerospace and France's Safran, is far from a bargain, renting in a similar range of $130,000 to $180,000 a month.
The problems with young retirements predate Spirit's collapse.
The 4-year-old Airbus plane that was torn down outside Phoenix in May is a key example. The aircraft was put in storage because of the engine recall, and it stayed until it was torn apart.
But the company's demise has brought more of its Airbus fleet to the market, forcing owners to figure out if it's worth the wait for engines or other parts.

CNBC visited AerSale's facility in Goodyear on a scorching day in late June, less than two months after Spirit collapsed, where dozens of the idle yellow planes were stored. It was so soon after the airline's demise that a former Detroit-based Spirit captain, Glenn Zecchin, popped in and asked about opportunities to ferry Spirit's aircraft to the desert, and to peek in on his former airline's planes.
"I knew the airplanes were there, and I wanted to see what happened," said Zecchin, who is now flying corporate jets.
A jet parked at the storage facility and maintenance hangar still had Spirit in-flight menus and safety cards in the bungee cord seatbacks. Pilot manuals were still in the cockpit.

Not all of these aircraft will be destroyed. Some companies that owned Spirit's planes before bankruptcy will just sell their parts, but some may keep the planes in storage. Other aircraft may go on to fly for other airlines, with potential carriers ripping out Spirit's tight 28-inch seat pitch for something roomier.

But as long as they're not flying, it means paying storage fees, which vary by aircraft type. Some planes in desert facilities — selected because the arid climate can preserve the aircraft better and avoid corrosion — can sit for decades.
Others won't make it back into the air if there's enough demand for the parts and too long of a wait to get the plane flying again.

"After you get rid of all the valuable equipment and sell it back into the aftermarket, what's really left is just a metal carcass that you will literally take a crane and crush," said AeroDynamic's Stengel. Then the owner can "sell it to recyclers that will make of it what they will, maybe into beer cans or something outside of aerospace."
Ascent's Querio said some owners opt to take that route.
"It's a little melancholy to watch it at times," he said. "But sometimes, it's kind of a thrill to ... see how fast an aircraft can be crunched up and sent off to the smelter."
— CNBC's Erin Black contributed to this report.

Retail investors who are trying to beat the market by buying individual stocks and complex exchange-traded funds may be better off with broad market index funds, according to Elm Wealth's Victor Haghani.

"I'm not sure that investors are that much more sophisticated than they were 30 years ago," the firm's founder and chief investment officer told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "We still are human beings and we're subject to certain kinds of biases — particularly extrapolation bias where whatever has happened recently in the past we tend to believe that it's going to continue into the future."
Haghani, who was a founding partner at hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, emphasizes cost-effective investment strategies as a priority at his current firm.

"It's an environment that continues to be tough for individual non-professionals to generate alpha," he said. "[Retail investors are] just very well served by having some exposure to broader index funds overall."
According to Haghani, access to elaborate strategies doesn't necessarily provide advantages.

"Whether it's Citadel or Jane Street or Hudson River Trading, they're just minting money every single day. So, it's an opportunity-rich environment — if you happen to have a billion dollars to spend on tech each year," he said. "If you're a retail investor sitting at home and trying to find opportunities, you have to realize that probably on the other side of your trades is [Citadel CEO] Ken Griffin or whoever, and it's probably not going to end all that well."
However, RBC Capital Markets' Valerie Grimba sees sophisticated funds playing a strategic role in retail investors' portfolios.
"More choice is ultimately a good thing," the firm's director of global ETF strategy said in the same interview.

She said funds holding 10 to 15 stocks can help investors participate in specific investment themes without having to identify their eventual biggest winner, while derivative-based products can be used to generate income in various ways.
But Grimba also emphasized that investors need to understand the holdings and trade-offs of the strategies they choose.
"It's more important than ever for an individual investor to understand what they're buying," she said. "You should be able to explain to your friend what it is in the ETF and what you're buying."
Clayface rolls into the box office fray but faces competition from the second weekend of You Can See Everything as the buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary expands.

Warner Bros. released director James Watkins’ body-horror feature Clayface in more than 3,400 North American theaters and it grossed $10.4 million domestically on Friday, including Thursday previews, adding $4.3 million internationally for the day. Earning an A- CinemaScore from audiences, Clayface could be headed for around $24 million domestically for the weekend, which would be just under the studio’s initial projection of $25 million to $30 million.

This marks the first DC Studios movie to launch since Supergirl had a disappointing opening of $37.1 million domestically over the summer on a $170 million budget. The $44 million-budgeted Clayface has impressed critics more than Supergirl, with a 76 score from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes and a 94 from audiences. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter, critic Frank Scheck called Clayface “a big swing that definitely pays off.” Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie star in the story of Matt Hagen (Harries), an actor who turns to a scientist (Ackie) for assistance when his face becomes disfigured.

You Can See Everything collected $6.1 million on Friday from 2,600 North American locations to bring its domestic cume to $31.7 million. The A24 film, which has been building awards buzz, adds to last weekend’s momentum and could collect $20 million in its sophomore frame. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Holmes widened after opening with $15 million from 855 theaters domestically, which gave it the highest-grossing launch for a release under 1,000 theaters since 2006’s Borat.

Looking to take third place is Laika’s stop-motion animated movie Wildwood, grossing $4.2 million Friday and heading to an expected $11.2 million for the weekend. Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay lead the voice cast for Travis Knight’s feature about a teen girl venturing to an enchanted forest to save her baby brother. Earning an A CinemaScore, Wildwood holds a dazzling 100 percent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with Scheck heralding it as “stupendous in every aspect.”

After winning the box office battle last weekend, Paramount and Legendary’s Street Fighter looks to land around $8.4 million with a roughly 73 percent decline to move its domestic cume to $46.7 million. Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji and Callina Liang lead director Kitao Sakurai’s adaptation of the Capcom video game centering on a combat tournament.

Likely to round out the top five is Black Bear’s romantic fantasy Wicker, which picked up $2.3 million domestically on Friday, including Thursday previews, from 1,471 North American theaters and is expected to open with $5.5 million. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard star in directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s movie about a woman in a quiet village who gets a wicker husband.
In his review for THR, critic Richard Lawson praised Wicker’s “winning mix of irreverence and compassion.” It holds a 94 score on Rotten Tomatoes from both critics and audiences.

Opening quietly in 880 North American theaters from Sony Pictures is Taika Waititi‘s Klara and the Sun, which made $300,000 and heads to around $725,000 for the weekend. Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams lead the adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel about a robot companion connecting with a sick girl. THR chief film critic David Rooney deemed it a “wretched mess.”
Additionally, Amazon MGM Studios releases Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G: Who Iz I? in just 125 theaters on only Friday and Saturday ahead of its Prime Video debut.
Amazon’s A Course Called Ireland was not supposed to be a Bill Murray TV show, but that’s pretty much what we got — not that Tom Coyne is complaining. (Murray is, a little.)

A Course Called Ireland, an adaptation of Coyne’s 2009 book of the same name, premieres Sunday on Paramount+. The six-episode, 30-minutes-per-episode series is as breezy as the Irish coast’s weather. Its original intention was to retrace the journey chronicled in Coyne’s bestseller — the golf writer once walked the island playing every golf course it had to offer — but this version of A Course Called Ireland became, as Murray grumpily laments in at least one episode to a director, “The Bill Murray Fucking Show.”
Murray has time for pretty much everyone who wants a photo — it is the production crew taking the professional videos he’d like to avert the lenses of.

“I’m heavy in the show. For an executive producer, that’s about as heavy as you can get,” Murray told The Hollywood Reporter. “I don’t want to complain about that. I did my complaining then. It’s too late to complain.”

I’m on a Zoom call with Murray, who is wandering the streets of Boston solo after sunset, and Coyne, who is sitting in a house in the Carribean. In a bucket hat and without a care in the world, Murray speaks kindly but candidly about making his buddy Coyne’s TV dream come true.

“I thought I was going to be an executive producer who would just show up and wait for the fresh croissants and stuff, not do much of anything,” Murray, who has only seen the first two episodes, explained. “If it comes back to being about Tom’s book, I’m going to be happy — I was not happy that they were sort of making it a little bit too much about me.”

Coyne is cool with whatever. He’s probably just relieved to have finally optioned this thing after 17 years of trying. I asked if he thinks the show gets made without the carrot of marketing it as a Bill Murray golf series.

“I’m realistic. I knew that when the producer bought it, that a Tom Coyne-headlined show was not going to be produced by Skydance Sports on Paramount+ and the BBC and all those things, right? I know that,” Coyne told THR. “So, yeah, Bill was a huge help to come along as a guest — as we envisioned it — a guest on my travels around Ireland.”

“The show, as it comes together, naturally it becomes more Bill-focused. But I’m not naive about why that’s the case. Bill’s amazing, and he’s amazing in the show,” he continued. “Whether it was Bill Murray or Charles Barkley or Shaquille O’Neal — it’s someone. It was never going to be ‘The Tom Coyne Show.'”
(For what it’s worth: Skydance, I’d still watch.)
It sounds like A Course Called Ireland could have starred Barkley or O’Neal — or Steph Curry, or Tom Holland or anyone, really.
“Every celebrity who golfs was brought up at some point,” Coyne said.

But Murray made the most sense. He and Coyne share Irish roots and they already play a lot of golf together — they even own a course together. Murray, Coyne and Jason Kelce of all people (Murray’s from Philly) own the historic, 9-hole Sullivan County Golf Club in the Catskills. (Kelce is among the guests in A Course Called Ireland, along with Chris O’Dowd and a few Murray brothers.)
“Bill’s the kind of friend…he looks out for people and knows that he can lend something to their lives of significance,” Coyne said.

That’s just what Murray has done here. There (Ireland), Murray saved his best moments for the locals. There was a time where Bill Murray Moments were up there with Chuck Norris Facts in terms of internet lore. Now, they’ve become almost the expectation among an adoring public whom, even more than a selfie, want a story. I asked Murray if the mainstreaming of his almost-mythical encounters has turned something special into a burden.

“If you’re living correctly, it’s not a burden. But if you’re stuck in something else, then yeah, it’s hard,” Murray said. “It’s just like another aspect of life. Something gets going, and you get attached to something — or something attaches to you — and you’re not free…to operate the way you wish to operate.”
Cell phone cameras have also stolen some of the magic. Juggling these impromptu meet cutes can be “a game of catch sometimes,” Murray said.

“Sometimes someone throws one too hard at you from too close, and someone throws one that you just can’t get to,” he explained the metaphor. “And sometimes you throw one and it hits them in the nose.”
And sometimes you get a well-earned mini-break from always being “on.” Those times are vital for rejuvenation — especially when you’re 75 years old.
Other times you fly commercial and it is what it is.
“Here it is again. It’s back,” Murray recalled thinking as he walked to his gate. “I’d had like four days without it. I felt like kind of refreshed.”

“I had a lot of energy, so I found myself having these sort of episodes with people in the airports. They’re fun,” Murray said. “It’s not always difficult. It’s just a much higher number of events than ordinary life. The percentages are the same — it’s just that the numbers are different.”
Maybe it’s just that Bill Murray is different.
A Course Called Ireland, produced by Skydance Sports and Stellify Media, premieres Sunday on Paramount+. In the U.K., the series will air on BBC Two, BBC One Northern Ireland and BBC iPlayer.
Quentin Tarantino had quite a surprise in store on Friday night.

The filmmaker made an appearance at AFI Fest in Los Angeles for a screening of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, sitting down for a Q&A afterwards about his hit movie. But just as the night seemed to be wrapping up, Tarantino surprised the crowd at the TCL Chinese Theater with a first look at The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, showing off the first 17 minutes of the follow-up film.

Tarantino wrote the script for Cliff Booth, with David Fincher stepping in to direct this time around. The new project sees Brad Pitt reprise his Oscar-winning role as stunt double Booth, and is set in 1977, eight years after the events of Once Upon a Time.

Before showing off the footage — which saw Booth working as a cinema projectionist while handling some more unsavory business on the side — Tarantino explained his decision to revisit the character in the first place.

“I tend to not remember good reviews of mine in quotes; I kind of remember the bad reviews in quotes, but I don’t really remember good reviews of mine in quotes. But one quote that I do remember somebody writing about Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, it was like, ‘This seems like the first world Quentin Tarantino has ever created that he would like to live in,’ and there is that aspect,” he told the crowd. “I loved the Cliff Booth character, I loved the way that Brad played him, and there was this aspect of him as sort of like a paperback hero. I could see like a series of paperbacks with Cliff Booth getting involved with this adventure or that adventure or something like that.”

Tarantino continued, “As time went on, I just thought about coming up with a different adventure, getting him in now a misadventure. I wanted to see what would happen with that.” He also noted how immersed he has become in the film’s world — having also written a Once Upon a Time novel — and explained, “I’ve got nothing to do but just invest in this mythology. I invested in it before I did the movie, and then I invested in it in the years since I’ve done the movie, just so I know the mythology. The audience doesn’t need to know everything, but it’s kind of nice that I know everything, and you can trust me that I know it.”

During the conversation Tarantino also revealed that “if I’m going to watch any of my movies, it would be this one,” and it’s a film that he can watch again and again. He added, “Don’t get me wrong, I love my stories. I really, really love my stories, and I invest in my stories. But I kind of like that this doesn’t really have a story. I like that you’re just hanging out with them.”

About to head into rehearsals for his upcoming play, Tarantino explained his current mindset is of being a writer first, as was put into action with opting not to direct Cliff Booth. “As I’m getting older, being a man of letters is more my thing,” he noted, “so screenplays and books and plays — everything except poetry.”
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is releasing in IMAX on Nov. 25 and streaming Dec. 23 on Netflix.

The owners of Elvis Presley‘s music have launched a legal war over artificial intelligence, suing AI giant Anthropic over accusations that it trained its models on hundreds of the legendary artist’s song without permission.

The new lawsuit, filed Friday (Oct. 23) and first reported by Billboard, claims that Anthropic, the tech behemoth behind Claude, infringed 274 of the rock legend’s copyrighted songs, including famed hits like “Can’t Help Falling in Love,” “A Little Less Conversation” and “Don’t Be Cruel.”

“The Elvis Plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” writes Richard Busch, the lead attorney behind the lawsuit. “The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs.”

Though music companies like Universal Music Group have already repeatedly sued AI companies for stealing their IP, the new lawsuits represents by far the most high-profile legal action filed on behalf of an individual musician — in this case, arguably the most famous recording artist of all time.

The case was filed by a unit of Authentic Brands Group, the licensing giant that largely controls the intellectual property rights to Elvis, including much of his song catalog, his brand trademarks and the rights to his name, image and likeness. It was co-filed by various other entities that own Elvis rights.

Like other AI firms, Anthropic is already facing numerous lawsuits over the process of “training” their models to create new ones, which involves ingesting millions of existing works without permission. AI companies say that process is protected by copyright’s fair use defense, but that issue remains pending across dozens of lawsuits — with billions of dollars in potential damages at stake.

Litigation over AI music has centered more on Suno, the leading AI song generator, which was sued in 2024 by all three major music companies over such training accusations. It eventually settled with Warner Music Group last year and has vowed to partner with the music industry, but is still facing contentious litigation from UMG and Sony Music. Anthropic, a far larger AI firm, has faced similar cases across creative industries, including from music publishers.

The new case Friday largely mirrors those earlier cases, claiming Anthropic illegally used music en masse to create technology that produces “unlicensed derivative works.” But it centers on what the Elvis plaintiffs call “some of the most groundbreaking, revolutionary, influential, and enduring musical compositions in human history.”

That includes “Can’t Help,” arguably Presley’s most famous song, “Don’t Be Cruel,” one of his early massive hits, and “Little Less,” which saw a resurgence in popularity due to a 2000s remix. The lawsuit also cites “All Shook Up,” “Return to Sender” and “(You’re The) Devil in Disguise”.
A rep for Anthropic did not immediately return a request for comment on Saturday.

Busch is no stranger to high-profile music cases. He represented Eminem in landmark cases in the 2000s over digital downloads, and later represented Marvin Gaye’s estate in a famous copyright case against Robin Thicke and Pharrell Williams, eventually winning a much-debated verdict that their “Blurred Lines” infringed Gaye’s “Got to Give It Up.”

From career milestones to new music releases to major announcements and those little important moments, Billboard editors highlight uplifting moments in Latin music. Here’s what happened in the Latin music world this week.
Maluma on Mental Health, Fatherhood and Learning to “Love Discomfort”

Maluma spoke candidly about therapy, anxiety, fatherhood and the challenge of balancing family life with a demanding career during the “Like Minded” conversation at Billboard Latin Music Week on Wednesday (Oct. 21). Moderated by Billboard’s co-chief content officer Leila Cobo, the BetterHelp-presented session also featured bilingual therapist Patricia Arrieta.

The conversation came shortly after the birth of Maluma’s second child, Orion, whom he said has brought him a new sense of calm and clarity. “I’ve finally been able to find that balance between my personal life and my artistic career,” he said. The Colombian star described therapy as an ongoing practice rather than a quick fix. “For me, therapy is being quiet, it is meditation, it’s constantly feeling uncomfortable and learning to love that discomfort,” he said.

Maluma acknowledged that he still experiences anxiety while managing his responsibilities as a father, artist, entrepreneur and leader of a large team. After undergoing a tension headache during an especially demanding week, he used ChatGPT to help organize his schedule and prioritize his well-being. “I started prioritizing my peace, lowering my burdens and stress,” he said. “I need at least four hours in the afternoon to spend with my family.”

He also spoke about moving away from extreme approaches to fitness and developing a healthier relationship with food and his body. “If you love yourself, you make good decisions,” he said. “My health is not negotiable.”

Reflecting on his latest album, Loco por Volver, Maluma said the project became part of his personal transformation. “It was the album that gave me back so many things I had lost,” he said. “The music transformed me.”
“Help is closer than we think,” he added.
Pablo Alborán & RIZA Turn a Latin Music Week Collab Into a Finished Song at Billboard Latin Music Awards

What began as a live songwriting experiment at last year’s Billboard Latin Music Week became a finished release — and then a Billboard Latin Music Awards performance on Thursday (Oct. 22). Pablo Alborán and RIZA delivered “Deditos Cruzados,” the dreamy collaboration they created during last year’s “Making the Hit, Live!” panel with producer Julio Reyes Copello and engineer Natalia Schlesinger.

Released Oct. 1, the song blends soulful vocals, Middle Eastern-tinged rhythms and lyrics about longing. Onstage, the pair performed from a warm, living room-inspired set, turning a creative experiment born in front of an audience into a full-circle musical moment. Check out “Deditos Cruzados” live below.
Nanpa Básico and Nella Bring Hope During Billboard Latin Music Awards After Colombia and Venezuela Earthquakes

Colombian artist Nanpa Básico and Venezuelan singer Nella delivered a moving rendition of “Todo Cambia,” the classic written by Julio Numhauser and famously popularized by Mercedes Sosa. Their Billboard Latin Music Awards performance on Thursday (Oct. 22) acknowledged the devastation caused by earthquakes that hit their home countries. Images of shattered buildings and concrete paved way to green plants emerging from the rubble. Nella sang beside the wreckage in a flowing brown gown, while Nanpa brought a cowboy-inspired touch to the bittersweet duet. As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.
So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.

“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.

No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.

“We'll definitely see more of these long-life bugs that are in every version of the software for the last decade or whatever,” says Jake Williams, vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy and a former NSA hacker. “But I think there’s only so much of this low-hanging fruit. There isn’t much else that has the specific reach of PHP. It’s a pretty wild attack surface—most other tools aren’t exposed to the internet by design.”

Researchers note, too, that even with frontier models, most examples of sophisticated AI-aided hacking also involve human expertise. As Ryan Austin, the Calif researcher who first discovered the PHP flaws, wrote this week, “No model is simply capable of unearthing ‘all bugs’ with simple prompts. At least for now.”

In short, security engineer and researcher Niels Provos says, everyone can dial back their freak-outs, at least a bit. “To be honest, I am not really worried,” he says, about AI finding an overwhelming number of historic bugs that are newly exploitable—or new vulnerabilities that couldn’t have been practically exploited without AI. “People have now been looking with AI for over a year, and it required a highly skilled team to find this one. I guess we will see whether I am completely wrong, but I doubt it.”

An experimental vaccine offers new hope to patients with melanoma, one of the most aggressive forms of skin cancer. The pharmaceutical companies Merck and Moderna released the results of a Phase 3 clinical trial that evaluated the efficacy of a personalized mRNA-based vaccine that, when combined with immunotherapy, reduced the risk of disease recurrence or death by 42 percent compared to treatment with the immunotherapy drug alone.

Georgina Long, medical director of the Australian Melanoma Institute and the study’s principal investigator, said in a statement that these results are “transformative” and “have the potential to make a foundational shift in how we treat patients with earlier-stage melanoma.”

The trial, known as INTerpath-001, included 1,137 people with high-risk melanoma who had undergone surgery to completely remove their tumors. The participants were divided into two groups. Those in the first group received only Pembrolizumab, a drug that helps the immune system detect and fight cancer cells, while those in the second group were treated with the same drug in combination with the mRNA vaccine, called Intismeran Autogene.

After monitoring the participants for an average of 24.6 months, the researchers determined that addition of the vaccine reduced the risk of cancer recurrence or death by 42 percent compared to Pembrolizumab alone.

The results also showed that the experimental treatment reduced the risk of the disease spreading to other parts of the body by 38 percent. At the end of the follow-up period, 82.2 percent of patients who received both treatments remained recurrence-free, compared with 70 percent of those who received Pembrolizumab alone.

“The results of the INTerpath-001 study represent a major breakthrough in the treatment of melanoma and, in particular, in the development of personalized medicine,” Eva Muñoz Couselo—who leads a melanoma research group at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology, in Barcelona and who was not involved in the study—told SMC Spain. “For the first time, a Phase III trial has demonstrated that an individualized therapeutic vaccine, designed on the basis of the molecular characteristics of each patient’s tumor, can significantly improve the outcomes of conventional immunotherapy.”

The laboratories explained that the vaccine was developed from a tumor sample taken from each patient, which was used to identify specific mutations that would create distinct proteins the immune system could learn to recognize in order to attack cancer cells. The scientists selected up to three of these molecular signatures per patient.

During the trial, some participants experienced mild side effects such as fever, fatigue, and pain at the injection site. These side effects were seen in earlier trials as well, and the Phase 3 findings demonstrate similar safety when the vaccine is used in the combination with Pembrolizumab.
“These results reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer,” Stéphane Bancel, CEO of Moderna, said in a statement.

The pharmaceutical companies emphasized that the vaccine is not designed to prevent melanoma but rather to reduce the risk of recurrence and death following prior medical treatment. They also noted that the therapy remains under investigation to validate its efficacy and obtain approval from health authorities before widespread use.

Most people diagnosed with melanoma have a high chance of survival, especially if detected early, but as one of the most common cancers, melanoma kills over 50,000 people globally each year. In theory, similar vaccines could be developed for other kinds of tumors in the future. Earlier this year, another trial demonstrated that personalized mRNA vaccines can greatly improve survival among patients with pancreatic cancer, one of the deadliest kinds of tumor.

“This is the major breakthrough, because conceptually it would make it possible to treat not only melanoma but also other tumors in which the immune system can be reactivated,” Marisol Soengas—a leading melanoma researcher at Spain’s National Cancer Research Center also not involved in the trial—told SMC Spain.

That doesn’t mean a cure for cancer is right around the corner. “The challenge is to ensure that this personalization can be scaled up to a large number of patients and that the cost is affordable for health care systems,” Soengas said. “It is logistically complex. It is literally a bespoke vaccine.”
