The best pet camera for you depends on what you value for your pet. Personally, I never knew I needed a pet camera, but after trying several models, I don’t think I can go into the office or on vacation without one set up at home. A home security camera can give you extra peace of mind when you’re out, and pet cameras specifically designed for our furry friends add helpful features, like the ability to follow your pet around, engage in play, and dispense kibble. Connected to an app on your phone and with cloud storage options, these pet cameras—including our top pick for most people (and pets!), the Furbo Mini 360° ($49), and our compact 360 rotating budget pick, Petcube Cam 360 ($47)—ensure you’ll never miss a moment in your pet’s life when you’re away (or at home).

For more peace of mind while you’re away from your pet, be sure to check out our related guides, like the Best Automatic Feeders, Best Cat Water Fountains, Best Automatic Litter Boxes, Best Indoor Security Cameras, and Best Outdoor Security Cameras.

Updated October 2026: I’ve added the SwitchBot Pan/Tilt Cam Plus 3K and Amazon Blink Mini 2K+ to Others Tested, and retested the Enabot Ebo Max FamilyBot. I’ve also ensured up-to-date links and prices throughout.

Enabot Ebo Max FamilyBot for $600: I’m usually a big fan of Enabot’s pet tech—especially its line of pet cameras, which are generally affordable and work consistently well without needing a pricey add-on cloud storage system. This camera is touted as an AI family companion that can recognize pets and household members, remember routines and preferences, and come when called. It also has the expected pet camera-on-wheels features, like two-way audio and video, night vision, and 4K imaging. During initial testing, the camera didn't charge properly on the dock and often froze or stopped charging. I got a second model to test, and it worked better—it handled tasks on command, returned to the charging station, and recognized my cats. However, I still don't think its AI-powered companion features are cool enough to justify that price tag. If price is no issue for you and you want a moving camera on wheels, it's worth checking out.

SwitchBot Pan/Tilt Cam Plus 3K for $50: I generally liked this pan/tilt camera, which offers a 360-degree horizontal field of view and a 115-degree vertical field of view, and can be mounted with the provided tools. It also has two-way audio, voice commands, and smart-home support like Amazon Alexa or Google Home. It has eight infrared LEDs that support enhanced night vision, with a range of up to 32 feet. Through the app, you can adjust camera settings for motion detection or tracking and switch to privacy mode when you want the camera to stop recording. However, it only works with 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi and, like many other cams on this list, requires a paid subscription plan to access enhanced features like AI recognition, smart event summaries, unlimited cloud storage, and access to historical recordings. It also required several firmware updates throughout testing and would freeze during updates. It also lagged when moving through the app and often froze for a prolonged period when first opening the app.

Amazon Blink Mini 2K+ for $40: This small, budget-friendly camera supports 2K video, 4X hybrid zoom, and color night vision. In his testing, reviewer Simon Hill found its motion detection reliable, but only with a subscription: $3 per month or $30 per year for one camera, or $10 per month or $100 per year for unlimited cameras. You can record locally by purchasing a Sync Module 2 ($50) and inserting a USB flash drive. Luckily, you don't need a subscription to record the motion-triggered footage from the camera to the Sync Module 2. You just need to insert an approved USB flash drive (up to 256 GB) into the Sync Module 2 to enable subscription-free local storage. Without a subscription, however, live viewing is limited to five minutes, recording is unavailable, videos load much more slowly, people/animal detection isn’t included, and you can’t share clips.

Enabot Ebo Air 2 for $199: The new model from Enabot is an improved interactive robot toy and camera on wheels from the brand’s lineup. It’s got a 2K HD camera, two-way audio, and a built-in laser toy, and you control the robot’s movements from your phone’s app. It’s lightweight and compact, and it can easily maneuver around objects. While acting as a pet camera, the robot also entertains (or scares or confuses) your pet by making animal noises, doing tricks like spinning and zigzagging, and displaying “emotions” via its front screen. It also has a built-in laser toy that my cats actually played with, along with key features like 24/7 video recording with smart playback, motion detection, and activity alerts.

Petcube Play 2 for $75: This Petcube camera attempts to combine popular laser toys that cats love with a pet security cam, with mixed results. Like many other cameras in the brand’s lineup, the Play 2 has excellent color and night vision, an extra-wide view, and two-way audio. The laser toy is supposed to auto-engage when motion is detected, but this often didn’t happen during my tests. When the laser did work and caught my cats’ attention, the feature turned off quickly. Plus, because the camera needed to sit high on a shelf to see the area, the laser was often too high for the cats to attempt to catch. You can manually play with the cat using the laser through the app, although it’s often laggy, and my cats ended up more perplexed than playful when the laser was on. It’s a solid camera, but the toy aspect falls a bit flat.

Furbo Mini for $25: I love this super-affordable, 360-degree-rotating basic pet camera. Furbo’s app is easy to use, the 1080 HD feed is clear, it can be mounted on a wall, and it has two-way audio. It’s powered via USB, but it works only with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, so beware. As with most other pet cameras, to access the full features—like smart detection, alerts, and access to historical video footage—you’ll need Furbo Nanny, the paid subscription service. Luckily, Furbo offers a 14-day free trial to see if the service is a good fit.

Petcube Bites 2 Lite for $80: With HD 1080p live video, night vision up to 30 feet, 8x zoom, two-way audio so you can talk to and hear your pets, and food-dispensing abilities, this pet camera has all of the bells and whistles. It also includes an easily detachable plastic treat dispenser that holds up to 1.5 pounds of kibble. You can toss treats remotely from the app, and you can also control the amount and distance. With the subscription service, the app alerts you when the device detects motion or sound and logs it with playback video. I like the customization options and clear video feed, but—like other Petcube devices—you need the extra Care plan to unlock all the best features.

Enabot Rola PetPal Robot Pet Companion for $200 (treat dispensing): A pet camera on wheels, this rolling model has the best of intentions, but the sometimes glitchy app makes the combo pet camera/toy/feeder a little unpredictable. Through the app, you can watch your pets on the security camera and drive the robot around, pressing buttons to do tricks and dispense treats. You can watch the camera feed live in the app, and you can also schedule recordings, which are viewable via cloud playback. It also assembles a 30-second “day in the life” compilation. The robot is also supposed to detect abnormal movement or sounds, like barking or broken glass, and send a smart alert to the owner with a timestamp while away from home. Through AI-powered pet recognition, the bot can also snap a picture of your pet, but the AI features were unreliable when I tested them.

Petcube Cam for $32: It's simple, compact, and doesn't have all the bells and whistles like more advanced models do, but it’s a great price for a reliable, basic pet camera. Like others in Petcube's lineup, it has a 1080p HD camera, night vision, and two-way audio. It sits on hinges and can angle up and down, with the option to flip the video feed in-app if you want to lay it horizontally. You'll need the brand's subscription Care plan to access any features beyond the live feed. You can set a “motion zone” to receive notifications only in a specific area, and you can connect your phone’s location to the app so you’re alerted more often when you’re away. You can also share the camera feed with others so they can watch remotely, and specify the footage you want to share. This camera is basic, but it delivers a high-quality camera feed and advanced extras that make it a steal at this price.

Catit Pixi Smart Mouse Camera for $51: This cutie looks like a miniature mouse with oversized, magnetic feet that attach to a metal stand. The mouse legs hinge so you can adjust the camera’s height and angle. While adorable, it’s expensive for what it is: The lens doesn't move, and it requires a microSD card to capture video beyond a live feed. With the SD card, you can scroll through recorded video to see activity from past days, record live footage, and save photos and videos to your smartphone’s camera roll. Even with the SD card, though, it was hard to pinpoint the exact time when reviewing footage. The live video feed can be laggy, and there were connectivity issues a few times. It’s a tad expensive at this price point for its (lack of) capabilities.

Closer Pets TreatView with Pet Camera for $100: With an HD camera, two-way communication, motion detection, a built-in memory card, and a one-cup storage for kibble or treats, which you can schedule or dispense at random—on paper, this pet camera has all of the bells and whistles. The video feed was always clear, though the audio was a bit laggy and hard to hear. The treat portions were huge, dispensing a heaping handful of kibble even at the lowest setting. The dispensing alert was super jarring, and my pets were frightened by it—there was no way to silence it. Because of the kibble-dispensing hole's placement, the camera is angled low, making it hard to see the area I wanted. This is an okay pet camera, but its additional features become a burden rather than an asset.

To find the best pet cameras to test, I first looked for security cameras with extra pet-specific features. I set up each camera individually, noting any difficulties with initial setup, Wi-Fi configuration, and the camera feed's speed and reliability. I tested each camera for at least a week (most for much longer) in various spots around my house, and I rigorously tested the extra features available on most of the cameras, like scheduled feedings, food-dispensing, playtime, and scheduled recordings, noting any issues I experienced. Over the months of testing, I went out of town several times and completely relied on these cams to keep an eye on my two children—I mean, cats.

Security cameras let you keep an eye on your house (and pet) while you’re away, but pet cameras often include additional pet-specific features, such as the ability to dispense treats and interact with your furry friend via a two-way speaker. These cameras with special features can help ease common pet issues like separation anxiety or boredom. The Enabot Rola PetPal Robot Pet Companion, for example, has attachments that let you remotely give your pet a treat or engage in “playtime.”

That's not to say you can’t use a security camera as a pet cam, but like any other smart home device that connects to Wi-Fi, it could be hacked and compromise your privacy. Make sure your Wi-Fi password is strong, and set up two-factor authentication in your camera’s app. It’s also a good idea to keep it turned off when you’re home, as an extra precaution.

The largest artificial intelligence (AI) firms increasingly understand that they are hostages of one another. If one firm pushes ahead recklessly, others may feel compelled to follow. If one deploys a dangerous model without adequate safeguards, others may see it as a green light to do the same.

The debate over AI has centered on what governments should do to regulate this frontier technology. That remains essential. But a more immediate question is emerging: Can the companies building these powerful systems take action independently before they lose credibility and suffer legal consequences?

That question no longer looks theoretical and is being recognized as an urgent challenge. We've already seen AI firms lose control of their models — for example, in Australia, a rogue AI hacked a government healthcare website. If we are not careful, it's only a matter of time before one of these incidents causes large-scale, real-world harm, like shutting down an electricity grid or municipal water system, or a mass misdiagnosis in a health system. If this trend continues, the entire industry could become tarnished.
But there is a blueprint for self-regulation in a risky business: the nuclear industry, which has built up layers of oversight, controls and self-scrutiny over decades.

Frontier AI may require something similar: private regulation among competitors that do not trust one another but have a mutual interest in preventing outcomes that could damage them all. This does not appeal to the better angels of human nature — it's self-preservation for the industry itself.

There is a historical precedent for this kind of arrangement. The nuclear sector did not become safe because every actor suddenly became benevolent. It became safer through a layered system of peer scrutiny, technical standards, information-sharing and external oversight. International organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which was established in 1957, emerged to coordinate monitoring and verification, while national regulators and industry bodies gradually built professional norms around catastrophic risk.

The result was not perfect safety, as the Chernobyl disaster in 1986 clearly attests. But nuclear governance architecture is designed around the recognition that in high-risk technological systems, one actor's failure can become everyone's problem. This was seen following Chernobyl: global nuclear safety increased significantly after the disaster, with upgrades to reactor designs, improved training and international monitoring networks.

And this movement to self-regulation also occurred in the U.S. nuclear sector, following the Three-Mile Island nuclear accident near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in 1979. The reactor suffered a partial meltdown after a relatively minor cooling malfunction. Investigations later revealed design flaws in instruments and alarms, along with inadequate emergency response training, were the root cause of the incident.

The event nearly killed the nuclear energy industry in the U.S., causing public support to fall from a record high of 69% in 1977 to 46%t in 1979. The entire industry suffered because of failures at one facility. In response, the U.S. nuclear industry established the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO) in December 1979 to improve operational safety.

The analogy to AI should not be overstated. Nuclear materials are easier to count than algorithms, and nuclear facilities are harder to hide than model weights. The outcomes of a catastrophic AI blunder are also less existential, although its use in weapon systems is not without risk. In September, an AI hallucination almost led to the U.S. intercepting a Chinese ship suspected of carrying nuclear material to Iran.

Yet the comparison remains useful because the core governance problem is similar. In both cases, competitors operate in an environment where the downside risk of unchecked rivalry is borne by society while the upside is private gain for these firms. The challenge is to create institutions that make restraint the rational default — even when no actor fully trusts the others, and the inner workings of the industry are not readily visible to outsiders.

For AI, that could mean reciprocal evaluation of frontier models before deployment, secure mechanisms for sharing safety information, agreed red lines around certain capabilities, and independent third parties empowered to audit compliance. Such mechanisms would not replace government regulation. They would instead serve as an intermediate layer: stronger than voluntary ethics statements but more adaptive and technically informed than legislation alone can often be in fast-moving domains. The state would act as a background enforcer.

AI executives appear willing to look for solutions too, with Elon Musk recently suggesting a peer-review system before advanced model release, and Demis Hassabis, co-founder and chair of Google DeepMind, putting forward a framework for an AI Standards Body, similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

Skeptics will object, with reason, that industry-led governance can become cartel behavior or public-relations theater. Companies may use "safety" language to entrench incumbency, slow rivals or deflect binding regulation. Those are real dangers. The lesson from nuclear history is not that private coordination works automatically. It is that private coordination works only when nested inside a broader system of transparency, verification and public authority. Without those elements, private regulation becomes little more than trust-me rhetoric.

Still, dismissing private regulation altogether would be a mistake. Governments do not yet possess the technical capacity, speed or international alignment needed to oversee frontier AI on their own. And if the leading labs already see themselves as bound together by shared exposure to catastrophic risk, that recognition can become the basis for institutional design. The question is how to turn mutual fear into durable rules.

- 'Autonomy always begins with something a human hands it': Who's responsible when an AI agent goes rogue?
- We're not about to awaken an evil digital god — AI is far more likely to end in a great disappointment

That is where the nuclear analogy is most powerful. It reminds us that industries facing existential hazards do not need perfect trust in order to cooperate. They need mechanisms that make cooperation preferable to defection. In practice, that means inspections, peer review, incident reporting, professional norms and a state-backed enforcement perimeter. AI governance is often discussed as if the only choices were laissez-faire innovation or heavy-handed state control. History suggests a third path: structured private coordination under public shadow.

The real opportunity, then, is not to celebrate the newfound (apparent) prudence of technology executives, it is to recognize what their comments reveal. When even fierce rivals begin to argue for mutual scrutiny, they are admitting that competition alone cannot govern the frontier. That admission should be treated not as reassurance but as evidence that the risk has become collective.

The policy task now is to build institutions that fit that reality. Governments should push for mandatory reporting, independent evaluation and legal backstops. But they should also encourage enforceable forms of peer oversight among the handful of firms whose systems may shape the trajectory of the technology. Frontier AI is becoming an industry in which the leading actors are hostages of one another. The nuclear age showed that such conditions can produce serious governance. The hope is that AI firms learn that lesson before they learn the cost of ignoring it at the peril of the public at large.

Akhil Bhardwaj is an Associate Professor of Strategy and Organization at the University of Bath, UK. He studies extreme events, which range from organizational disasters to radical innovation. Akhil is interested in the epistemological problem of understanding the underlying dynamics that lead up to these events. He also studies how thinking can be improved as well as the implications of AI adoption in the context of strategic management, entrepreneurship, and high-risk systems. His work is philosophically grounded in pragmatism. Prior to joining academia, Akhil has worked as an engineer and manager at CAT., Inc and consulted as a SOX compliance analyst in the U.S.
October's full "Hunter's Moon" is about to rise, and skywatchers will get two great chances to see it appear on the eastern horizon around sunset.

Although it officially turns full at 12:11 a.m. EDT on Monday (Oct. 26), the Hunter's Moon will appear almost perfectly full as it rises on both Sunday (Oct. 25) and Monday evenings, giving skywatchers two opportunities to observe it.

October's full moon is nicknamed the Hunter's Moon because it was traditionally a signal for hunters to prepare for the coming cold winter by hunting, slaughtering and preserving meat, according to Time and Date. That's an Anglo-Saxon name; Native American names for October's full moon include the Drying Rice Moon, the Falling Leaves Moon and the Freezing Moon.

The first chance to see the Hunter's Moon comes just before sunset on Sunday, when the almost-full moon will rise in the east. The second opportunity comes on Monday, when the moon — still essentially 100% illuminated — will again rise just after sunset. Because it will be in a slightly darker sky, Monday's moonrise will likely be more dramatic.
As it rises Sunday, the moon will appear in the constellation Aries, and Saturn will be to its upper right. On Monday, it will rise above the Pleiades open cluster (M45).

For the best view on either evening, find somewhere with a clear view low to the eastern horizon and be in position shortly before moonrise where you are. An elevated viewpoint, open field or coastline is ideal because buildings, trees and hills can delay the moment the moon becomes visible.
Although the full moon will look magnificent with the naked eye, a backyard telescope or good stargazing binoculars can help you zoom in on various lunar features.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Hunter's Moon may appear unusually large thanks to the "moon illusion," which makes the moon seem bigger when it's seen beside familiar objects, such as trees and buildings, near the horizon. The illusion stems from the fallacies of how our brains use distance to perceive size.

October's Hunter's Moon isn't a supermoon, but it comes immediately before a notable sequence of four consecutive supermoons. The first will be the next full moon, the Beaver Moon, on Nov. 24, followed by full moons in December, January and February. A supermoon occurs when a full moon happens while the moon is relatively close to Earth in its slightly elliptical orbit, making it appear somewhat larger and brighter than average.

The Nazca Lines are the most famous geoglyphs in the world. Dating back around 2,000 years and reaching a combined length of more than 800 miles (1,300 kilometers), they depict a variety of motifs, including humans, animals, geometric shapes, plants and flowers. These designs were constructed on the arid hills and valleys of coastal Peru by the Nazca people between 200 B.C. and A.D. 500, long before writing was used in the region.
It's not clear exactly how many Nazca Lines there are, but they number in the thousands, with new geoglyphs continuing to be discovered with the help of AI.

Scientists have been debating this question since the lines were first formally investigated in the early 20th century. Although the definite answer remains unknown, experts have proposed various reasons for the famous geoglyphs.

There "are many ideas out there about their function and meaning," Ana Nieves, a professor of art history at Northeastern Illinois University, told Live Science in an email. "If you look at the area's geoglyphs closely, though, there are different styles of geoglyphs, some are relatively larger and some smaller, some are on hillsides while some are on the pampas. It is not likely that a single explanation would apply to all."
A vast array of theories for the lines' uses have been proposed over the years, with the most outlandish of these suggesting that they were sites for aliens to land spaceships.
More grounded theories link the lines to cultural and religious practices.

"The question of why the geoglyphs exist is difficult to answer, given that we lack any type of preserved oral or written testimony," Karsten Lambers, an art history professor at the University of Augsburg in Germany, wrote in an essay published in the book "Los geoglifos: imágenes y escenarios en el desierto de Nazca y Palpa [The Geoglyphs: images and settings in the desert of Nazca and Palpa]" (University of Augsburg, 2017). It's possible that the uses for the geoglyphs changed over time, he added.
One suggestion is that they were initially used to mark routes for travelers and caravans and later became places for gathering and feasting.

In a 2026 study, researchers noted that some of the earlier Nazca geoglyphs were constructed on hillsides, seem to be located on trails, and "were visible from considerable distances." This means the geoglyphs may have been used to mark travel routes and indicate areas that were good for temporary camps. The team suggested that the markings became places for gathering and feasting.

Another idea is that the geoglyphs were used to match astronomical alignments to serve as a kind of calendar. In December 1941, historian Paul Kosok examined the lines and determined that they had astronomical alignments. Mathematician Maria Reiche followed up on Kosok's work, examining the Nazca Lines for more than 40 years to identify many geoglyphs she believed have an astronomical relationship to various celestial bodies, a research team noted in a 2021 paper. Yet after analyzing the geoglyphs, the modern-day team found that only a relatively small number had a possible alignment to a star or solar event such as a solstice.

"The results suggest that the geoglyphs, as a whole, certainly cannot be interpreted as a calendar system," the team wrote. However, this doesn't discredit the idea that the Nazca Lines had an astronomical significance, Christiane Richter, a researcher at the University of Applied Sciences in Germany and first author of the 2021 paper, told Live Science in an email.

Since the paper's publication, Richter and her team's research has indicated that around 8% of the geoglyphs have some form of lunar alignment. It is "highly probable that celestial bodies played a role in the creation of the drawings," Richter said in an email.

Offerings such as ceramics, crabs, corn and earrings made from Spondylus shells (a genus of bivalves known as thorny oysters) were also placed on low rock platforms near some of the geoglyphs, especially those shaped like trapezoids, Lambers noted in his paper. Spondylus shells are normally found farther north, in Ecuador, but during El Niño events, they can appear farther south, in Peru. These shells, alongside crabs and corn, tend to be associated with water and fertility, Lambers noted.

Whatever the reasons for their construction the Nazca Lines are awe inspiring today. Lambers wrote in his essay that the Nazca people who built them "succeeded in transforming one of the driest deserts in the world, over the course of many centuries, to serve the region’s inhabitants as an expression of their cultural ideas and a setting for their social activities."

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.
SpaceX appears to have lifted restrictions the Ukrainian military’s of use Starshield — the military-grade version of the company’s Starlink internet system.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara told reporters that Starshield appears to be working normally again, although the military is still conducting tests and has not received an explanation for the restrictions.

This follows a 10-day period where Ukrainian drones would lose internet connectivity when flying at speeds of around 100 miles per hour, resulting in the military losing control of some drones, while others became more vulnerable because they were flying more slowly.

President Donald Trump reportedly called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Wednesday and asked him to restore Starshield service. Both Trump and Musk have criticized Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, with Musk recently posting, “Zelensky has gone too far.”
“Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately,” Musk said. “This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact.”

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.

Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.

Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.

Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.

In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.

It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.

As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?

I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?

But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.
I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?

One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.

Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.

At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.
I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?

I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.

But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!

Though the results could yet surprise us, it’s very likely the key story of the 2026 midterm elections will be the Republican Party’s loss of support from non-MAGA elements of the electorate who temporarily backed Donald Trump in 2024. To that extent it’s not just a matter of the White House party predictably losing ground in a midterm, which happens far more often than not. It’s a tale of trends reversing themselves that robbed Trump and his cohort of what many thought might be a political realignment making the GOP the majority party for years. So it’s worth a closer look: How, exactly, did Trump alienate these onetime supporters? Here are some tentative answers.
Trump’s 2024 coalition was never as big as he claimed

The president has incessantly exaggerated his winning share of the electorate in 2024. On Election Night, he claimed an “unprecedented and powerful mandate.” Shortly after taking office, he told supporters he had “achieved the most epic political victory our country has ever seen” and “the biggest mandate in 129 years,” and one of his spokespeople boasted he had “decisively won every battleground state and became the first Republican to win the popular vote in 20 years,” lines he would repeat often on Truth Social. In fact, he narrowly won the popular vote by 1.5 percent, far short of the usual 10 percent threshold for a “landslide,” which was smaller than the margins of victory for Joe Biden in 2020, Barack Obama in 2012 and 2008, and George W. Bush in 2004 (and smaller, for that matter, than Hillary Clinton’s popular-vote margin over Trump in 2016). Winning all seven battlegrounds is no big accomplishment, either; these were very close states, which is why they were called battlegrounds. Suffice it to say that Trump’s victory was legitimate but no great shakes by any historical standard.
Some of Trump’s gains were circumstantial, not a realignment

What had some Republicans buzzing about a “realignment” were the gains Trump posted among Hispanic, Black, and under-30 voters. The size of these gains varied by sources, but probably the most reliable, Pew’s “verified voters” analysis, showed Trump gaining 12 percent among Hispanics compared to 2020 (and 20 percent compared to 2016); 7 percent among Black voters (and 9 percent since 2016); and 4 percent among under-30 voters (and 11 percent since 2016). Considering how aggressively reactionary Trump had been in the intervening years, these were indeed impressive numbers in those demographic groups and cause for concern among Democrats, who had arguably taken them for granted. But Trump has now squandered these gains by every measurement we have.
The high price of breaking cost-of-living promises

Hispanic, Black, and under-30 voters are on average more economically vulnerable than other Americans, and there’s not much question a big part of their pro-Trump trend in 2024 involved unhappiness with Joe Biden’s record on inflation and Trump’s promises to lower the cost of groceries, fuel, and housing. He was not able at all to keep those promises, which were not realistic to begin with. While this isn’t the only reason he’s lost ground with these voters, it is clearly important, and it’s hard to overstate the depth of his failure. According to the latest high-quality New York Times–Siena survey of likely voters, Trump’s job-approval numbers on “the cost of living” are 20 percent approval and 79 disapproval (with 65 percent strongly disapproving) among Hispanics, 3 percent approval and 91 percent disapproval (with 88 percent strongly disapproving) among Black voters, and 13 percent approval and 86 percent disapproval (with 73 percent strongly disapproving) among under-30 voters. There is no way to sugarcoat these numbers on the most important issue of the midterms.
Latinos are unhappy with mass deportation

It was reasonably clear that the Latino/Hispanic voters who trended Republican in 2024 supported Trump’s border-control policies (most still do) and believed his claims that he would deport only violent criminals. But again, Trump broke his promises. A March 2026 Equus survey of Latinos found that by “a wide 65-30 margin, Latinos believe Trump’s actions on immigration ‘are going too far, and instead of deporting criminals, he is targeting the types of hardworking immigrants who strengthen our nation.’” The same survey showed 72 percent of Latinos weren’t happy with ICE, “whether that means they support reforming ICE to prevent violence and ensure accountability (37%) or abolishing ICE because it is out of control and no training or accountability could reform it (35%).” The Times-Siena poll showed 60 percent of Hispanics “strongly disapproving” of Trump’s immigration policies overall.
Trump has offended Black voters as much as possible

If you are a Republican who wants to increase your party’s fragile beachhead with Black voters, here are some things you should probably avoid doing: (1) devoting all the civil-rights organs of the federal government to a fight against alleged discrimination against white people; (2) virtually criminalizing diversity efforts in federal or federally supported hiring; (3) successfully encouraging the U.S. Supreme Court to atomize the Voting Rights Act of 1965; (4) successfully encouraging southern state legislatures to dismantle congressional and state legislative districts that elected Black people to office; and (5) making white Afrikaners from the former apartheid state of South Africa the one remaining recognized beneficiary of refugee status. That the Trump administration has done all these things helps explain why in the Times-Siena survey only 7 percent of Black voters gave the president a positive job-approval rating while 78 percent strongly disapprove.

Aside from being very sensitive to living costs, young voters are famously disinclined to support wars of choice (i.e., those that aren’t a matter of national self-defense), perhaps because they are often of the same generation as those who are dying or risking their lives in such wars. Trump’s war of choice against Iran is generally unpopular; according to the Times-Siena survey, 33 percent of likely voters support the war while 66 percent disapprove (57 percent disapprove strongly). Young voters really hate it, with only 9 percent supporting it (and just one percent supporting it strongly) and 86 percent disapproving of it (75 percent strongly). No wonder 79 percent of under-30 voters disapprove of Trump’s overall job performance (71 percent strongly).
Trump is now only focused on his base, because it’s all he has left

No wonder the president is traveling from red state to red state to rally his most loyal MAGA supporters to show up at the polls and mitigate his party’s losses. He has deliberately chosen to alienate everyone else, including voting groups that were open to changing sides. At this rate, Trump will leave the GOP in worse shape than he found it.

Scientists have discovered a distinct subtype of cell in the prostate, and it could help solve the mystery of why the gland enlarges with age.
This natural phenomenon is called benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and it tends to occur in just one region of the prostate.
But scientists still don't understand why.
Now, researchers at Johns Hopkins University have found a possible culprit hiding around the urethra.
Using single-cell RNA sequencing, the team has identified a population of prostate cells that are particularly abundant in this region, especially in cases of BPH.
The findings are published in The Journal of Pathology.

"Although BPH affects millions of men worldwide, scientists still do not fully understand why it develops primarily in a region of the prostate known as the transition zone, while other regions of the gland remain relatively unaffected," explains senior author Vasan Yegnasubramanian.
The transition zone is the part of the prostate that surrounds the urethra.
If this area enlarges with age, it can constrict the passage, making urination slower and more sporadic.

It's the most common prostate problem in men older than age 50, and while changes to hormone levels, inflammation, and cellular growth probably play a role, no one really knows why, at a cellular level, BPH occurs.

Urologist Charles Welliver at Albany Medical College was not involved in the recent study, but in an interview for the Urology Care Foundation's podcast in August, he explained that BPH isn't due to swelling.
"Benign prostatic hyperplasia is just an increase in the number of cells within the prostate," said Welliver.
"So, the cells don't get bigger, there's an increase in the number."
Now, scientists think they have figured out which units might be behind that cellular surge.
Researchers at Johns Hopkins analyzed noncancerous prostate tissue from 10 men who had prostate cancer.
Samples came from the three major zones of the prostate, and researchers carefully analyzed which genes were turned on or off in nearly 130,000 individual cells.
In tissues from the transition zone and in samples from BPH, researchers found a distinct cell population that was rare in other parts of the prostate.
These cells are a subtype of basal cells called WIF1+, and they are transcriptionally and anatomically distinct to the rest of their family members.
Scientists say they display a unique gene expression profile, and RNA sequencing and staining show that they are markedly enriched in the transition zone of the human prostate.
Some genes associated with WIF1+ cells respond to androgens like testosterone and are involved in signaling pathways that influence prostate growth and development.

"Together," the authors write, "the molecular signature, zonal distribution, and pathway enrichment suggest that transition-zone-enriched WIF1+ basal cells may contribute to BPH pathogenesis by promoting epithelial and stromal remodeling."
The researchers also speculate that by dampening inflammation and a growth-signaling pathway called WNT, these cells could help explain why prostate cancer starts less often in the transition zone.

"The analysis revealed that these cells possess molecular features associated with tissue remodeling that could contribute to prostate enlargement as well as an ability to communicate with neighboring cells, suggesting they may help establish the unique biological environment of the transition zone," says first author Rulin Wang.
When Wang and colleagues analyzed publicly available datasets, they found more evidence to support their results.
Enlarged prostate gland tissues were enriched with WIF1+ basal cells.
The gene signature of these abundant basal cells was also distinctly altered.
Wang says this raises the possibility that these cells "contribute to the regional processes that make the transition zone particularly susceptible to BPH."
For now, that's just a hypothesis, but it's one that Wang and colleagues think deserves further investigation.
Future studies, for instance, could examine the functional roles of WIF1+ basal cells in the development of enlarged prostate glands.
If these cells really do play a direct role in BPH, they could become future drug targets.
The research has been published in The Journal of Pathology.
The Air Force Office of Special Investigations is looking for a few good Airmen to swap jobs and become special agents.

No, they won’t get the 007 James Bond code—but they could learn to conduct counterintelligence and investigate procurement fraud and major crimes, OSI spokesperson Trevor Saylor told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

The office is looking to recruit agents from backgrounds other than law enforcement—it’s seeking Airmen with less than 11 years in service, with some exceptions, and is calling for applicants from other job fields in part because other areas of expertise can prove valuable in the unique types of investigations OSI conducts.

“A maintainer may understand an issue involving an aircraft or weapons system, while a contracting or acquisitions professional may recognize a process or irregularity relevant to a fraud investigation,” Special Agent Jennifer Holland, an OSI recruiter, said in a recent release. “Intelligence professionals may bring experience analyzing adversaries, identifying patterns and working with sensitive information.”

As threats to the Department of the Air Force cross traditional boundaries between criminal investigations, counterintelligence, cyber activity, and technology protection, that range of experience has become more relevant, Holland said.

Current threats and demands placed on OSI have “placed a renewed focus on defending the homeland, strengthening deterrence, protecting critical capabilities and preserving military advantages to generate combat power,” according to the release.
Skills such as foreign language proficiency, cybersecurity expertise and advanced computing skills are helpful, but not required or all that is needed.

“We’re looking for Airmen capable of exercising independent judgment, communicating with people from different backgrounds, managing competing priorities and documenting investigative activity with precision,” Holland said.
- Technical sergeants who exceed the 11-year limit may be considered on a case-by-case basis and should pursue a time-in-service waiver through their local AFOSI detachment before applying.
- First-term Airmen must also meet applicable retraining window requirements.

- First-term Airmen assigned within the continental United States who are serving four-year enlistments may generally apply from the first duty day of the month in which they complete 35 months of their current enlistment through the last duty day of their 43rd month.
- For Airmen serving six-year enlistments, the corresponding window is from the 59th through the 67th month.

- First-term Airmen assigned outside the continental United States generally must apply between 12 and 15 months before their date eligible to return from overseas. They must also enter their 35th month of service, or 59th month for six-year enlistees, on or before that date.
- Applicants on a current Control Roster or with a current Unfavorable Information File are not eligible.
- Applicants must be worldwide qualified and have a current passing fitness assessment without exemptions or a profile.
- OSI does not require enlisted applicants to have a college degree.
Traditionally, law enforcement, cyber defense, healthcare, and logistics Airmen have had success translating their skills into the special agent role, Saylor wrote.
The recruitment effort isn’t from any shortage or operational gaps, Saylor said. Instead, it is part of an ongoing effort to maintain a “highly credible, robust force” of agents.
“We remain fully postured and staffed to meet all operational requirements,” Saylor wrote in an email.
OSI isn’t targeting a specific job field, and the application process is open to all Airmen who meet the criteria.
The office evaluates using the “Whole Airman” concept, Saylor wrote.

The concept focuses on evaluating Airmen as well-rounded individuals across their military and personal lives, using tools such as Enlisted Performance Reports and special duty selections, with an emphasis on leadership, job performance, self-improvement, base/community involvement, and well-being aspects tied to Airman fitness.

If an Airman submits their application package correctly and follows the USAF Personnel Center windows to secure a release from their current job, their AFSC Career Field Manager will be the final authority to approve or deny their request to move to special agent selection and training.
- Apply online, complete documentation, and secure your commander’s recommendation.
- AFOSI requests your career-field release, though approval is not guaranteed.
- Approved applicants undergo suitability screening at their local unit.
- Candidates complete interviews and background investigations before final selection.
- The application process takes about three to six months.
If selected, the Airman then gets a short-term Assignment Limitation Code while they go through vetting and onboarding for special agent training, Saylor wrote.

Newly retrained Airmen-turned-agents will train at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Ga., to learn the fundamentals of federal criminal investigations before completing OSI-specific training.
They’ll then be put into specialties such as counterintelligence, procurement fraud, and major criminal investigative roles once they join their units, Saylor wrote.
“For roles in AFOSI’s cyber defense positions, AFOSI vectors Agents who show promise in the field into the specialized cyber fields upon the completion of probation,” Saylor wrote.
Most agents will begin their 15-month probationary period working felony-level criminal investigations and counterintelligence operations.
While some may specialize in certain areas, all special agents are expected to work interchangeably in a variety of missions and types of investigations.
Special Agents often travel more than many in the Air Force as part of their job and sometimes work high-stress cases that involve violent crime, fraud, and national security threats.
To mitigate burnout, Saylor wrote that OSI proactively supports personnel through a structured career progression plan and uses embedded wellness resources.

“Upon completing an initial probationary period of approximately 15 months focused on general criminal and counterintelligence work, agents have the opportunity to transition into specialized investigative sections,” Saylor wrote. “This structural pathway provides variety in their assignments and a deliberate break from the initial high-tempo investigative grind.”
OSI also has its own embedded chaplain corps and psychologists to provide ready access to mental health support, he wrote.

The NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) program has created 18 new awards to support visionary ideas to improve aerospace technologies in areas ranging from the exploration of the solar system to understanding the universe.

The 18 NIAC Phase I awards total $3.2 million. Each award provides up to $175,000 for a nine-month initial investigation. The NIAC projects are about early-stage concept development and are not considered official NASA missions.

“NASA has outlined an ambitious vision for the future of space exploration, we’re returning the Moon to stay, advancing to Mars, and pushing to deepen our understanding of space,” said Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology division within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Achieving that will require more than incremental technological advancement. It means we need great leaps. These awards are the kinds of innovation the world needs NASA to help foster.”

As an innovation incubator, NIAC funds early development of potential breakthrough technologies. Concepts for award consideration must have both transformative potential and possible feasibility for eventual implementation.

“Every innovation, every leap in technology, starts with a seed of an idea,” said Phillip Williams, NIAC’s acting program executive. “The NIAC program allows NASA to germinate those seeds and determine if there’s something that could be grown to benefit future space missions and our nation’s aerospace economy.”

As NASA and its partners push for sustained lunar presence, some of the 2026 awardees focused on ways to help explore the Moon and build infrastructure there. These include a system to support hovering robots to explore lava tubes under the Moon’s surface, a method to manage temperatures for small mobile exploration robots, and a way to incorporate radioisotopic heat sources into suits to help keep astronauts warm when operating in the Moon’s nearly two-week-long lunar nights.

Other concepts focus on exploring some of the solar system’s most remarkable features. Venus, with its hot atmosphere, presents an imposing challenge for research vehicles, so one NIAC awardee explores methods for hardening instruments for longer missions.

Two other concepts could help study planetary rings. One would use a swarm of 10,000 tiny satellites to map and analyze the rings of Saturn, while another would create a system for collecting samples from rings such as those circling Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

Some NIAC awardees will look far beyond the solar system, exploring ways to power interstellar spacecraft, map out continents on exoplanets, observe the photon rings around black holes, and detect subtle gravitational waves to explain how galaxies formed. Others will work to answer questions directly related to life on Earth, like the potential use of spaceborne dust to reduce solar radiation, and awareness about the debris orbiting Earth.
Researchers, known as NIAC Fellows, will investigate their concepts and identify potential challenges and opportunities for further development.
The 18 selections for 2026 NIAC Phase 1 grants are:
- Saptarshi Bandyopadhyay, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, California: Dimming the Sun Using Controllable Dust Cloud to Reduce Solar Insolation (DimSun)
- David Bugby, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory: Combinatory Architecture offering Neomobility, on-Venus Adaptability, and Survivability (CANVAS)
- A.C. Charania, Zeno Power Systems, Inc., Washington: Extended Astronaut Radioisotope-EVA in Nighttime and Deep-space Icy Landscapes (EARENDIL)
- Anish Damodaran, University of Central Florida, Orlando: PS21: Transforming Submillimeter Space Interferometry with Photonic Technologies
- Artur Davoyan, University of California, Los Angeles: Coilable Stacked Solar Sails for Very High delta-V Missions
- Daniel Drew, University of Hawaii, Honolulu: Solid-state Propulsion for Autonomous Reconnaissance of Karst (SPARK)
- Gilly Elor, Stone Aerospace, Inc., Del Valle, Texas: Power-over-Fiber to Enable a Lunar Underground eXplorer (LUX)
- Zhaoyan Liu, NASA Ames Research Center, California’s Silicon Valley: Quantum Wind Lidar Applications for Planetary and Earth Science Missions
- Jeff Nosanov, Orbital Velocity, LLC, Decatur, Georgia: OBLIVIAN: Observing Black hole LIght Via Intensity cOrrelatioN (OBLIVIAN)
- Keunhan Park, University of Utah, Salt Lake City: Plasmon-Enhanced Radioisotope Thermophotovoltaic (PRTPV) Power Generation for Interstellar Missions
- Austin Phoenix, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, Blacksburg, Virginia: Efficient variable Conductivity Lunar Insulator for Passive Surveyor Environmental Control (ECLIPSE)
- Marco Quadrelli, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory: PRAXIS: Planetary Rings Autonomous EXploration with In-situ Sampling (PRAXIS)

- Benjamin Schafer, Rarefied Technologies Inc., Albuquerque, New Mexico: Photophoretic Tracers for Near-Space Remote Sensing at 30-100 km Altitudes
