BendPak Inc. has announced the opening of its third distribution center, enabling delivery in two days or less to 92% of the U.S. population.

The new facility in Milford, Conn., serves New England, the Mid-Atlantic states and parts of the Great Lakes region. BendPak’s other regional hubs are in Santa Paula, Calif., serving the western half of the country, and Theodore, Ala., which now covers most of the Midwest and South. The optimized network brings next-day or two-day shipping to 40 states and Washington, D.C.

By further decentralizing inventory storage and integrating predictive stocking algorithms across all three hubs, BendPak reduces order fulfillment and shipping transit times, curbs secondary shipping emissions and minimizes the regional delays that traditionally disrupt national supply chains.

“This Northeast distribution center marks a milestone in our commitment to customer-centric growth,” said Derek Burns, director of distribution center operations – East for BendPak. “In addition to scaling our footprint, we’re redefining what reliability looks like for our dealers and end-user customers. Reaching 92% of Americans in two days or less means our customers get what they need, when they need it, with unprecedented speed.”

Over the last nine years, BendPak has expanded its product portfolio and geographic footprint. It has introduced new brands including Autostacker, JackPak, Ergochair and APEX, as well as products like OctaFlex and AP Series two-post lifts, Mobi-EVS Series EV battery lifts and Coolee portable air coolers.

During that time, the privately held company expanded its Santa Paula manufacturing and distribution center twice, bringing the facility to more than 400,000 square feet. It also established a new global headquarters in Agoura Hills, Calif., and increased its Alabama operations from a single distribution center in Theodore into a multi-building campus. Earlier this year, BendPak completed Phase 1 of its Donald R. Henthorn Industrial Complex in Mobile County, Ala.

“In today’s marketplace, business moves faster than ever, and BendPak is positioned to outpace it,” said Jeff Kritzer, president and CEO of BendPak. “Our Northeast expansion is just the latest step in our long-term plan to continuously refine our logistics network to optimize delivery times and best serve our customers.”
For more information on BendPak, visit bendpak.com.

Presenting the 2026 Class of BodyShop Business Women in Collision, highlighting an exceptional group of female collision repair professionals who are making meaningful contributions in the industry. This year’s class represents an impressive range of organizations, from collision facilities to manufacturers and suppliers.

The collision repair industry has traditionally been male-dominated, but women are increasingly making their mark across virtually every corner of the business. From repairing vehicles on the shop floor and managing high-performing collision centers to developing business strategies, supporting repairers and building companies of their own, women are helping shape where the industry goes next. Their career paths are as varied as the roles they hold, demonstrating there is no single route to building a successful career in collision repair.

That diversity is evident in the 2026 Class of BodyShop Business Women in Collision. Some of this year’s honorees grew up around body shops or automotive businesses, while others arrived in collision almost by accident after beginning careers in fields such as accounting, healthcare and education. Their accomplishments include competing in SkillsUSA, growing family businesses, developing future industry talent, leading large collision operations, advocating for independent repairers and helping shop owners strengthen or transition their businesses. Despite those different backgrounds, common themes emerge: taking chances, embracing uncomfortable challenges, continually learning, and recognizing the value of strong mentors and relationships.

Perhaps most importantly, these women aren’t simply building impressive careers for themselves. They’re developing employees, mentoring the next generation, strengthening businesses and demonstrating the breadth of opportunities available to women entering the industry today. Their advice to those following them is equally powerful: ask questions, take risks, don’t fear failure and don’t wait until you feel completely ready to step forward.
Stephanie Steelman – Body Technician, DCR Systems

How did your collision career begin? I started learning the basics of collision repair in high school. I was able to compete in the SkillsUSA collision repair competition at the national level and was awarded 4th place. After high school, I had the opportunity to start working as my father’s apprentice.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? Getting my first job at DCR Systems after working for my dad. It felt good, having built the confidence in myself and the skills I had developed to go off on my own. I couldn’t be more proud of what I continue to build for myself with DCR Systems. The team at DCR has mentored me, provided me with many training opportunities and helped me grow in my skills.

What would you tell your younger collision self? It’s okay to fail. Repairing cars isn’t easy, and it takes a lot of trial-and-error to improve yourself. Take the feeling of being stumped and use it as encouragement to network, seek new ideas and try different techniques.
Leila Hobart – Associate Strategy & Portfolio Manager, OEC

How did your collision career begin? Four years ago, I joined OEC’s Repair Technologies team alongside some of the best mentors in the industry. I didn’t come from automotive — my background is in healthcare and education — but the mission hooked me: helping repairers deliver safe, proper repairs that protect vehicle owners.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? There are several that come to mind, including building OEM partnerships and leading WIN’s virtual conference, but the one closest to my heart is building OEC’s repair education program and helping schools put tools and training in the hands of the next generation of talent in our industry.

What would you tell your younger collision self? Take chances! It’s okay to end up somewhere different than your post-college plan. I went from an audiologist, to managing college programs, to shaping strategy in collision. Though I’ve worn different hats, I’ve found a throughline I’m passionate about — working with great people and making a true difference.
April Lausch – Collision Center Manager, Faulkner Collision Center

How did your collision career begin? After college, I began my career with a business background and accepted an office manager position at a collision center. I quickly developed a passion for the industry, learning every aspect of the repair process. That experience inspired me to grow professionally and build a long-term career in collision repair.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? Helping build a strong team and creating opportunities for others to grow. Seeing employees develop their skills, advance their careers and deliver exceptional repairs while providing outstanding customer service has been the most rewarding part of my career.

What would you tell your younger collision self? Believe in yourself, stay curious and never stop learning. Don’t be afraid to ask questions or take on new challenges. Every experience, even the difficult ones, will help you grow into a stronger leader and a better advocate for your team and the collision repair industry.
Wendy Patrick – Vice President of Store Operations, Gerber Collision & Glass

How did your collision career begin? I started in the industry at 17, working in an independent body shop. I never expected it to become my career, but I quickly realized I loved the work, the people and the constant opportunity to learn. That experience sparked a passion that has stayed with me ever since.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? I’m proud of the opportunities I’ve had throughout my career, but what means the most to me is helping others grow. Watching people gain confidence, step into leadership roles and succeed in ways they may not have imagined has been the most rewarding part of my journey.

What would you tell your younger collision self? Be curious, stay open to learning and don’t be afraid to ask questions. Trust that every challenge will teach you something valuable. Build strong relationships, lead with integrity and remember that the way you treat people will define your career more than any title ever will.
Syndey Feehan – General Manager, Fix Auto Maple Grove

How did your collision career begin? I graduated high school in 2020 and was working towards an internship with a State Farm agent. The testing facilities closed due to COVID, and I had to figure out what I wanted to do — wait or figure something else out. My dad offered me a CSR position at one of our shops, and I found my groove. Six years later on the admin side and I love what I do now more than ever!

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? I’m most proud of the family legacy that I get to help carry on. My brothers and I are the third generation, and the family dynamic is really what I believe sets us apart from our competitors. To work alongside my dad, brothers and husband every day is such a gift. To be able to achieve metrics like the no. 1 GEICO ARX store in the country and having all three of our stores scoring a 99-100 RPM score for State Farm is a testament to our dedication to our work and the grit we have in all that we do.

What would you tell your younger collision self? Be confident in your abilities. Learn all that you can. Watch your own bobber. Always ask questions. It’s okay to be uncomfortable — growth can be scary. Have a thankful heart. You don’t have to do this; you get to do this!
Rachel James – Founder, Torque Financial

How did your collision career begin? My path started in automotive and aviation as a technician before I discovered collision repair at a Chevy/Hyundai dealership. It was a fluke thing really, some employees left and there was a gap on the body shop side and the owner asked if I could go over to collision and help. I quickly fell in love with the creativity, problem-solving and craftsmanship behind collision repair — and I’ve been passionate about the industry ever since.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? I’ve been blessed with some great moments, but nothing ever compares to helping blue-collar professionals build stronger businesses, overcome debt or save money for their future.
What would you tell your younger collision self? Don’t underestimate where this industry can take you, ask more questions and save more money!
Nada Jokic – Business Consulting Services Manager, AkzoNobel

How did your collision career begin? I like to say I stumbled into the industry. Shortly after college, I joined DuPont on a one-year project transitioning distributors and body shops from microfiche to PC-based paint formula retrieval. Soon after, when we began building a body shop management system, I parked myself in shops to better understand the business. That’s where I developed a real appreciation for the industry and, especially, the hardworking, down-to-earth people in it.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? Looking back, I can’t point to any one accomplishment. What has given me the most satisfaction is hearing shop owners tell me we’ve helped them grow their businesses. From DuPont’s body shop management software to AkzoNobel’s business consultants today, helping our customers succeed has always been the most rewarding part of my career.

What would you tell your younger collision self? I don’t think I’d change much. If I could tell my younger self one thing, it would be to get involved with WIN sooner. Early in my career, I worked with very few women and didn’t realize how much that would change. Today, there are so many talented women leading and shaping this industry, and I’m grateful to now be part of WIN.
Kena Dacus – Owner, Dacus Auto Body & Collision Repair

How did your collision career begin? My path into collision repair wasn’t exactly traditional. I earned a degree in business administration from Wichita State University and began my career in accounting. In 2015, I joined my husband Chris full-time at Dacus Auto Body, just three months after he had opened. Chris brought the technical expertise, and I brought a love of numbers, business strategy and organization. Over time, I became involved in nearly every aspect of the company. What began as joining our family business grew into a genuine passion for the collision industry, its people and the opportunities we have to make it stronger.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? I’m most proud of what Chris and I have built together. We’ve grown from one collision repair location into two locations and launched Dacus Towing & Recovery, but I’m equally proud of the team and culture we’ve developed along the way. Personally, I’m also proud that my involvement has grown beyond our own businesses. Having served as president of the Kansas Auto Body Association and now on the SCRS board of directors has given me the opportunity to advocate for independent repairers and help strengthen the industry that has given our family so much.

What would you tell your younger collision self? Take more risks. Speak up sooner, trust your instincts and don’t wait until you feel completely ready — because you may never feel completely ready. My greatest growth has come from stepping outside my comfort zone, trying something new and being willing to fail and learn as I went. I would also remind myself that I didn’t need to be an expert before I could contribute something valuable. The industry needs different perspectives, and the skills that make you different may ultimately become some of your greatest strengths.

How did your collision career begin? I grew up in my dad’s motorcycle and used car dealerships. After his bankruptcy, I worked for Mattos, a regional paint jobber in the Washington D.C. area while attending college and became fascinated with body shops. Later, while selling cars, my dealer principal asked where else I’d like to work. I said, “The body shop.” The rest is history.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? Building and selling our process-driven collision centers in 2015 was incredibly rewarding. Then came my 2.0 career—founding Consolidation Coach. What began as a part-time venture has become a leading, woman-owned M&A advisory firm in collision, allowing me to advocate for owners during one of their biggest life decisions.

What would you tell your younger collision self? Staying power is what it takes to be successful. There will be hard times and curves in the road. Success takes vision, strength and positivity, especially when staying the course is difficult. And never let being the only woman in the room make you question whether you belong there.
Shyllo Michaelis – Chief Strategy Officer, Texas Collision Centers

How did your collision career begin? In 2010, I was recruited by Service King Founder Eddie Lennox after having been at Farmers Insurance for 15 years. I was hired to grow the Houston market as a business development manager for Service King.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? By far, my greatest accomplishment is the development of people … and women in particular. Mentoring and then witnessing the growth of fellow teammates and helping them learn their full potential is so satisfying!

What would you tell your younger collision self? I would tell my younger self to be more confident in this male-dominated space. The industry is evolving, and women now have a greater stake in the game. Women I know and love in collision repair are crushing it! I love to see it!
Laura Kottschade – Chief Operating Officer, Jerry’s Abra Auto Body & Glass

How did your collision career begin? I was born and raised in the collision repair industry. From spending afternoons at the shop and taking tow calls while my parents plowed snow, I was always around it. The Monday after college graduation, I officially started in the parts room, learning the business from the ground up.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? It’s hard to choose just one. From navigating production through COVID and unprecedented parts delays to receiving the WIN Cornerstone Award, helping grow the WIN Scholarship Program, becoming COO of our family shop and serving as WIN chair 20 years after my mom, it’s all incredibly humbling.

What would you tell your younger collision self? I’m only 33, so this is something I still remind myself: hold yourself to high standards, but don’t let one mistake define you. Own it, be honest, fix it, learn from it and grow. Mistakes happen; what matters is how you respond, take responsibility and move forward. I’d also tell myself that work-life balance matters. Burnout is real, and climbing out of it can be a long, difficult process. It’s okay to leave something on your desk and finish it tomorrow. Not everything has to be solved today. Taking care of yourself doesn’t mean you’re less dedicated — it allows you to show up better for your team, your customers and yourself.
Natalie Zjac – Vice President of Business Development, Crash Champions

How did your collision career begin? My collision repair career began in 2014 when I met our founder and CEO, Matt Ebert, through a mutual friend. His passion and vision for the business were contagious, and with my background in sales and marketing, we took a chance on each other. That decision changed the course of my career and ultimately my life.

What is the proudest accomplishment of your career? I always try to encourage our teams to pause and celebrate wins because we tend to move quickly from one challenge to the next. Looking back, I’m most proud of being part of the founding team that helped build one of the largest collision repair companies in the country. It’s been an incredible journey and has shaped my growth as an employee, leader and person.

What would you tell your younger collision self? Embrace change and focus on bringing value wherever you can make the biggest impact. Stay curious, keep learning and be open to new opportunities along the way. Some of the most rewarding experiences and greatest growth will come from paths you never expected to take.

Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.

The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.

More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.
Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.
The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.
More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.
The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.

Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.

"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."
Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.
What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.
"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.

Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."
French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?

The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.

"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Sebastian Roche, a researcher at France's National Centre for Scientific Research who specializes in comparing police forces across Europe.
He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.

"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."
Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.
Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.

"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."

According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.
French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.
However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."
The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.
DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.

"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."
Experts are critical of the police's actions.
"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."
Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark

The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.

Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.
"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."

BELLEVUE, Wash., Oct. 15, 2026 — Agile Space Industries, a leading provider of in-space chemical propulsion solutions, has expanded into the Seattle metropolitan area with the opening of a new office in Bellevue, Washington. The expansion builds on Agile’s continued growth, extending its engineering capabilities and strengthening its presence in one of the nation’s most established aerospace and technology markets.

Located at Sunset North in Bellevue, the new 5,470-square-foot office will initially accommodate 7 employees, with the capacity to grow to approximately 30 as Agile expands its regional operations. Agile Chief Technology Officer Jake Mills will be based at the Bellevue office, reinforcing the company’s commitment to establishing a strong engineering and leadership presence in the region.

“Seattle has a remarkable concentration of aerospace talent, innovative companies and organizations advancing the space industry,” said Jake Mills, chief technology officer at Agile Space Industries. “Establishing a presence here allows us to tap into that expertise, strengthen industry relationships and build on the capabilities we’re developing across Agile to support our customers and their missions.”

The Bellevue office will focus on engineering and program management, supporting the development and delivery of advanced propulsion systems for government and commercial space missions. As the team grows, Agile expects to broaden its technical expertise and support an expanding range of propulsion programs.

Beyond its engineering talent, the Seattle region offers an established network of aerospace companies, industry partners and investors. Agile’s presence in this ecosystem creates opportunities to strengthen customer relationships, develop new partnerships and engage with the broader business and investment community as the company pursues its long-term growth objectives.

The expansion also creates opportunities for experienced aerospace professionals looking to work on complex propulsion challenges in a collaborative, hands-on engineering environment. Agile’s teams contribute to programs spanning early development through qualified flight hardware, with the opportunity to help shape technologies supporting the next generation of space missions.

The Bellevue office joins Agile’s headquarters in Durango, Colorado, and operations in Pennsylvania and Oklahoma. Together, these locations support Agile’s growing capabilities in propulsion design, manufacturing and testing, positioning the company to serve an expanding range of commercial and government space customers.

Agile Space Industries develops advanced chemical propulsion solutions that enable spacecraft to move, maneuver, and operate in space. From early concepts to qualified flight hardware, Agile brings together propulsion expertise, additive manufacturing, and in-house testing to rapidly solve complex challenges and accelerate development. Agile partners with leading aerospace companies and the U.S. Government on spacecraft and launch vehicle programs. Learn more at agilespaceindustries.com.

When the European thermal-imagery company constellr began working with Space Inventor on its next generation of satellites, some of the most important details of the spacecraft had yet to be finalized.

The Munich-based firm knew it wanted its HiVE, or High-precision Versatile Ecosphere, constellation to measure temperatures from space with the precision needed for agricultural applications and urban planning. But the requirements for the payload’s size, weight and power were still evolving.

That presented what can be a familiar tradeoff in the small satellite community. Work on satellite buses often begins before every detail of a payload has been finalized. If engineers lock in the spacecraft design too early, the payload may need to conform to the bus. If the payload needs new iterations, the bus may require an extensive – and expensive – redesign.

But Space Inventor, the Danish manufacturer, took a different approach. Instead of demanding the payload fit a standardized satellite bus, it adapted its BIG CAT 600 bus as constellr’s requirements evolved.

“We needed a platform built around the payload, not the other way around,” said Marius Bierdel, constellr’s co-founder and vice president of program management. “Space Inventor’s system-level approach means our thermal sensors perform exactly as designed once they’re in orbit.”

That ability to repeatedly modify the spacecraft is the centerpiece of Space Inventor’s pitch to operators who need to build payload-centric mini-constellations. Unlike megaconstellations numbering in the hundreds or thousands, mini-constellations typically range from a few satellites to a few dozen and can target specific geographies or niche capabilities.

“These are high state-of-the-art payloads that often are still in development when we start building the bus,” said Jan Smolders, the chief commercial officer at Space Inventor. As one batch is being built, he said, Space Inventor is already applying lessons learned to the design of the next.
“The standardization is in the satellite modules, not in the bus,” he added.
Mini-constellations occupy a middle ground in the satellite market.

Their smaller scale offers flexibility. Operators may want to incorporate lessons from the first satellites into later iterations. Or, as technology advances, they may want to upgrade the instruments.
Space Inventor designed its BIG CAT family of services for exactly those moments.

The BIG CAT 100, 300 and 600 platforms are sized for different spacecraft classes, but each is configurable rather than fixed. That means if a mission suddenly needs more power, improved pointing performance or a new communications capability, Space Inventor can often accommodate these changes by swapping out bus modules, rather than redesigning a spacecraft from scratch.

That philosophy of iteration is especially helpful in rapidly changing fields such as thermal imaging, space domain awareness and in-orbit servicing. It also means Space Inventor can avoid locking in a design around requirements developed years before launch.
Space Inventor pairs its modular approach with another strategy: making most of its components itself.

The company manufactures nearly all of its components – with the exception of propulsion – in house at its factory in Aalborg, Denmark, offering more control over its design and less exposure to the volatility of the supply chain.

If a new requirement calls for a modified PCB, Space Inventor can update the design, machine a revised housing, assemble the new component and test the change, all under the same roof. Such a change ordered from an outside supplier might take about six weeks. Space Inventor can make the same change in roughly one week, Smolders said.
“Because we make everything in house, we can easily add new modules to facilitate changing requirements, very fast,” he said.
This gives Space Inventor tighter quality control and reduces exposure to supply chain shortages.

Space Inventor also maintains a stock of its components, allowing it to offer next-day shipping. That reduces the risk that a small component or a supplier delay holds up the production of a spacecraft.
For mini-constellation operators, this model makes it easier to change later satellites based on what they’ve learned from earlier ones.
The same configurable approach that Space Inventor uses for commercial missions also underpins its offerings for the defense community.
Rather than only offering military customers a satellite bus, the company can pair a BIG CAT platform with a mission-specific payload to provide a turnkey system.
Space Inventor’s defense-specific Apex Predator series includes BC Lynx and BC Leopard, two turnkey surveillance solutions built on its BIG CAT platform.

Lynx is designed to detect radio-frequency emissions, geolocate their source and identify activity that may warrant further investigation. Leopard can then be tasked with capturing high-resolution optical or thermal imagery in the same area.
The approach follows a “tip-and-cue” model, with one sensor identifying a potential target and then directing another sensor to collect more detailed information.

The company has also developed a business case for detecting and investigating maritime activity in the heavily trafficked Baltic Sea, bordered by NATO members and Russia. There, Lynx satellites can identify anomalous RF emissions that could reveal dark vessels or help locate sources of GPS spoofing. It can then cue a Leopard satellite to collect additional intelligence.
This space-based approach to surveillance, Smolders argues, offers a cost-effective complement to expensive drones and stealth aircraft that can only monitor a relatively contained area at once.

“For the cost of one or two F-35s, you can actually get the intelligence to tell those planes where to go,” he said. “Affordable, proven ISR capability is ready to deploy in Europe today, with Space Inventor at the forefront of turning that capability into operational missions, but the decision-makers need to know about it.”

In the automotive aftermarket, growth is often associated with adding more: more products, more inventory, more suppliers and more resources. However, adding more doesn’t always lead to growth. In fact, adding more can introduce unnecessary complexity, making growth more difficult. The most successful businesses understand where they create the greatest value and have the discipline to direct resources toward those priorities.

Inventory management is one area where this can be seen. Healthy inventory turns consistently for suppliers and distributors, whereas chronically slow-moving inventory can signal that resources are not creating enough value for customers. Even inventory that isn’t moving still requires dollars to acquire, manage, store and move through the operation, and these costs can add up quickly, especially when the product isn’t generating meaningful sales.

As an important proactive action, suppliers and distributors should consistently review inventory investment and turns to help identify which products are creating value and where resources can be better focused to help drive growth.

The purchase price is easy to measure, and too often, businesses try to sell for the most and buy for the least. But greater value can come from understanding what partners need and where their challenges exist.

For distributors, there’s also value in building deeper relationships with a focused group of suppliers. During periods of supply disruption or elevated demand, manufacturers and other suppliers naturally prioritize their most important customers. These relationships create opportunities to support each other’s businesses better while establishing mutual trust and confidence.

The critical learning from this example is the importance of building relationships that are strategic rather than simply transactional. The most important question is: How can we change the way we do business to benefit both sides beyond the purchase order’s value? When distributors and suppliers understand each other’s businesses well enough to answer this question, the relationship can become stronger and create better economics for both sides.

Simplification also extends to how distributors serve their customers. By providing more flexibility in terms of how customers purchase and receive products, distributors can help customers manage their inventory more efficiently while maximizing their dollars and warehouse space.

That same principle can extend across the broader supplier relationship. When customers can access more of what they need in smaller quantities and combine categories into fewer shipments, they can simplify ordering and receiving, turn inventory faster and manage working capital and space more effectively.

For Highline Warren, we start with a simple question: What do we want to be known for? We want customers to know that they can rely on us to deliver products on time and in full. Consistently delivering on those priorities builds credibility and can make a supplier more integral to the customer’s process, turning focus into a foundation for growth.

Understanding where a business creates value can also help identify its next growth opportunity. For suppliers and distributors, one of the easiest, fastest and most economical ways to grow is to sell existing products to existing customers. The relationship is already established, the supplier understands the customer, and the customer already knows the value the supplier provides. From there, a business should look at the broader market and consider how products or categories it already carries can help address another need.

For example, a retailer may buy several product categories from one supplier while sourcing other products elsewhere, even though the same supplier already carries those products. The overlap creates an opportunity to grow by leveraging existing products and capabilities.

Growth frequently happens in concentric circles: first by strengthening existing relationships, then by expanding into adjacent opportunities that align with proven capabilities. Businesses that consistently deliver value earn the right to broaden those relationships over time.

Growth isn’t always about adding more; often, it comes from getting more from the products, capabilities and relationships a business has already established. Businesses disciplined enough to focus on this approach are better positioned to support customer needs, further strengthen relationships and create opportunities for mutual success.

Oct. 24 (UPI) -- On this date in history:
In 1901, daredevil Annie Edson Taylor became the first person to go over Niagara Falls in a barrel.

In 1929, $5 billion in market values were swept away in the greatest selling wave in the history of the New York Stock Exchange. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 would mark the beginning of a 10-year Depression which would affect the entire Western world.
In 1931, New York City's George Washington Bridge opened to public traffic.
In 1962, the blockade of Cuba was in effect, with a ring of U.S. warships and planes under orders to block by whatever means, further aggressive arm deliveries to Fidel Castro.
In 1992, the Toronto Blue Jays become the first Major League Baseball team based outside the United States to win the World Series.

In 2002, police arrested two suspects in a three-week series of Washington-area sniper attacks that killed 10 people and wounded three others. John Allen Muhammad, 41, and John Lee Malvo, 17, were found sleeping in a car at a rest stop near Frederick, Md. Both were convicted. Muhammad was executed and Malvo sentenced to life in prison.
In 2003, an era in aviation history ended when the supersonic Concorde took off from New York to London on its final flight.

In 2009, U.S. President Barack Obama declared a national emergency related to the outbreak of the H1N1 flu virus, also known as swine flu, to aid local authorities in dealing with the pandemic. Medical officials put the American death toll at 530 with thousands hospitalized.
In 2012, a 41-mile final stretch of Texas Highway 130, a toll road from Mustang Ridge, south of Austin, to Seguin, opened with the highest speed limit in the United States -- 85 mph.

In 2012, Hurricane Sandy made landfall for the first time, in Jamaica, killing two people there. The storm would go on to cause tens of billions of dollars in the northeast United States and kill more than 200 people along its path.

In 2021, Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Tom Brady made his record 600th touchdown pass during a game against the Chicago Bears. During the game, the ball was given to a fan, who returned it to the team in exchange for a replacement game ball and a $1,000 gift certificate to the team store. Experts told UPI the original ball was likely worth $500,000 to $1 million. Brady retired in 2022 with 649 touchdown passes.
In 2022, silent movie actor Anna May Wong became the first Asian American to be featured on U.S. currency as part of the U.S. mint's American Women Quarters Program.

In 2024, Grammy award-winning rapper Lil Durk, recognized as the creative leader of Chicago's "drill" hip-hop scene, was arrested and held without bond in Florida on a charge of murder for hire. He pleaded not guilty to the charge.

Oct. 24 (UPI) -- Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat in the Bavarian Alps was gutted by fire, and one man has been arrested.

The Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest, caught fire Friday night, setting off alarms at 9:25 p.m. local time in nearby Traunstein. Firefighters arrived to find the building engulfed in flames.

Fire trucks had some difficulty getting access to the site "due to the local conditions," authorities said. The building is about 6,000 feet up in the Kehlstein mountain, and visitors had to access it via a long tunnel leading to an elevator that travels up about 40 stories. Only specially designed buses have regular access to the road to the tunnel.
The fire was still burning early Saturday, police said, with about 200 emergency personnel on the scene. No injuries were reported.
Police said Saturday that the building wasn't likely salvageable. They also offered no details about the person arrested, saying the investigation was ongoing.

The building was completed in 1938 and was a guesthouse for Nazi officials and their visitors. Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films showing him as a lover of animals and nature.
It became a tourist attraction in the 1950s, and until Friday offered Alpine views and a restaurant. The Kehlstein mountain is a subpeak of the Hoher Gӧll, which overlooks the town of Berchtesgaten.

Farther down the mountain is the Obersalzburg Documentation Center, which tells the story of the building and Nazi use of the site and offers entrance to some of the mountain tunnels where Nazis hid during the war.
The Kehlsteinhaus and the mountain tunnels and bunkers were graffitied by Allied soldiers who liberated the area.

Iran has increased efforts to target U.S. personnel in the Middle East and other countries, according to a memo sent by the Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
The memo warned that “the lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages.”
A U.S. official confirmed the authenticity of the memo first reported by Axios.

The intelligence comes days after sources told NBC News the U.S. military has been quietly scaling back its troop presence at bases across the Middle East. The State Department ordered a further reduction in staff at multiple diplomatic posts in the region, including in Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Jordan, according to a State Department official.
Those posts have already been placed on a “restricted operations” status and have been functioning with limited staffing since the start of the war.

Clayton told Rubio in the memo that the risk is “relevant to more individuals than are currently cleared to receive this information,” adding: “We will make every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so you can share it with State Department personnel at your discretion.”

The reduction of American forces and diplomatic personnel is similar to drawdowns at bases and embassies that the Defense Department and the State Department initiated around the start of the war with Iran in February.

“When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment,” a U.S. official said. “The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on Restricted Status in the region.”

President Donald Trump said this week that he was considering another operation against Iran, after months of strikes on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and limited progress toward a long-term ceasefire.

“We may do another little Epic Fury,” he told a rally in Florida on Friday, referring to the U.S. name for the initial wave of strikes. “If they’re smart, they’ll just say, let’s get down to business,” he added.
His comment came after senior U.S. military officials presented Trump with options for new strikes in Iran.

Among the military options presented to Trump in recent weeks are major strikes against the tunnels or entrances of Iran’s nuclear facilities, such as at Pickaxe Mountain, or against its strategic islands, according to one of the U.S. officials and a former U.S. official with knowledge of the options.

They said some of the options include targeting Kharg Island — which is home to the vast majority of Iran’s oil production, making it an economic lifeline for the country — and Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran had proposed a fresh deal last month to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days. Trump publicly rejected that proposal without giving a specific reason, saying Iran wanted a deal “because they’re losing so badly.” He also accused Iran of seeking to drive up oil prices ahead of the midterm elections.
“We don’t care about U.S. midterm elections,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said. “We care about our national interests.”

On Wednesday, the chiefs of mission at multiple U.S. diplomatic posts in the Middle East were notified that their posts would begin operating with reduced staff, the two U.S. officials said. The State Department also announced Wednesday that the U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia is under “ordered departure,” meaning it will operate only with emergency staff.

“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote on X.

LONDON — Police in the British capital said Saturday that they received a letter containing allegations about the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019, but did not tell other law enforcement agencies.
Authorities in the Philippines confirmed this week that they are investigating Thomas Markle over claims that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home. He has denied the allegations.
Meghan said in a statement Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations and that she was previously informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018.

A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan Police said a review of records confirmed that the force received a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”

“It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex,” the statement added. “The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”
The statement did not say whether any investigation took place or if any further action was taken.
The force said it was reviewing the incident and considering whether to refer itself to the United Kingdom’s Independent Office for Police Conduct.
Asked about the discrepancy between the two statements on the date of the letter, a spokesperson for Meghan told NBC News she “may have been mistaken by a few months.”

The allegations against Thomas Markle were first reported Thursday by The Sun, a British tabloid, which reported that his son had informed police after he said he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home.

The Sun published a photo it said showed the son, Thomas Markle Jr., signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
In a statement Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated.

“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, whose relationship with her father has been limited and fraught in recent years. He did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018, drawing widespread media scrutiny.

She said the letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018 “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”
Meghan added that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
The elder Markle, 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

His daughter Samantha Markle also dismissed her brother’s allegations, telling the Daily Mail that “there is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever. ... He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
NBC News did not immediately receive responses to requests for comment from Markle Jr. or Samantha Markle — Meghan’s half-siblings.
NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for Markle Sr., who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery.

In a statement, the FBI said it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”
The Philippines’ justice department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to “provide further details at this time.”
Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States.

The couple last week made their first joint public appearance since returning to the U.K., visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Harry, however, has said recently that he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”

PARIS — More than 100,000 people marched in Paris on Saturday over school funding and soaring living costs, challenging President Emmanuel Macron’s government as police fired tear gas and water cannons near the end of the protest.
Paris police estimated turnout at 110,000, with demonstrators mobilizing despite restrictions that confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center.

Police used tear gas in several cities, including Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, and Strasbourg, and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Marseille, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march’s endpoint.

The Paris prosecutor’s office said 64 people had been arrested in connection with Saturday’s demonstration and 40 placed in police custody. Those arrested included six minors. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said.

The unrest is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: the far-right National Rally has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for them.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had announced a nationwide deployment of up to 70,000 officers, backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.

Authorities had confined the Paris march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center. An Associated Press journalist saw tens of thousands of people marching from Porte d’Italie early in the afternoon. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters in raincoats carrying flags and handmade placards.
After reaching the authorized endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some demonstrators tried to continue toward Place de la Nation, but police blocked their path, French media reported.
Camille Chesnier, 27, said she had been unable to find work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.
“There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it’s very tough,” she said.
A small protest became a national movement

What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris has grown into a national movement. Students demanding better schools and workers seeking higher wages and pensions have brought anger over living standards into the final months of President Emmanuel Macron’s presidency.
Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.
Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.
Police changed the Paris route Friday. At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a 135-euro ($150) fine.
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, said she had been joining protests for more than 30 years but had never seen a march start at Porte d’Italie.
“They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters,” she said. “But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools.”

In Marseille, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities. Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier.
Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Thousands also marched Saturday in Orléans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Marine Le Pen’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.

Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
Nuñez acknowledged Monday that police had lost control in some cities during last weekend’s unrest. He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.
More than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday. Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over the weekend.

Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician’s shop.
“I got the call last night,” he said. “The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life.”
Major museums, including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — were shuttered Saturday.
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system.
Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.

Public middle and high schools lost 15.4 million teaching hours in the 2024-25 school year because absent teachers were not replaced, according to Education Ministry figures. That amounted to 7.5% of scheduled teaching time.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.
“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people,” said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University.
Premier Roger Cook has visited South Hedland for the first time since an inquest into the deaths of three local children was announced.
He was met by residents angered by reports of child protection failings.
The state government says there has been progress, while community elders urge more collaboration.

South Hedland residents have confronted the West Australian Premier during a five-hour visit to the northern town — his first since the state government announced a coronial inquest into the deaths of three local children.

The renewed investigation into Margaret Hawke's 2022 killing of her 10-year-old daughter, seven-year-old son and four-month-old baby came after sustained political and media pressure over failures by WA's Department of Child Protection.

Recent weeks have seen a steady stream of political drop-ins to South Hedland, more than 1,600 kilometres north of Perth, with the premier arriving on Saturday to declare a contractor had been selected to construct a long-promised $22 million MRI facility.
However, the spotlight remained on reports first appearing in The Australian newspaper that up to 15 children had been living unsupervised in a state-owned home until September.

The Premier was accompanied by Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski — her fourth trip to South Hedland in nine weeks — for an agenda dominated by closed-door discussions with government agencies and their partners.

"You've gotta come back sit with us here, camp with us and roam the streets with us, so they can see for themselves what's actually happening," said Nyamal-Pitjikarli elder Doris Eaton, who spoke with the pair at a snap meeting during their visit.
"You can't see it from Perth, you can't do fly in and fly out."
Departing talks with community organisation Hedland Aboriginal Strong Leaders, Mr Cook and Ms Stojkovski came under fire from a community member who identified herself as a former foster carer.
"When is the department going to be accountable and when are you going to speak to the community?" she said.
The ABC spoke with multiple other residents who expressed their frustration with the government response.
"I get confronted by people all the time. That's part of the job," Mr Cook said.
"But I fully appreciate that everyone wants to see things improve."
There were no policy announcements about child protection during the premier's visit, nor did he meet with families impacted by the crisis.
Mr Cook said the emphasis was on consulting with the people "who are delivering the services in the community".
The ABC understands Dorothy Papertalk, mother of Margaret Hawke and the children's grandmother, declined an invitation to meet with the premier.
Ms Papertalk led the campaign for an inquest, which was denied by the coroner in 2025. Ms Papertalk has requested privacy at this time.
"There are a range of families that are receiving good services, there's others that we can improve," Mr Cook said.
"The department's in a process of continuous improvement all the time."

When questioned, Ms Stojkovski could not point to how many full-time equivalent staff positions had been filled since it was revealed in WA Parliament the Pilbara region had 11 child protection caseworker vacancies.
A relief team has been sent to South Hedland in response.
"Having those senior staff from the group, the relieving team, is really important and it's been very helpful for our staff here on the ground," Ms Stojkovski said.
The minister expects to be handed an assurance review of recommendations made in the wake of the Hawke murders by the end of the month.
On Thursday, WA Commissioner for Children and Young People Jacqueline McGowan-Jones tabled a scathing assessment of the state's child protection system in parliament.
The report considered the experiences of 19 children who were placed into a secure care centre multiple times and made 56 recommendations.
"If children are brought into out-of-home care, it is because they are apparently at risk at home," Ms McGowan-Jones told the ABC.
"They were equally, if not more so, at risk, being brought into the state system."
WA opposition leader Basil Zempilas said it was "insulting" that the premier was not visiting affected families.
"I am absolutely astounded after nine weeks of this being in the national spotlight, the premier has finally gone up — finally — but is not meeting with any families," he said.
"This is a shocking and ignorant lack of leadership."

Problems with the Elon Musk-owned Starlink and Starshield came after Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.

Met Police says it received letter about Meghan Markle's father in 2019 but didn't share with other agencies
London's Metropolitan Police has confirmed it received a letter with "a number of claims" against Meghan Markle's father in January 2019.
A spokesperson said the Met Police did not share the letter with other agencies.
It comes amid allegations that child sexual abuse material was found at Thomas Markle's former home in the Philippines.
Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet
Domestic politics appear poised to trigger a new phase of war with Iran
The warning signs are flashing red with indications that once the ballots are counted in the U.S. midterm elections, the United States and Israel will relaunch their war with Iran.
The next round of attacks could be more devastating than the first, warn analysts.

"A renewed war seems almost inevitable," said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Middle East and Iran analyst whose earlier warnings and cautions about the risks of a direct conflict with Iran were largely borne out by events.

Citrinowicz, who worked for Israel's military as an intelligence official for more than two decades, had initially warned that any U.S. and Israeli attack on the Islamic regime would not likely lead to regime change but would instead end up engulfing the entire region in a wider conflict — an assessment that proved true.
In an interview with CBC News, he said that assessment still holds.
"The problem is there is no silver bullet solution to the impasse we are now at in the Persian Gulf and in front of Trump he has only bad and worse options."

Under U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their countries broke with decades of restraint and shadow warfare and launched two distinct wars with Iran over the past 18 months.
Iranian women look at a building, which was damaged in a U.S. and Israeli strike in March, in Tehran on Aug. 22. (Reuters)
The first in June 2025 began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, lasted 12 days and ended with a fragile ceasefire.

The conflict roared back to life in February of this year following a massive U.S. military buildup in the region. It began with Israel's strikes against Iran's senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Citrinowicz, who's with Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said a third round of war could be the worst yet, based on what Iranian officials are telegraphing.

"They will attack the energy facilities in the Gulf. But more than that, they will cause significant damage to civilian infrastructure, communications, as well as cutting off the internet lines going under [the] Hormuz Strait," he said.
He said there is even a possibility that Iran could push some of its massive land army into the fight with limited assaults against Gulf countries that house U.S. bases, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.
"We'll see a regional war with Iran investing a lot in attacking the U.S. presence in the region to cause maximum economical damage to the U.S. international economy."

Smoke rises from a burning vessel, following what the U.S. Central Command said was a strike on an Iranian-affiliated dhow, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, in this still image taken from a video released on Oct. 14. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters)

While both sides have largely avoided fresh strikes against each other's bases or territory since the summer truce collapsed, the conflict remains active. The U.S. imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran has continued to target commercial shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy costs.

Posting on Truth Social Thursday, Trump blamed Iran for trying to artificially drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, elections that many pollsters believe will see Trump's Republicans lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.
"They are even making up fake hits, mines and everything else," said Trump, implying that Iran is exaggerating the extent of the damage it's causing.

A report published this week by the Washington, D.C.,-based Critical Threats Project alongside the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also suggested Iran is trying to use strikes on shipping to weaken Trump's position heading into the elections.

"The increase in Iranian attacks on vessels is part of the ongoing Iranian campaign to pressure the United States to meet Iranian demands, including control over the Strait, by driving up global prices," the report said.
People walk on the beach, with vessels in the Strait of Hormuz visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Oct. 13. (Razieh Poudat West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

Iran's government wants relief from punishing sanctions, reparations for the damage caused by earlier U.S.-Israel strikes, the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and the right to keep its supplies of enriched uranium.
Mediators with Pakistan and Qatar have spent weeks trying to push diplomatic solutions to get the two sides talking again, but to no avail.
For both Netanyahu and Trump, the war with Iran remains unfinished business.

The Islamic regime not only remains in power, but its leadership has also proven remarkably adept at adapting to both the military strikes and the economic blockade imposed by the West.

"The war in some respects has probably persuaded Iran's leadership to double down on their commitment to the revolutionary ideology that has really forged this regime," said Suzanne Maloney, a vice-president and director of the foreign policy program at the Washington, D.C.,-based Brookings Institution.
Like Citroniwicz, she said if war resumes, Trump won't be able to easily contain it.
"The retaliation as we've seen will come not just from Iran, but from its proxies and partners in the region," she said, referring to the Houthi militias in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Iran's goal won't just be to hit back at U.S. military targets but also soft economic targets, such as airports, that could undermine Gulf countries for years to come, she said.
Maloney and Karim Sadjadpour, a prominent Iran expert with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, were speaking on an online Carnegie panel about the future of the war in Iran.
"I genuinely don't think that President Trump has a clear idea in his head what he's trying to achieve," said Sadjadpour.
"I don't see any possibility of what Trump is looking for — which is like a knockout punch, a military strike — which will essentially force the Iranians into a compromise or capitulation."
Trump claimed his justification for the initial attacks on Iran was to ensure the country doesn't get a nuclear weapon.

At the time, while Iran possessed enough enriched uranium to theoretically pursue a weapon, many independent experts and U.S. intelligence sources believed it was still likely months away from doing so — and perhaps more importantly, that the regime's supreme leader had not yet made the definitive political decision to cross the nuclear threshold.
Since those initial June 2025 strikes, the human cost of the war has been severe.
Western NGOs claim the death toll in Iran is well over 7,000, including civilians and government figures who have been killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.
Lebanon has also suffered an especially heavy toll, with local media reporting more than 4,000 fatalities.
Twenty-one U.S. service members were killed, mostly by Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf, while more than 70 Israelis have died.
People drive near a billboard depicting U.S. President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran on Sept. 16. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)
There have also been deaths throughout the Gulf countries, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Iraq and Yemen.
The New York Times and other U.S. media are reporting the Pentagon is working on a new battle plan for the possible next round of attacks — but whether Trump will ultimately authorize it is unknown.
Israel's leadership, on the other hand, has made no secret of its push to restart the conflict, with Netanyahu explicitly stating his desire to bring down the Iran regime by "finishing the job."
Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in the coming days, and whether he hangs onto his job could end up in a photo finish.

Relaunching the war with Iran could offer him a tactical way to stay in power; even if his party loses seats, a widening security crisis could lead to the creation of an emergency unity government with members of the opposition, said Citrinowicz.

"The real risk is that Netanyahu will involve his political considerations together with some other operational development in Iran that he is going to not necessarily invent, but probably [inflate]," he said.
A shopkeeper works at his shop in a local market in Tehran on Sept. 26. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
"And this combination will lead to an unnecessary attack against Iran."
Sadjadpour from the Carnegie panel said there is no obvious military way out of the impasse and says Trump's maximalist goals have closed down diplomatic options as well.

"I believe there's a pretty clear formula under which it [Iran's government] compromises," said Sadjadpour. "It's when it faces what I would describe as existential economic pressure, coupled with a clear, limited diplomatic exit.
"If you're asking them to change their identity, that's not going to succeed."
Israelis are leaving the country in record numbers. Could a looming election accelerate the trend?
A February study found 99,000 Israelis left the country in 2023 and 2024
Sitting at his desk in a sun-filled apartment in Tel Aviv, economist Itai Ater pored over data that shows more Israelis have left the country over the past three years than ever before.

Those have been tumultuous years for the country of around 10 million people, with war, economic uncertainty and a prime minister plagued by corruption charges whose trial started in 2020 and still hasn't reached a verdict.

Ater, a professor at the Coller School of Management at Tel Aviv University, says these departures could accelerate depending on the outcome of next week's legislative elections, destabilizing the country's economy and causing ripple effects throughout the region.

"Israelis are thinking, 'do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?'" Ater said. "Unfortunately, and I understand, I sympathize with their answers, many of them realize that the answer is no. And that's why they're leaving."

In February, Ater and his colleagues published a study using data collected from the Central Bureau of Statistics that found 99,000 Israelis left the country between January 2023 and December 2024. The study looked at Israelis who left for at least three consecutive months and stayed out of the country for more than 270 days during the first year of their departure.
Ater says he understands why people might want to leave: 'Israelis are thinking, "do I want to raise my kids in a country like this?"' (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

According to the data, 50,000 left in 2023, a year that saw Hamas militants storm southern Israel, killing roughly 1,200 people and kidnapping another 250. Israel responded by embarking on a devastating military campaign in the Gaza Strip that continued until a fragile ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, though Israel still controls roughly 60 per cent of the enclave and engages in regular military activity there.
In 2024, 49,000 left. Ater says preliminary data shows the trend continued in 2025, and he believes the looming election could push those numbers even higher in 2026.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been a defining figure in Israeli politics for the past three decades and is by far the country's longest serving leader, is once again vying for power.

Polls suggest his far-right bloc will fall short of the requisite 61 seats in the Knesset to form a government and that a rival bloc headed by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, is currently in position to secure the most seats. As of now, Eisenkot's coalition is expected to be short of a majority.
